會試錄序

嘉靖二十有六載，是爲丁未。天子朝羣后于萬邦，萬邦之士與計偕者四千三百人有奇，景附闕下，願爲帝臣，求試于有司。春二月，禮部尚書臣費寀、侍郎臣許成名、臣崔桐以聞。上命學士臣承恩、臣治往主試事。同考則侍讀臣朴，編修臣璣、臣貞吉、臣晟、臣訥、臣儀、臣景淳、臣樹聲，檢討臣材、臣以勤、臣穼，都給事中臣大同、臣綸、
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

The twenty-sixth year of Jiajing was the dingwei year [1547]. The Son of Heaven received in audience the lords of the myriad regions. More than 4,300 scholars from those regions, traveling with the delegations bearing accounts to the capital, gathered like shadows beneath the palace gates. Wishing to become servants of the Emperor, they sought examination by the responsible authorities. In the second month of spring, the Minister of Rites, your servant Fei Cai, and the Vice Ministers, your servants Xu Chengming and Cui Tong, reported this to the throne. His Majesty ordered the Hanlin Academicians, your servants Cheng’en and Zhi, to preside over the examination. The Associate Examiners were the Hanlin Expositor-in-Waiting, your servant Pu; the Hanlin Compilers, your servants Ji, Zhenji, Sheng, Ne, Yi, Jingchun, and Shusheng; the Hanlin Examining Editors, your servants Cai, Yiqin, and Sen; and the Chief Supervising Secretaries, your servants Datong and Lun …

事咸慎簡以充臣等肅將

右給事中臣雲鴈、署郎中臣鳳、主事臣時春、臣維嶽。監試則御史臣綬、臣儲秀，暨諸執事，咸慎簡以充。臣等肅將明命，矢心勤事，三試之，仰遵宸斷，取中式者三百人。故事有錄，錄其氏名及其文之可傳者以獻。臣承恩謹序其端。
臣海隅側陋，遭逢聖明，備位宮長，不能竭忠殫力，報塞萬分之一。夙夜兢惕，私心惓惓，圖惟薦賢舉能，倣古上臣事君以人之義。廼今躬親
translation_en:
…Right Supervising Secretary, your servant Yunyan; Acting Bureau Director, your servant Feng; and Bureau Secretaries, your servants Shichun and Weiyue. The examination was overseen by Investigating Censors, your servants Shou and Chuxiu. These men, together with all the other functionaries, were carefully selected to fill their posts. We respectfully carried out the illustrious command, pledging ourselves to diligent service. We examined the candidates in three sessions and, reverently following the imperial decision, selected three hundred successful candidates. Established practice calls for a record, preserving their names and those of their writings worthy of transmission, to be presented to the throne. Your servant Cheng’en respectfully supplies this prefatory account.
Your servant, an obscure man from a remote coastal region, has had the good fortune to live under a sagely and enlightened ruler and to occupy the position of head of the palace establishment [?]. Yet I have been unable to devote such loyalty and effort as would repay even one ten-thousandth of the favor received. Anxious and vigilant morning and night, I earnestly ponder how to recommend the worthy and advance the capable, emulating the principle by which the great ministers of antiquity served their sovereign through the men they brought into his service. Now, personally undertaking…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
其任臣幸甚幸甚先是嘉靖
辛卯臣嘗典試南畿後六年
典試
京畿獲觀文於兩都人士及茲
夫合天下士試之獲盡觀四
方之文殊狀異態隋珠和璧
競爽並耀讜論嘉猷層見疊
===
出究天人之原恢皇王之緒
明道德之歸探性情之秘文
有經緯之方武有戡定之畧
錯綜六藝揮霍百家若覽職
貢方物畢陳筐篚稠疊玉帛
紛錯若閱輿圖都邑具列名
山大川棊布星羅昭然指掌

典試

===
出究天人之原恢皇王之緒
明道德之歸探性情之秘文
有經緯之方武有戡定之畧
錯綜六藝揮霍百家若覽職
貢方物畢陳筐篚稠疊玉帛
紛錯若閱輿圖都邑具列名
山大川棊布星羅昭然指掌
punctuated: 其任，臣幸甚幸甚！先是，嘉靖辛卯，臣嘗典試南畿，後六年，典試京畿，獲觀文於兩都人士。及茲，夫合天下士試之，獲盡觀四方之文。殊狀異態，隋珠和璧，競爽並耀；讜論嘉猷，層見疊出。究天人之原，恢皇王之緒，明道德之歸，探性情之秘。文有經緯之方，武有戡定之畧，錯綜六藝，揮霍百家。若覽職貢，方物畢陳，筐篚稠疊，玉帛紛錯；若閱輿圖，都邑具列，名山大川，棊布星羅，昭然指掌。
translation_en: …this responsibility: your servant is most fortunate, most fortunate! Previously, in the xinmao year of Jiajing [1531], your servant presided over the examination in the Southern Metropolitan Region; six years later, I presided over the examination in the Northern Metropolitan Region. Thus I was able to read the writings of scholars from the two capitals. Now, with scholars from throughout the realm assembled for examination, I have been able to survey fully the writings of all four quarters. In their varied forms and distinctive styles, they are like the pearl of Sui and the jade of He, vying in brilliance and shining together. Forthright arguments and excellent counsels appear in succession. They investigate the origins of Heaven and humankind, extend the legacy of emperors and kings, clarify the ultimate purport of the Way and virtue, and explore the mysteries of human nature and feelings. In civil affairs, they offer methods for ordering the realm; in military affairs, strategies for pacification. They weave together the Six Arts and range freely through the Hundred Schools. It is like viewing the prescribed tribute: local products are all displayed, baskets are piled high, and jade and silk mingle in profusion. It is like examining a map: capitals and cities are all set out, famous mountains and great rivers arrayed like pieces on a chessboard and stars in the sky, as clearly discernible as the palm of one’s hand…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
也天下之大觀備矣臣觀萬
國之會朝也分封而别壤殊
途而異轍及其戾止不敢後
先者大一統也羣士之敷言
也人殊其才性異其尚及其
合并莫敢異致者會
皇極也同文同軌之治猗歟盛哉
===
臣惟天下之生久矣宇宙貞
元之會唐虞三代以来僅僅
可數也是故至治之世不可
屢值
明聖之主能幾遇哉我
太祖高皇帝應
天受命驅逐胡虜而有天下正乾

===
臣惟天下之生久矣宇宙貞
元之會唐虞三代以来僅僅
可數也是故至治之世不可
屢值
明聖之主能幾遇哉我
太祖高皇帝應
天受命驅逐胡虜而有天下正乾
punctuated:
也。天下之大觀備矣。臣觀萬國之會朝也，分封而别壤，殊途而異轍；及其戾止，不敢後先者，大一統也。羣士之敷言也，人殊其才，性異其尚；及其合并，莫敢異致者，會皇極也。同文同軌之治，猗歟盛哉！

臣惟天下之生久矣。宇宙貞元之會，唐虞三代以来，僅僅可數也。是故至治之世，不可屢值；明聖之主，能幾遇哉！我太祖高皇帝應天受命，驅逐胡虜而有天下，正乾
translation_en:
…Thus the grand spectacle of all under Heaven is fully displayed. Your servant observes that when the myriad states assemble at court, they come from separately enfeoffed territories, following different routes and tracks. Yet upon their arrival, none dares fall behind or move ahead of the prescribed order: this is reverence for the great unity. When the assembled scholars set forth their views, each differs in talent, and their dispositions differ in what they esteem. Yet when their views are brought together, none dares pursue a divergent aim: they converge upon the august standard. A realm governed with a common script and uniform carriage tracks—ah, how flourishing!

Your servant reflects that life under Heaven has endured for a long time. Yet since the ages of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties, the moments when the cosmos passes from completion to renewal can scarcely number more than a few. Thus an age of consummate governance is not often encountered; how many times can one meet an enlightened and sagely ruler? Our Emperor Taizu Gao received the Mandate in accordance with Heaven, expelled the northern barbarians, and took possession of all under Heaven, setting right Heaven…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
坤之大統昭日月之重明豐
功偉烈超出千古
聖子
神孫繩繩繼繼百八十年于茲矣
我
皇上
天縱
===
聖神誕膺
寶曆深仁厚澤丕冒遐邇際天
所覆極地所載莫不顒顒然
向風承德一統之治
皇極之行愈隆愈盛固其所哉然
則士生
今日豈非千載而一時也夫太

坤之大統，昭日月之重明，豐功偉烈，超出千古。聖子神孫，繩繩繼繼，百八十年于茲矣。
我皇上，天縱聖神，誕膺寶曆，深仁厚澤，丕冒遐邇。際天所覆，極地所載，莫不顒顒然向風承德。一統之治，皇極之行，愈隆愈盛，固其所哉！然則士生今日，豈非千載而一時也？夫太
translation_en:
…the great succession of Heaven and Earth, illuminating the renewed radiance of sun and moon. His magnificent achievements and mighty deeds surpassed those of all preceding ages. His sage sons and divine descendants have continued the succession without interruption, for one hundred and eighty years down to the present.
Our Emperor, endowed by Heaven with sagely and divine qualities, has gloriously received the imperial mandate. His profound benevolence and abundant blessings amply encompass both far and near. Throughout all that Heaven covers and Earth supports, none fail to turn reverently toward his influence and receive his virtue. The government of a unified realm and the implementation of the sovereign’s supreme standard grow ever more exalted and flourishing—as indeed they should! Thus, for scholars born in this age, is this not an opportunity that comes but once in a thousand years? Now, the great…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
平之業以人而致亦以人而
守
國家求賢是急登進諸士將何
爲也臣用敢告曰
祖宗豐芑作養之仁
皇上禮樂陶鎔之化諸士漸被乆
矣兹當脫迹巖穴感奮風雲
===
致身之始其將何居夫士莫
先尚志而審所効法臣聞虞
有九官周有十人皆聖賢之
選也諸士能紹其芳躅矣乎
諸士實生虞周之時非是則
何式主司非是亦莫敢以告
先資自獻諸士則既已自許

punctuated: 平之業，以人而致，亦以人而守。國家求賢是急，登進諸士，將何爲也？臣用敢告曰：「祖宗豐芑作養之仁，皇上禮樂陶鎔之化，諸士漸被乆矣。兹當脫迹巖穴，感奮風雲，致身之始，其將何居？夫士莫先尚志，而審所効法。臣聞虞有九官，周有十人，皆聖賢之選也。諸士能紹其芳躅矣乎？諸士實生虞、周之時，非是則何式？主司非是亦莫敢以告。先資自獻，諸士則既已自許
translation_en: …The enterprise of great peace is achieved through worthy men and likewise preserved through them. The state makes seeking worthy men its urgent concern; to what purpose does it advance you gentlemen? Your servant therefore ventures to address you thus: “You gentlemen have long received the ancestral emperors’ benevolent nurture—like the cultivation of luxuriant millet—and Your Majesty’s transforming influence through rites and music. Now, as you emerge from secluded caves and cliffs, stirred to action by this auspicious conjunction of wind and cloud, and begin to devote yourselves to service, what position will you take? For a scholar, nothing comes before elevating his aspirations and carefully considering whom to emulate. Your servant has heard that under Shun of Yu there were nine officials, and under the Zhou ten men, all chosen from among sages and worthies. Can you gentlemen follow in their illustrious footsteps? You indeed live in an age like that of Yu and Zhou: whom else, then, should you take as models? Nor would those presiding over the examination venture to commend any other models to you. In coming forward to offer yourselves on the strength of your prior qualifications [?], you gentlemen have already pledged yourselves…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
矣許而弗克終主司者之所
懼也諸士念哉爲人臣而享
有禄位邦家之基生民之命
社稷之寄諸士與有闘矣無負爾
所學無忝爾所舉無棄爾今
日之言慎乃恒德敬爾官守
陳力宣猷以弼
至治衍
宗社億萬年無疆之休主司有厚
望焉諸士尚其懋哉臣不佞
頃奉
明詔仰見
皇上慎重賢科務期得人至意惕
然恐不勝任諸士式克念爾
alt_text:

社稷之寄諸士與有關矣無負爾
所學無忝爾所舉無棄爾今
日之言愼乃恒德敬爾官守
陳力宣猷以稱
===
至治衍
宗社億萬年無疆之休主司有厚
望焉諸士尚其懋哉臣不佞
頃奉
明詔仰見
皇上愼重賢科務期得人至意惕
然恐不勝任諸士式克念爾
punctuated:
矣。許而弗克終，主司者之所懼也。諸士念哉！爲人臣而享有禄位，邦家之基、生民之命、社稷之寄，諸士與有闘矣。無負爾所學，無忝爾所舉，無棄爾今日之言。慎乃恒德，敬爾官守，陳力宣猷，以弼至治，衍宗社億萬年無疆之休。主司有厚望焉，諸士尚其懋哉！
臣不佞，頃奉明詔，仰見皇上慎重賢科、務期得人至意，惕然恐不勝任。諸士式克念爾
translation_en:
… Yet to pledge yourselves and fail to carry through is what we who preside over the examination fear. Consider this, gentlemen! As servants of the ruler enjoying official stipends and rank, you share responsibility [?] for the foundations of the state, the lives of the people, and the charge of the altars of soil and grain. Do not betray your learning, disgrace your selection, or abandon the words you have spoken today. Carefully maintain your constant virtue and attend reverently to your official duties. Exert your strength and give effect to sound plans, thereby assisting consummate government and extending the boundless blessings of the ancestral temples and the altars of state for countless millions of years. We who preside over the examination have great hopes for you. Gentlemen, strive earnestly!
Your untalented servant recently received the illustrious edict and perceived with reverence Your Majesty’s profound concern for the examination that selects worthy men, and your earnest determination that it should secure men fit for service. In trepidation, I feared that I could not discharge this responsibility. If you gentlemen can duly bear in mind your …

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
主司告誡則臣等奉
法承
令之責庶幾少逭矣乎
掌詹事府事資治尹正議大
夫吏部左侍郎兼翰林院學
士孫承恩謹序

主司告誡則〔臣〕等奉
法承
令之責庶幾少逭矣乎
掌詹事府事資治尹正議大
夫吏部左侍郎兼翰林院學
士孫〔承恩〕謹序
punctuated:
主司告誡，則臣等奉法承令之責，庶幾少逭矣乎？

掌詹事府事、資治尹、正議大夫、吏部左侍郎兼翰林院學士孫承恩謹序。
translation_en:
…the admonitions of your examiners, then might we, your servants, perhaps escape some measure of blame in discharging our responsibility to uphold the law and carry out your commands?

Preface respectfully composed by Sun Cheng’en, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Administrator for Assisting Government, Grand Master for Proper Counsel, Left Vice Minister of Personnel, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.

text:
嘉靖二十六年會試
知貢舉官
資政大夫太子少保禮部尚書兼翰林院學士費寀〔子和江西鉛山縣人辛未進士〕

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Twenty-sixth Year of Jiajing (1547)

Officials in Charge of the Examination

Fei Cai, Grand Master for Aid in Governance, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Rites, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zihe; he was from Yanshan County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year (1511).

Xu Chengming, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites. His courtesy name was Siren; he was from Liaocheng County, Shandong, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year (1511).

Examiners

Sun Cheng'en, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Administrator for Aid in Governance (zizhi yin), Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, and Left Vice Minister of Personnel, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhenfu; he was from Huating County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year (1511).

Zhang Zhi, in charge of the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, and Left Vice Minister of Personnel, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Wenbang; he was from Chaling Subprefecture, Huguang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinsi year (1521).

Associate Examiners

Guo Pu, Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhifu; he was from Anyang County, Henan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year (1535).

Li Ji, Hanlin Academy Compiler, with the rank of Gentleman for Serving in Literature. His courtesy name was Bangzai; he was from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year (1535).

Zhao Zhenji, Hanlin Academy Compiler, with the rank of Gentleman for Serving in Literature. His courtesy name was Mengjing; he was from Neijiang County, Sichuan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year (1535).

Pan Sheng, Hanlin Academy Compiler, with the rank of Gentleman for Serving in Literature. His courtesy name was Siming; he was from Xinchang County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Yan Ne, Hanlin Academy Compiler, with the rank of Gentleman for Serving in Literature. His courtesy name was Minqing; he was registered in Wu County, Zhili, was a native of Changshu County, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Gao Yi, Hanlin Academy Compiler, with the rank of Gentleman for Serving in Literature. His courtesy name was Zixiang; he was from Qiantang County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Qu Jingchun, Hanlin Academy Compiler, with the rank of Gentleman for Serving in Literature. His courtesy name was Shidao; he was from Changshu County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year (1544).

Lin Shusheng, Hanlin Academy Compiler, with the rank of Gentleman for Serving in Literature. His courtesy name was Yuji; he was from Huating County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Wang Cai, Hanlin Academy Examining Editor, with the rank of Gentleman for Summoned Service (zhengshi lang). His courtesy name was Zinan; he was from Xincheng County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Chen Yiqin, Hanlin Academy Examining Editor, with the rank of Gentleman for Summoned Service (zhengshi lang). His courtesy name was Yifu; he was from Nanchong County, Sichuan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

translation_en:
Chao Li, courtesy name Junshi, was an Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service. He was from Kaizhou, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in 1541.

Zheng Datong, courtesy name Jiewu, was Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel. He was from Putian County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1529.

Li Lun, courtesy name Deyan, held the rank of Gentleman for Fulfilling Service and was Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Rites. His registered domicile was Huai’an Guard under the Wanquan Regional Military Commission; he was a native of Yingshang County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

He Yunyan, courtesy name Shibin, held the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service and was Right Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Works. He was from Fenshui County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.

Chen Feng, courtesy name Yubo, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and was a Secretary acting as Director of the Guangxi Bureau in the Ministry of Justice. His registered domicile was the Nanjing Rear Guard of the Reserve; he was a native of Kuaiji County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1535.

Li Shichun, courtesy name Yiyuan, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and was a Secretary in the Bureau of Personnel Appointments in the Ministry of Personnel. He was from Guangzhou, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Wu Weiyue, courtesy name Junbo, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and was a Secretary in the Jiangxi Bureau of the Ministry of Justice. He was from Xiaofeng County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Examination Inspectors:

Huang Shou, courtesy name Gongpei, held the rank of Gentleman for Rendering Service and was an Investigating Censor for the Shandong Circuit. He was from Ningxia Central Garrison Guard, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1529.

Chen Chuxiu, courtesy name Shunbi, held the rank of Gentleman for Rendering Service and was an Investigating Censor for the Shandong Circuit. He was from Nan’an County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1532.

Proctors:

Li Chong, courtesy name Rucheng, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites. He was from Jingyang County, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Zhang Huan, courtesy name Maoshi, held the rank of Gentleman for Upright Service and was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites. His registered domicile was Changzhou County, Zhili; he was a native of Wu County and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Officials in Charge of Printing Examination Papers:

Wu Chun, courtesy name Yirong, held the rank of Grand Master for Upright Service and was a Vice Director acting as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites. He was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Yuan Gun, courtesy name Buzhi, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and was a Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites. He was from Wu County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Officials in Charge of Receiving and Keeping Examination Scripts:

Li Huang, courtesy name Zhonglai, held the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service and was a Central Secretariat Drafter. He was from Renqiu County, Zhili, and was a student admitted by virtue of an official’s status.

四書
固天縱之將聖又多能也
中也者天下之大本也和也者天下之達
道也致中和天地位焉萬物育焉
禹思天下有溺者由己溺之也稷思天下
有饑者由己饑之也是以如是其急也

君子黃中通理正位居體美在其中而暢

第壹場

四書

固天縱之將聖，又多能也。

中也者，天下之大本也；和也者，天下之達道也。致中和，天地位焉，萬物育焉。

禹思天下有溺者，由己溺之也；稷思天下有饑者，由己饑之也，是以如是其急也。

易

君子黃中通理，正位居體，美在其中，而暢於四支，發於事業，美之至也。

節，亨，剛柔分而剛得中。

聖人以此齋戒，以神明其德夫！

和順於道德而理於義，窮理盡性以至於命。

書

安汝止，惟幾惟康，其弼直；惟動丕應，徯志。

以昭受上帝，天其申命用休。

厥田惟中下，厥賦貞，作十有三載乃同。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Heaven has indeed endowed him with the capacity to become a great sage, and he also possesses many abilities.

Equilibrium is the great foundation of all under Heaven; harmony is the universally followed Way of all under Heaven. When equilibrium and harmony are fully realized, Heaven and Earth take their proper places, and all things flourish.

Yu thought that whenever anyone under Heaven drowned, it was as though he himself had drowned them. Ji thought that whenever anyone under Heaven went hungry, it was as though he himself had caused their hunger. This is why they acted with such urgency.

Book of Changes

The gentleman embodies the yellow of the center and comprehends principle; he occupies his proper position and abides in his essential form. Beauty resides within him, spreads through his four limbs, and manifests itself in his undertakings. This is beauty at its utmost.

Restraint: success. The firm and yielding lines are apportioned, and the firm obtains the central position.

Through this the sage purifies himself and observes abstinence, thereby making his virtue spiritually luminous!

They accord harmoniously with the Way and its virtue and are ordered according to righteousness; they fathom principle and fully realize their nature, thereby reaching an understanding of Heaven’s decree.

Book of Documents

Rest securely in your proper place; attend to the first stirrings of affairs and to conditions of ease, and let those who assist you be upright. Whenever you act, there will be a great response, as people await your intention.

Thus illustriously receive the mandate of the Lord on High; Heaven will renew its mandate with blessings.

Its fields were of the lower-middle grade, and its tax assessment was of the lowest grade. Only after thirteen years of cultivation did it reach the same standard as the other regions.

無有作惡遵王之路

punctuated:
無偏無陂，遵王之義；無有作好，遵王之道；無有作惡，遵王之路。
庶政惟和，萬國咸寧。

詩
麟之趾，振振公子，于嗟麟兮！
天保定爾，俾爾戩穀；罄無不宜，受天百祿。降爾遐福，維日不足。
神之格思，不可度思，矧可射思！
奏鼓簡簡，衎我烈祖。

春秋
公會齊人、宋人救鄭。〔莊公二十有八年〕
秋，楚公子嬰齊帥師伐鄭。公會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、杞伯救鄭。八月，戊辰，同盟于馬陵。〔成公七年〕
季孫宿會晉侯、鄭伯、齊人、宋人、衛人、邾人于邢丘。〔襄公八年〕秋，七月，辛巳，豹及諸侯之大夫盟于宋。〔襄公二十有七年〕
春，王正月，舍中軍。〔昭公五年〕秋，七月，季孫
translation_en:
Without partiality or deviation, follow the king’s righteousness. Do not indulge personal preferences; follow the king’s Way. Do not indulge personal aversions; follow the king’s path.
Let the many affairs of government be harmonious, and all the states will be at peace.

Book of Odes
The qilin’s feet! Virtuous are the lord’s sons. Ah, the qilin!
Heaven protects and establishes you, granting you happiness and prosperity. Everything accords with what is fitting; you receive Heaven’s hundred blessings. It sends down lasting blessings upon you, as though the days were insufficient.
The spirits’ coming cannot be fathomed; how much less may they be treated with disrespect!
The drums sound, resounding and strong, gladdening our illustrious ancestor.

Spring and Autumn Annals
The duke joined men of Qi and Song to relieve Zheng. 〔Twenty-eighth year of Duke Zhuang.〕
In autumn, Prince Yingqi of Chu led an army to attack Zheng. The duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi 齊, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, and the Earl of Qi 杞 to relieve Zheng. In the eighth month, on the wuchen day, they jointly concluded a covenant at Maling. 〔Seventh year of Duke Cheng.〕

…Yiru, Shu Gong, and Zhongsun Jue led an army to attack Ju. 〔Tenth year of Duke Zhao.〕

Record of Rites
The Son of Heaven takes virtue as his carriage and music as his charioteer. The feudal lords deal with one another through ritual propriety; the great officers establish their relative order through rules; the servicemen assess one another through trustworthiness; and the common people sustain one another through harmony. This is the flourishing of All under Heaven.
When accomplishments are reported to Heaven in sacrifice, phoenixes descend and tortoises and dragons arrive. When offerings are made to the Supreme Lord at the suburban sacrifice, wind and rain are regulated, and cold and heat come in their proper seasons.
Rites and music accord with the essential nature of Heaven and Earth and give expression to the potency of spiritual powers. They bring down the spirits above and raise those below, consolidating the forms of both the subtle and the gross, and governing the proper relations between father and son, ruler and minister.
When the gentleman acts reverently, he uses sacrificial vessels. Thus he does not neglect the appointed days and months or disregard divination by tortoise shell and milfoil, and he serves his ruler and superiors with reverence. Consequently, those above do not treat the people disrespectfully, and those below do not behave irreverently toward their superiors.

punctuated: 皇上者乎？試舉其大者，與諸士共揚搉焉。往者建明堂大享之典也，議初下，章縫之士莫不顧愕咨度，吐哺而思，無所授簡，蓋兢兢乎其難也。我皇上親灑宸翰，作《或問》一篇，頒諸朝堂，授于有司，不崇朝而曠世之典定，百代之疑决矣。仰而誦之，大義炳若日星，妙悟英斷，微詞奧旨，蔚然六經矣。豈啻考三王、俟後聖而不謬不惑哉！我皇考睿宗皇帝盛德如周文王，我皇上嚴父之孝比諸武王，備美極盛，越二千年而再見者也。夫士生聖代，親覩大典之成，習服大訓，必有能紬繹其義而鋪張其盛者矣。與夫往古立制之詳畧、裁義之當否，幸皆精白陳之，用觀博雅之學。
translation_en:
…His Majesty? Let us take up the greatest of these matters and discuss them together with you gentlemen. When the ceremonial institution of the Great Sacrifice in the Hall of Light was being established, and the proposal was first circulated, the scholars in their ceremonial caps all looked at one another in astonishment and deliberated. They spat out their food to ponder it, yet no one could be entrusted with the writing tablets: so apprehensive were they of its difficulty. His Majesty personally took up the imperial brush and composed a piece entitled Questions and Answers (Huowen), promulgating it at court and delivering it to the responsible officials. Before the morning was over, a ceremony unparalleled for ages had been settled, and doubts persisting through a hundred generations resolved. Reverently reading it, we find its great principles as brilliant as the sun and stars. Its marvelous insight and discerning judgments, its subtle language and profound meaning, possess the rich splendor of the Six Classics. How could it merely meet the standard of being tested against the Three Kings without error and awaiting a later sage without misgiving?

Our late imperial father, Emperor Ruizong, possessed glorious virtue like that of King Wen of Zhou. His Majesty’s filial devotion in honoring his father compares with that of King Wu. Such consummate excellence and supreme splendor have appeared again after more than two thousand years. You gentlemen, born in this sage age, have personally witnessed the completion of this great ceremony and have studied and followed these great instructions. Surely some among you can unravel their meaning and fully expound their magnificence. Together with these matters, set forth with utmost sincerity and clarity the elaborateness or simplicity of institutions established in antiquity, and whether the judgments of ritual propriety underlying them were fitting, so that we may assess your broad and refined learning.

所謂得之之形勢乎人人能爲諸生道古
punctuated: 問：古之有天下者，成功之後，皆有象功之舞，所以示子孫以其始得之之形勢，著不忘也。如唐太宗自詫其七德之舞，不苟作，意亦若此。夫太宗不足言也，不見孔子告賓牟賈以武王之事乎？我祖宗以神武取定天下，其攻取形勢，大畧古所未有也。夫我太祖高皇帝之提劒而起也，自北而南，經營審顧而基成矣。於是右麾而西，左麾而東，則始轉北嚮矣。又右麾而東，左麾而西，中立而整嚴，再指而北，無有當之者矣。我成祖文皇帝之靖難而興也，一旦決策，不崇朝而定其國中，其基固矣。於是捨之而趨東北而復南，正之竒也；又捨之以趨西北而再南，竒之竒也。屢出擾之，其後也，乘之而益南，而無有當之者矣。凡此非所謂得之之形勢乎？今欲爾諸生道古
translation_en:
Question: The rulers of antiquity, after accomplishing the conquest of All under Heaven, all had dances that represented their achievements. These showed their descendants the circumstances and strategic configurations through which they had first acquired the realm, making them manifest so that they would not be forgotten. For example, Emperor Taizong of the Tang himself boasted of his Dance of the Seven Virtues: it was not composed casually, and its intent was likewise of this kind. But Taizong hardly merits discussion. Have you not seen what Confucius told Binmou Jia about King Wu?

Our imperial ancestors conquered and pacified All under Heaven through their divine martial prowess. The strategic configurations of their campaigns were, in their broad outlines, unprecedented in antiquity. When our Emperor Taizu Gao rose with sword in hand, he moved from north to south, planning his operations and carefully considering his position, until his foundation was established. Then he waved his command to the right and moved west, and to the left and moved east; only then did he turn northward. Again he waved his command to the right and moved east, and to the left and moved west. Holding the center with his forces disciplined and in good order, he once more directed them northward, and none could withstand him.

When our Emperor Chengzu Wen rose to quell the troubles, he settled upon his strategy one day and, before the morning was over, secured his own domain, making his foundation firm. He then left it to hasten northeast and return south: this was an unorthodox maneuver within orthodox operations. Again he left it to hasten northwest and once more turn south: this was an unorthodox maneuver within unorthodox operations. He repeatedly sallied forth to harass the enemy; afterward, exploiting the opportunity, he advanced farther south, and none could withstand him.

Are not all these instances of what is called the circumstances and strategic configurations through which the realm was acquired? Now we wish you students to expound upon antiquity…

有俾於我聖天子保大思艱之助，則以何義？夫孔子居常，則述其周之先王，爾諸士舉我帝制，又何讓焉？

問：圖以畫卦，書以敘疇，世儒皆能言之矣。然稽之易，首言圖書而不詳所始，則所謂河圖授羲、洛書錫禹者，其說果何所本？漢儒亦何據以之分屬易範耶？今考之，圖之畫卦，其陰陽竒偶之理，易具之矣。若範出於書，則方位名數皆不可強而通者，豈其說果成於附會歟？而宋儒因是作皇極內篇以立範數，豈神禹所敘、箕子所陳，其用止於明數矣乎？夫圖書分屬，而易範之作不同時，則有謂圖書同出，聖人則圖書以畫卦者，又豈無見而云？世儒不知據經，而類求之緯候之說，至以九十互言圖書，以資異論，豈皆穿鑿附會者始之，而諸說因是以張
translation_en:
…to help our sagely Son of Heaven preserve his great dominion and remain mindful of its difficulties: by what principles would you do so? Confucius, in his ordinary discourse, recounted the deeds of the former kings of his Zhou dynasty. Why, then, should you gentlemen hesitate to cite the institutions of our imperial dynasty?

Question: The Chart served to draw the trigrams, and the Writing to set out the categories: scholars today can all speak of this. Yet, when we examine the Book of Changes, it first mentions the Chart and the Writing without detailing their origins. On what, then, is the claim that the River Chart was bestowed upon Fu Xi and the Luo Writing granted to Yu actually based? On what grounds, too, did Han scholars assign them respectively to the Book of Changes and the Great Plan? If we now examine the Chart’s use in drawing the trigrams, the principles of yin and yang, odd and even, are fully present in the Book of Changes. But if the Great Plan derives from the Writing, its directions and positions, names and numbers cannot all be made to correspond by force. Could this account indeed have arisen from strained associations? Moreover, a Song scholar proceeded on this basis to compose the Inner Chapters on the Supreme Standard (Huangji neipian), establishing the numerical system of the Great Plan. Could the purpose of what the divine Yu set out and Jizi expounded have been confined to elucidating numbers? Now, if the Chart and the Writing belong to separate works, and the Book of Changes and the Great Plan were not composed at the same time, could those who say that the Chart and the Writing appeared together, and that the sage took them as models in drawing the trigrams, have spoken without any insight? Scholars today do not know to ground themselves in the classics, but generally seek answers in the prognostic theories of the apocryphal texts. They even interchange nine and ten in speaking of the Chart and the Writing, lending support to divergent interpretations. Could all this have originated with those who forced connections and strained explanations, with the various theories consequently taking this as their basis…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
本歟爾諸士究心理學是必有折衷前
聞以是正諸家之說者幸究言之毋自
諉曰尊所聞也
問儒者抱業求自見於世其於當時之務
未有不究心者試舉近日
廷謨之大者二事與多士商之
國家財賦倚於東南轉漕山東入于通惠歲
輸大司農者四百萬石此
祖宗定制也頃以災歔之故稍從折變邊圉告
===
棘間亦藉為餽給然
國儲則漸損矣
皇上責成計部必全復舊徵誠治安之長策也
而或者則慮應邊之不裕或謂諸邊餽
給原不麗於太倉或又謂邊郡逋負之
久凶饉之仍而調募之眾多非取助于
太倉不可然歟否歟茲欲使內儲不移
外餉恒足其策安在歟
國家邊防重於西北慎守東勝達于黑山阻

國儲則漸損矣
皇上責成計部必令復舊徵誠治安之長策也
而議者聞之慮邊之不裕或謂諸邊餽
給原不賴於太倉或又謂邊郡逋負之
久而餽之倘而調募之衆多非取助於
太倉不可然歟否歟茲欲使內儲不移
外餉恒足其策安在歟
國家邊防重於西北慎守東勝達于黑山阻
punctuated:
本歟？爾諸士究心理學，是必有折衷前聞，以是正諸家之說者。幸究言之，毋自諉曰尊所聞也。
問：儒者抱業，求自見於世，其於當時之務，未有不究心者。試舉近日廷謨之大者二事，與多士商之。
國家財賦倚於東南，轉漕山東，入于通惠，歲輸大司農者四百萬石，此祖宗定制也。頃以災歔之故，稍從折變；邊圉告棘，間亦藉為餽給。然國儲則漸損矣。皇上責成計部，必全復舊徵，誠治安之長策也。而或者則慮應邊之不裕，或謂諸邊餽給原不麗於太倉，或又謂邊郡逋負之久、凶饉之仍，而調募之眾多，非取助于太倉不可。然歟？否歟？茲欲使內儲不移，外餉恒足，其策安在歟？
國家邊防重於西北，慎守東勝，達于黑山，阻
translation_en:
…a foundation for them? You scholars devote yourselves to the study of principle; surely you have weighed earlier teachings and can thereby correct the various schools’ explanations. Please discuss this exhaustively, without excusing yourselves by saying that you revere what you have been taught.
Question: Confucian scholars cultivate their learning and seek to distinguish themselves in the world; none fails to give close attention to the affairs of his time. Let us take two major matters recently deliberated at court and discuss them with you scholars.
The state relies on the southeast for its fiscal revenues. Grain is transported through Shandong and into the Tonghui Canal; four million shi are delivered annually to the Minister of Revenue. This is the established system of our imperial ancestors. Recently, owing to disasters [?], some payments have been allowed to be commuted. When emergencies arose on the frontier, these resources were also occasionally used to supply it. Yet the state’s reserves have consequently dwindled. His Majesty has charged the Ministry of Revenue with fully restoring the former levies: this is indeed a long-term strategy for good government and peace. Some, however, fear that resources will be insufficient to meet frontier needs. Some say that supplies for the various frontiers were never chargeable to the Court of the Imperial Granaries; others argue that, given the long-standing arrears of the frontier commanderies, repeated famines, and the large numbers of troops transferred and recruited, assistance from the Court of the Imperial Granaries is indispensable. Is this so, or not? If we now wish to keep the central reserves from being diverted while ensuring that frontier military provisions are always sufficient, what strategy should we adopt?
The state’s frontier defenses are concentrated in the northwest. Carefully guarding Dongsheng and extending to Heishan, relying on …

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
河為固者二千餘里此
祖宗舊疆也往者制禦稍疎失其險阨黠虜日
盛因得出入河套而邊患遂日深矣
皇上嘉納邊臣欲恢還故土誠纘承之鴻烈也
而或者顧慮大虜之難逐或謂逐之可
以復至洪河之險與虜共之或又謂河
濡烽堠之遠轉餉之費士馬單脆效昔
時之守為難然歟否歟兹欲使虜可久
絶我可恒守其策安在歟夫錢穀甲兵
===
皆學者之所當講況將出而施用之日
其責有不得辭者願陳其畧
問夷狄之禍久矣三代以後漢唐之治為
盛考之當時叛服不常當其畏威逺遁
也莫然猶思所以制之創五郡以斷匈
奴右臂築三城以拒默啜中昬今以
國家之盛强不之圖而飆舉烏集時竊邊徼
虽屢受挫於口後亦不制竊據于海西
吉囊巢穴於河套西番分布于甘肅比

祖宗舊疆也往者制禦稍疎失其險阨黠虜日

以復至洪河之險則虜兵之或又謂河

絕我可恒守其策安在歟夫錢穀甲兵

問夷狄之禍久矣三代以後漢唐之治爲
盛考之當時叛服不常當其畏威遠遁
〻莫然猶思所以制之創五郡以斷匈
===

□□□□□□□□□□□□□□
□□□□□□□□□□□□□□
吉崇與大於河套西番分布于甘肅
punctuated:
河為固者二千餘里，此祖宗舊疆也。往者制禦稍疎，失其險阨，黠虜日盛，因得出入河套，而邊患遂日深矣。皇上嘉納邊臣，欲恢還故土，誠纘承之鴻烈也。而或者顧慮大虜之難逐，或謂逐之可以復至，洪河之險與虜共之；或又謂河濡烽堠之遠，轉餉之費，士馬單脆，效昔時之守為難。然歟否歟？兹欲使虜可久絶，我可恒守，其策安在歟？夫錢穀甲兵，皆學者之所當講，況將出而施用之日，其責有不得辭者，願陳其畧。

問：夷狄之禍久矣。三代以後，漢唐之治為盛。考之當時，叛服不常，當其畏威逺遁也，莫然猶思所以制之，創五郡以斷匈奴右臂，築三城以拒默啜，中昬。今以國家之盛强，不之圖，而飆舉烏集，時竊邊徼，虽屢受挫於口後，亦不制，竊據于海西，吉囊巢穴於河套，西番分布于甘肅，比
translation_en:
…with the river forming a defensive barrier for more than two thousand li: this is the former territory of our imperial ancestors. In the past, control grew somewhat lax, and we lost its strategic strongpoints. The crafty enemy grew stronger by the day and consequently gained access to the Hetao, entering and leaving at will; frontier troubles thus became daily more severe. His Majesty graciously accepted the proposals of frontier officials and wished to recover the former territory—truly a magnificent undertaking in carrying forward his ancestors’ achievements. Yet some worry that the powerful enemy will be difficult to expel. Some say that even if expelled, they can return, since the defensive advantages of the great river are shared with them. Others say that the remoteness of the river’s beacon posts [?], the expense of transporting provisions, and the weakness of our troops and horses make it difficult to maintain the defenses as in former times. Is this so or not? What policy would enable us to exclude the enemy for a long time and maintain our defenses permanently? Finance, grain supplies, arms, and warfare are all matters that scholars ought to study. Moreover, when you enter office and put your learning into practice, these are responsibilities you cannot decline. Please set out the essentials.

Question: The calamities caused by the Yi and Di peoples have persisted for a long time. After the Three Dynasties, government flourished most under the Han and Tang. Examining those times, we find that these peoples alternated unpredictably between rebellion and submission. Even when they feared imperial might and fled far away, measures to control them were still considered [?]. Five commanderies were established to sever the right arm of the Xiongnu, and three cities were built to repel Mochuo [the following 中昬 is unclear]. Now, despite the flourishing strength of our state, no plans are made against them. They rise like a whirlwind and gather like crows, periodically making incursions into the borderlands. Although repeatedly repulsed at [unclear place or phrase: 口後], they remain uncontrolled and occupy Haixi without authorization. Jinang has his lair in the Hetao, and the Western Fan are spread across Gansu [the final 比 is unclear] …

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
其故何歟夫當時之將若魏尚李廣耿
恭段熲張奐皇甫規之徒特一太守刺
史校尉之任耳而震懾強虜坐制諸羌
今大將擁旄憲臣開府而虜騎長驅狼
奔豕突往歲喋血于太原繼又鳴鏑於
宣府繼又飲馬於涇原矣懸軍深入兵
家所忌彼獨不畏者何歟且宣元之世
而叩關納欸稽顙稱臣遣子入侍今以
聖治之隆
===
聖化之遠而夷情反覆變詐不常假市貢為窺
伺之計譯番文無真正之言花當則脅
求添貢把兒孫則深入虜掠今諸番先
期擾動糜費廩餼邊臣不能阻回至煩
朝廷切責此其悖慢甚矣豈天厚其毒而潰
之歟將佑啟
神功駿烈以成中興之盛也諸士子藏器待時
久矣行將與謀帷幄之中其何以佐修
攘之計乎願試陳之以觀濟時之畧

久矣行將與謀帷幄之中其何以佐修
攘之計乎願試陳之以觀濟時之畧
punctuated: 其故何歟？夫當時之將，若魏尚、李廣、耿恭、段熲、張奐、皇甫規之徒，特一太守、刺史、校尉之任耳，而震懾強虜，坐制諸羌。今大將擁旄，憲臣開府，而虜騎長驅，狼奔豕突，往歲喋血于太原，繼又鳴鏑於宣府，繼又飲馬於涇原矣。懸軍深入，兵家所忌，彼獨不畏者何歟？且宣、元之世，而叩關納欸，稽顙稱臣，遣子入侍。今以聖治之隆，聖化之遠，而夷情反覆，變詐不常，假市貢為窺伺之計，譯番文無真正之言。花當則脅求添貢，把兒孫則深入虜掠。今諸番先期擾動，糜費廩餼，邊臣不能阻回，至煩朝廷切責，此其悖慢甚矣！豈天厚其毒而潰之歟？將佑啟神功駿烈，以成中興之盛也？諸士子藏器待時久矣，行將與謀帷幄之中，其何以佐修攘之計乎？願試陳之，以觀濟時之畧。
translation_en: …What is the reason for this? Generals of those times, such as Wei Shang, Li Guang, Geng Gong, Duan Jiong, Zhang Huan, and Huangfu Gui, held only the posts of governor, regional inspector, or commandant, yet they struck terror into powerful foes and held the various Qiang peoples in check with ease. Today, great generals bear their command banners and censorial officials establish headquarters, yet enemy cavalry penetrate far into our territory, rushing like wolves and charging like boars. In past years they shed blood at Taiyuan; then their whistling arrows sounded at Xuanfu; then they watered their horses at Jingyuan. To send an isolated army deep into enemy territory is something military strategists shun. Why do these enemies alone have no fear of it? Moreover, in the reigns of the Han emperors Xuan and Yuan, they came knocking at the frontier gates to offer allegiance, bowed their foreheads to the ground and declared themselves subjects, and sent their sons to attend at court. Today, despite the grandeur of Your Majesty’s sage rule and the far-reaching influence of your transforming virtue, the foreigners are fickle in their intentions and endlessly deceitful. They use trade and tribute as a pretext for spying out opportunities, and their translated documents contain no truthful statements. Huadang uses threats to demand additional tribute missions, while Ba’ersun penetrates deep into our territory to take captives and plunder. Now the various foreign peoples arrive before the appointed time and cause disturbances, waste provisions, and cannot be turned back by the frontier officials, so that the court has been troubled to issue stern reprimands. Their defiance and insolence are extreme! Is Heaven allowing their poisonous wickedness to grow so that it may bring about their collapse? Or will it lend its aid and open the way for Your Majesty’s divine achievements and magnificent deeds, bringing a glorious restoration to fruition? You scholars have long kept your abilities in reserve, awaiting your opportunity. Soon you will participate in deliberations within the command tent. How would you assist plans to strengthen internal governance and repel foreign enemies? Please set forth your views, so that we may assess your strategies for meeting the needs of the times.

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
固天縱之將聖又多能也
秦梁
同考試官都給事中鄭批縱與又二字最難發揮
枯則不暢蔓則不切是篇詞簡而意完異乎
諸子者之作矣錄之
同考試官檢討晁批議論精確理趣完粹
足占有本之學錄之
===
同考試官編修潘批善發子貢之意而詞
格古雅蓋深造有得者
同考試官侍讀郭批意精詞雅論語義之
最佳者宜錄以式
考試官學士張批說聖與多能處明盡
考試官學士孫批發揮精到
賢者言聖人之道達諸天而不可以小知也蓋
聖人之道天道也以多能為聖則其知也亦小
矣此子貢之告太宰所以有天縱之說歟其意

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
曰天之於人也有所厚有所不厚斯人之於天
也有所能有所不能何則流行賦予聖人之於
人同類也而知愚賢不肖之等異焉惟聖人則
以其身而立天地民物之極聰明睿智自生民
以来未之或盛者殆非人所能與盖天縱之以
聖而聖人之所不能違焉者矣降衷秉彝聖人
之性與人同也而仁知百姓之見拘焉惟聖人
則以其心而體天地萬物之理生知安行其聖
神之妙不可以名者有非人所能及盖聖人不
===
自限於天而天亦不能為之限焉者矣是故自
其大者觀之聖則無所不能然不知渾然全體
之中自具夫泛應曲當之用才全德備不可以
偏長目也夫所謂多能者乃其事之餘耳豈足

之極聖神功化殆難以方所求也夫所謂聖者

道之至而天所成也謂夫子為聖者似足以知

punctuated: 曰：天之於人也，有所厚，有所不厚；斯人之於天也，有所能，有所不能。何則？流行賦予，聖人之於人，同類也，而知愚賢不肖之等異焉。惟聖人則以其身而立天地民物之極，聰明睿智，自生民以来未之或盛者，殆非人所能與，盖天縱之以聖，而聖人之所不能違焉者矣。降衷秉彝，聖人之性與人同也，而仁知百姓之見拘焉。惟聖人則以其心而體天地萬物之理，生知安行，其聖神之妙不可以名者，有非人所能及，盖聖人不自限於天，而天亦不能為之限焉者矣。是故自其大者觀之，聖則無所不能，然不知渾然全體之中，自具夫泛應曲當之用，才全德備，不可以偏長目也。夫所謂多能者，乃其事之餘耳，豈足以盡聖道之全哉？自其小者觀之，多能亦可以言聖，然不知一才一藝之美，不可語天道精微之極，聖神功化，殆難以方所求也。夫所謂聖者，一以貫之者耳，又何止於多能之小哉？盖聖者，道之至而天所成也，謂夫子為聖者，似足以知
translation_en:
…It says: Heaven is generous toward some people and less generous toward others; people, in their relation to Heaven, likewise have things they can and cannot do. Why is this? In the flowing forth and bestowal of Heaven’s endowments, the sage belongs to the same kind as other people, yet distinctions arise between the wise and foolish, the worthy and unworthy. The sage alone, through his own person, establishes the supreme standard for Heaven and Earth, the people and all things. His keenness of perception and sagely wisdom, unsurpassed since humankind first came into being, are surely beyond what others can match. This is Heaven’s granting him sagehood, something even the sage himself cannot contravene. In receiving the moral nature bestowed from above and possessing its constant norms, the sage’s nature is the same as other people’s; yet the benevolent, the wise, and the common people are constrained by their respective views. The sage alone, through his mind, embodies the principles of Heaven and Earth and the myriad things. He knows them from birth and acts upon them with ease. The ineffable subtlety of his sagehood and spiritual power lies beyond the reach of others. Thus the sage does not let himself be bounded by Heaven, and Heaven itself cannot set bounds upon him.

Accordingly, viewed from its greater aspect, sagehood means being capable of everything. Yet this view fails to recognize that within its undivided wholeness there already resides the capacity to respond to every circumstance with exact appropriateness. Complete in ability and fully endowed with virtue, the sage cannot be characterized by any particular excellence. What are called his many abilities are merely incidental accomplishments. How could they suffice to encompass the whole Way of the sage? Viewed from its lesser aspect, many abilities may also serve as grounds for speaking of sagehood. Yet this view fails to recognize that excellence in a single talent or skill cannot express the utmost refinement and subtlety of Heaven’s Way. The transformative achievements of the sage’s spiritual power can scarcely be sought within fixed bounds. What is called sagehood is simply that which is threaded through by a single principle. How could it be confined to the lesser matter of many abilities? Sagehood is the culmination of the Way, brought to fulfillment by Heaven. To call the Master a sage would seem sufficient to know…

…the Master, yet fail to understand that his sagehood actually derives from Heaven. Accomplishments are the peripheral aspects of the Way, encompassed within its greatness. Those who describe the sage as possessing many accomplishments not only fail to understand Heaven; they also fail to understand the sage. Alas! The Grand Steward’s understanding was shallow. Yet can Zigong, who spoke of Heaven’s endowment, be said to have understood the Master deeply? For the sage can, through the Way, attain to Heaven, but Heaven cannot reserve the Way exclusively for the sage. Heaven can endow the Master with sagehood, yet the Master himself is not conscious of having been so endowed by Heaven. I suspect that Zigong’s understanding had not reached this point. Otherwise, why would the Master have been so earnest in instructing Ci—that is, Zigong—about dispensing with speech, and about learning below and attaining understanding above?

The Doctrine of the Mean says that the Way is fully present in the human mind: to realize one’s mind to the utmost is to realize the Way to the utmost. For the mind comprehends the Way, uniting Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things into one. If one can realize one’s mind to the utmost, the work of establishing things in their proper places and nurturing them reaches completion. How could this depend on anything external? Zisi’s meaning is this: There is no Way outside the mind anywhere under Heaven; the gentleman practices the learning of realizing the mind to the utmost. Consider the single mind of a person. In its original substance, free from any leaning or inclination, it is called equilibrium. This equilibrium is precisely what Heaven confers upon people as their nature. Though still and unmoving, it already contains the roots from which joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure arise. title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
□□不假於人而無所不周矣非天下之達道
□夫道之具於人心其體用如此君子於此誠
能存戒懼於不睹不聞之時約而至於至靜之
中不使有一毫之偏倚則極其中而大本立矣
辨善惡於隱微幽獨之地精而至於應物之處
不使有一毫之差謬則極其和而大用行矣由
是吾心之中即天地之中吾心既不違於中則
天地亦不能違吾心而有所不位矣陰陽動靜
各止其所殆與心而同其神乎萬物之和即吾
===
心之和和既極於吾心則萬物亦不能違吾心
而有所不育矣懽忻交通充塞無間殆與心而
一其化乎蓋至是而體道之功無以加矣然皆
始於心焉向使須臾之不敬一念之未純則與
天地不相似而萬物且違之矣况得而位育之
哉此君子所以貴有盡心之學也雖然堯舜之
道亦不過此危微精一之訓萬世治天下之法
也後世心學不明去道益遠而唐虞之化不復
見者豈不可深慨哉此子思所以憂天下而作

punctuated: □□不假於人而無所不周矣，非天下之達道□？夫道之具於人心，其體用如此。君子於此，誠能存戒懼於不睹不聞之時，約而至於至靜之中，不使有一毫之偏倚，則極其中而大本立矣；辨善惡於隱微幽獨之地，精而至於應物之處，不使有一毫之差謬，則極其和而大用行矣。由是，吾心之中即天地之中，吾心既不違於中，則天地亦不能違吾心而有所不位矣。陰陽動靜，各止其所，殆與心而同其神乎！萬物之和即吾心之和，和既極於吾心，則萬物亦不能違吾心而有所不育矣。懽忻交通，充塞無間，殆與心而一其化乎！蓋至是而體道之功無以加矣，然皆始於心焉。向使須臾之不敬，一念之未純，則與天地不相似，而萬物且違之矣，况得而位育之哉！此君子所以貴有盡心之學也。雖然，堯舜之道亦不過此，危微精一之訓，萬世治天下之法也。後世心學不明，去道益遠，而唐虞之化不復見者，豈不可深慨哉！此子思所以憂天下而作
translation_en: …[?] It does not depend upon others, yet extends everywhere without omission. Is this not the universally prevailing Way of all under Heaven [?]? Such are the substance and functioning of the Way inherent in the human heart. If the gentleman can truly maintain caution and apprehension when nothing is seen or heard, gathering himself inward until he reaches utter stillness and allowing not the slightest deviation or bias, he will bring his equilibrium to its fullest extent, and the great foundation will be established. If he distinguishes good from evil in what is hidden and subtle, even in solitude, refining his discernment through to his responses to things and allowing not the slightest error, he will bring his harmony to its fullest extent, and the great functioning will be realized. Thus the equilibrium of my heart is the equilibrium of Heaven and Earth. Once my heart does not depart from equilibrium, Heaven and Earth likewise cannot diverge from my heart and leave anything out of its proper place. Yin and yang, movement and stillness, each rest in their proper places: do they not share the heart’s wondrous efficacy? The harmony of the myriad things is the harmony of my heart. Once harmony reaches its fullest extent within my heart, the myriad things likewise cannot diverge from my heart and leave anything unnourished. Joyfully communicating with one another, pervading everything without a gap: do they not become one with the heart in their transforming activity? At this point, the achievement of embodying the Way can advance no further; yet it all begins in the heart. Had there been even a moment’s lack of reverence or a single impure thought, one would no longer accord with Heaven and Earth, and the myriad things would diverge from one. How, then, could one bring them to their proper places and nurture them? This is why the gentleman prizes the learning that fully develops the heart. Even so, the Way of Yao and Shun goes no further than this. Their instruction concerning the precariousness of the human heart, the subtlety of the heart of the Way, refinement, and singleness is the method for governing all under Heaven for ten thousand generations. In later ages, the learning of the heart became obscured, people departed ever further from the Way, and the transforming influence of Tang and Yu was seen no more. Is this not cause for profound lament? This is why Zisi, concerned for all under Heaven, composed…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
命之禹則夫所以生斯民於昏墊者固禹之責
矣是故禹之心以為溺天下之民者水也所以
拯之使不至於溺者則予之責也以拯溺為責
而天下猶有溺焉是予之責未盡耳溺非予溺
之而誰溺歟懷襄之勢一日未順利巢窟之民
一日未衽席則禹之憂在天下無一日而忘矣
稼穡之任以命之稷則夫所以生斯民以粒食
者固稷之責矣是故稷之心以為養天下之饑
者食也所以教之使不至於饑者則予之責也
===
以養民為責而天下猶有饑焉是予之責未盡
耳饑非予饑之而誰饑歟待哺之民一日未安
飽黍稷之藝一日未蕃熟則稷之憂在天下無
一日而忘矣夫禹稷之任責之不可辭也禹稷
之憂心之不能已也以不能已之心加之以不
可辭之責則其所以救民之患者其容以不急
哉是故乘四載而荒度導百川而東下汲汲乎
惟欲奠之於平土之上而後已蓋禹既為天下
懷己溺之憂則不得不為天下拯有溺之患矣

punctuated: 命之禹，則夫所以生斯民於昏墊者，固禹之責矣。是故禹之心以為：「溺天下之民者，水也；所以拯之使不至於溺者，則予之責也。以拯溺為責，而天下猶有溺焉，是予之責未盡耳。溺，非予溺之，而誰溺歟？」懷襄之勢一日未順利，巢窟之民一日未衽席，則禹之憂在天下，無一日而忘矣。稼穡之任以命之稷，則夫所以生斯民以粒食者，固稷之責矣。是故稷之心以為：「養天下之饑者，食也；所以教之使不至於饑者，則予之責也。以養民為責，而天下猶有饑焉，是予之責未盡耳。饑，非予饑之，而誰饑歟？」待哺之民一日未安飽，黍稷之藝一日未蕃熟，則稷之憂在天下，無一日而忘矣。夫禹稷之任，責之不可辭也；禹稷之憂，心之不能已也。以不能已之心，加之以不可辭之責，則其所以救民之患者，其容以不急哉？是故乘四載而荒度，導百川而東下，汲汲乎惟欲奠之於平土之上而後已。蓋禹既為天下懷己溺之憂，則不得不為天下拯有溺之患矣。
translation_en:
…entrusted it to Yu, so the task of preserving the people's lives amid the engulfing flood was assuredly Yu's responsibility. Thus Yu thought: “What drowns the people of the world is water; rescuing them so that they do not drown is my responsibility. If rescuing the drowning is my responsibility, yet people in the world still drown, this means only that I have not fully discharged my responsibility. If it is not I who have drowned them, then who has?” As long as the surging floodwaters had not been brought to flow freely in their proper courses, and the people dwelling in nests and caves had not been settled comfortably on sleeping mats, Yu's concern remained with the world: not for a single day did he forget it.

The charge of sowing and harvesting was entrusted to Ji, so the task of sustaining these people with grain was assuredly Ji's responsibility. Thus Ji thought: “What nourishes the hungry people of the world is food; teaching them so that they do not go hungry is my responsibility. If nourishing the people is my responsibility, yet people in the world still go hungry, this means only that I have not fully discharged my responsibility. If it is not I who have caused their hunger, then who has?” As long as the people awaiting nourishment were not secure and well fed, and the planted millets had not grown abundantly and ripened, Ji's concern remained with the world: not for a single day did he forget it.

The charge borne by Yu and Ji was a responsibility they could not decline; their concern arose from hearts that could not rest. When hearts that could not rest were joined to responsibilities that could not be declined, how could they fail to act urgently to save the people from calamity? Thus Yu traveled by the four modes of conveyance to survey the land far and wide, and guided the many rivers eastward. He labored urgently, wishing only to settle the people securely upon level ground before he would rest. Since Yu felt concern for the world as though he himself had caused its people to drown, he could not but rescue those in the world who faced the peril of drowning.

…He assessed the suitability of high ground and lowlands and distinguished the properties of the five grains, striving urgently to bring the people into a state of adequate food and warmth, and only then to rest. Since Ji felt concern for the hungry throughout the realm as though he himself were hungry, he could not but relieve their hardships. Yu and Ji passed their doors three times without entering because they truly wished to devote themselves to all under Heaven. How could they have been fond of exhausting themselves?

Alas! Heaven brings forth sages and worthies for the people's sake; thus their hearts never forget the people under Heaven for even a day. Yet their circumstances differ. 文言於坤之六五著其内外之善而贊其合一
之盛也夫君子之道内外合一而體用無間也
積於中而發於外其斯以為盛乎文言什坤爻
六五而以君道言之若此夫黄裳者中順之象
也中順者君所具之德也以中言之不偏不倚
===
而體全於未發之前惟精惟一而迹泯於先幾
之始淵乎其凝天命而涵衆理之會通也湛乎
其行達道而具萬事之條理也有黄之象焉故
曰黄以言乎中之色也以順言之無好無惡不
恃位而居物之先不驕不亢每虛己以受人之
感退然養其至和而勢不足以汩其真也夷然
安於後動而物不足以亂其守也有裳之象焉
故曰裳以言乎下之飾也夫中順雖有内外之
殊而其道則無二致盖中所以立順之體而順

In the way of the noble man, inner and outer are united, and substance and function admit of no separation. What accumulates within manifests itself without: is this not what constitutes its fullness? Now, the yellow lower garment symbolizes centrality and compliance. Centrality and compliance are virtues possessed by the ruler. As for centrality, he inclines to neither side, and its substance is whole before feelings arise. Utterly discerning and single-minded, he leaves no trace at the outset, before the first incipient stirrings. How profound his consolidation of Heaven’s mandate, encompassing the convergence and interconnection of all principles! How deep his practice of the universally applicable Way, embodying the ordered patterns of all affairs! Here is the image of yellow; hence the text says “yellow,” referring to the color of the center.
As for compliance, he has neither likes nor dislikes, and does not rely on his position to place himself ahead of others. Serenely content to act after others, he cannot be disturbed by external things in what he steadfastly maintains. Here is the image of the lower garment; hence the text says “lower garment,” referring to the adornment of the lower body.

…is the means by which compliance gives expression to the operation of centrality. Thus, when the virtue of centrality resides within, it is accumulated through utmost sincerity, and its impulse to manifest itself cannot be concealed. Preserved within as the virtue of Heaven, it cannot but take outward form as the kingly Way. From this it permeates the four limbs, and the bearing of virtue flourishes; it issues forth in undertakings, and the beneficent influence of virtue spreads widely. A majestic bearing that is exceedingly illustrious, extending even to providing a model for the many lords and thereby revealing the radiance of civil virtue—all this has its foundation in profound tranquillity. The generous ease of administering government, extending even to providing a standard for the nine regions and thereby accomplishing transformation through nonaction—all this results from wholehearted reverence. Is this not the utmost excellence of a ruler’s virtue?

Because its cultivation is already deep, the resources drawn from encountering the source extend far in their application, and nothing can obstruct them. Because its operation is already effective, the subtle efficacy of preserving the spirit concentrates virtue [?], making it ever more exalted. Substance and function are both fully present, and virtue and achievement alike attain their greatest flourishing. This may be called the utmost excellence, beyond which nothing can be added. When the line statement says, “Supreme good fortune,” does it not refer to this?

Yet the ruler embodies the Way of Qian, the Creative; why, then, should he draw upon Kun, the Receptive? The Ways of Heaven and Earth differ in form but share the same principle. Thus simplicity is what brings to completion the capacity for knowing through ease, while utmost compliance is that through which utmost vigor operates. In their essentials, these Ways merely complement one another to achieve centrality. Thus the principles of ease and simplicity are apprehended, and one establishes one’s place between Heaven and Earth.

translation_en:
…yet cannot be regarded with aversion. Righteousness is the differentiated manifestation of the Way and its virtue in their functioning. The Book of Changes follows what is fitting for each affair and thing, measuring it against the standard of centrality and correctness. In distinguishing degrees of right and wrong and clarifying the consequences of success and failure, it encompasses complexity without overstepping bounds and unfolds distinctions in keeping with their proper names. Thus, it speaks of the utmost movement under Heaven, yet cannot be thrown into disorder. Such is what is meant by the Changes encompassing substance and function in their entirety. Accordingly, although the differentiated principles of all under Heaven number in the myriad, none fails to be fully investigated through the Changes. Through it one discerns the causes of the hidden and the manifest and understands the way of day and night; Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things can no longer conceal their true circumstances. Although the natures endowed upon people and things differ greatly, none fails to be fully realized through the Changes. In understanding them, nothing remains unclear; in dealing with them, nothing is inappropriate. Through shaping, completing, grading, and regulating them, each is made to accord with its proper way.

Yet the heavenly mandate is also the source from which principle and nature emerge. When no principle remains unexplored, the Changes, by comprehending all and excluding nothing, becomes wholly integrated with the reality that flows unceasingly. Is not that which lies below form the substance of that which lies above form? When no nature remains unrealized, the Changes, by bringing each thing to completion without omission, participates in the transformations of the Supreme Ultimate, which are free from falsity. Is not the utmost transformation the functioning of the utmost numinousness? Such is what is meant by the Changes penetrating the subtle workings of both the manifest and the hidden. Viewed thus, the Way of Heaven cannot be made clear without the Changes, and the Changes could not have been composed by anyone other than the sages. Heaven, the Changes, and the sages—what separation could there be among them? To consider it further, the Changes is the human heart-mind. Since people cannot all be sages, the sages composed the Changes to instruct them, so that through it all might recover their own heart-minds…

translation_en:
…that is all. If people truly apprehended their own minds, the Changes could be dispensed with. Jing Fang made it shallow through images and numbers; Wang Bi dissipated it through abstruse emptiness. Thus the Way of the Changes was torn apart throughout the world.

Book of Documents

“Rest securely in your proper stopping place; attend to incipient developments and to repose, and let your assistants be upright. In your actions, respond fully to those awaiting the fulfillment of your intentions, thereby illustriously receiving the favor of the Lord on High. Heaven will renew its mandate to you with blessings.”

Chen Yan

When a great minister explains to his ruler the essentials of attending carefully to his position, he must carry his account through to the fullest effects of such efforts. Could the harmonious response of Heaven and humanity possibly be attained by chance? I imagine that the meaning of Great Yu’s admonition to Shun was as follows: Occupying Heaven’s throne is difficult; one cannot fail to exercise care. But what should the work of exercising such care entail? For truly…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
心為萬化之原不得其止則心之所以危也必
閑邪以存誠順適乎道心之正主敬以直內允
孚乎天德之純存於心者欲其無邪慝焉事乃
一心之用不審于事則動之所以妄也必惟幾
以省其發而致嚴于理欲之分惟康以省其安
而深憂乎悔吝之介見於行者欲其無繆戾焉
而又左右之臣皆以正君為急繩愆糾繆非徒
美之是將也以責難為恭明諫顯諍非惟善之
是承也謹位之功如此由是徵諸庶民則神道
===
之感通有以妙鼓舞之術王猷之允塞有以神
倡率之機將見聖人有作而物咸覩之推之無
不準也大君有命而民皆宜之動之無不化也
其心悅誠服殆有預待乎未事之先者矣由是
質諸上帝則冲漠無朕之理自我信之光明下
濟之神自我凝之將見有道之君足當天心之
眷有以介景福于無疆無虞之世自獲佑命之
隆有以錫純嘏于不替其篤厚不忘殆非有出
于圖度之私者矣夫下而得民則帝位出于民

punctuated: 心為萬化之原，不得其止，則心之所以危也。必閑邪以存誠，順適乎道心之正；主敬以直內，允孚乎天德之純。存於心者，欲其無邪慝焉。事乃一心之用，不審于事，則動之所以妄也。必惟幾以省其發，而致嚴于理欲之分；惟康以省其安，而深憂乎悔吝之介。見於行者，欲其無繆戾焉。而又左右之臣，皆以正君為急，繩愆糾繆，非徒美之是將也；以責難為恭，明諫顯諍，非惟善之是承也。謹位之功如此，由是徵諸庶民，則神道之感通，有以妙鼓舞之術；王猷之允塞，有以神倡率之機。將見聖人有作，而物咸覩之，推之無不準也；大君有命，而民皆宜之，動之無不化也。其心悅誠服，殆有預待乎未事之先者矣。由是質諸上帝，則冲漠無朕之理，自我信之；光明下濟之神，自我凝之。將見有道之君，足當天心之眷，有以介景福于無疆；無虞之世，自獲佑命之隆，有以錫純嘏于不替。其篤厚不忘，殆非有出于圖度之私者矣。夫下而得民，則帝位出于民
translation_en:
…the mind is the source of all transformations. If it fails to rest where it should, this is what makes it precarious. One must ward off depravity to preserve sincerity, conforming to the rectitude of the moral mind; one must maintain reverence to make the inner self upright, truly according with the purity of Heaven’s virtue. What is preserved within the mind must be free of evil and perversity. Affairs are the workings of this single mind. If one does not scrutinize affairs, this is what makes action reckless. One must attend to the first stirrings and examine their emergence, rigorously distinguishing moral principle from selfish desire; one must attend to well-being and examine one’s ease, remaining deeply concerned about the threshold of remorse and humiliation. What appears in conduct must be free of error and contrariness. Furthermore, the ministers at the ruler’s side must all regard correcting their sovereign as urgent. In checking faults and rectifying errors, they do more than promote his fine qualities; regarding the demand that he accomplish difficult things as true respect, they remonstrate openly and dispute forthrightly, doing more than merely support his good deeds.

Such is the work of attending carefully to the throne. If its effects are tested among the common people, the spiritual Way’s power to evoke a response enables the subtle art of inspiring them; the full realization of kingly guidance gives wondrous efficacy to the workings of leadership. Then one will see that when the sage acts, all beings look to him: wherever his example is extended, none fail to take it as their standard. When the great ruler issues commands, the people all find them fitting: wherever his influence moves them, none fail to be transformed. Their heartfelt delight and sincere submission seem already to await him before any undertaking has begun.

If this is then verified before the Lord on High, the principle that is silent, formless, and without trace is made manifest through oneself; the luminous spiritual power that descends to aid those below is concentrated through oneself. Then one will see that a ruler who possesses the Way is fully worthy of Heaven’s loving regard and thereby receives great blessings without limit. An age free from troubles naturally obtains abundant divine aid and favor, and thus pure blessings are bestowed without cessation. Such steadfast generosity and unfailing remembrance surely do not arise from selfish calculation.

Now, when one wins the people below, the imperial throne derives from the people…

translation_en:
…cherished and upheld in the people's hearts, becomes all the more secure. By gaining Heaven's favor above, the imperial position, favored and protected by Heaven's heart, becomes all the more firmly established. In sum, all this results from cultivating both the inward self and outward conduct. Can the emperor fail to attend to the work of guarding his position with care? Consider further: Shun occupied the throne as a great sage—what an age was that of Youyu! Yet Yu still earnestly admonished him to guard his position with care, invoking Heaven's mandate and the people's hearts as evidence. The minister did not forget to offer loyal counsel merely because order had already been achieved; the ruler did not slacken in accepting good advice merely because he was already a sage. Those above and below labored with solicitude, and ruler and ministers trusted one another. Was this not why their flourishing government of supreme harmony stood unrivaled through the ages?

“All affairs of government are harmonious; the myriad states are at peace.”
Zhou Rudou

Associate Examiner Zheng, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “It speaks well of harmonious government and a peaceful people. Reading it feels like personally encountering the flourishing age of Tang and Yu.”
Associate Examiner Chao, Examining Editor, comments: “Classically grounded and dignified, without frivolity; it can serve as a model.”
Associate Examiner Pan, Compiler, comments: “Clear, polished, and classically elegant; it should be recorded as a model.”
Associate Examiner Guo, Expositor, comments: “Concise in wording and refined in meaning—an outstanding composition.”
Examiner Zhang, Academician, comments: “It describes almost exhaustively the flourishing government and transforming influence of Tang and Yu.”
Examiner Sun, Academician, comments: “Even and fluent, clear and apt.”

The worthy king cites the flourishing government and transforming influence of the age of the sages to show the excellence of establishing offices. Establishing offices is the means of seeking good government. In the age of the sages, governmental affairs were harmonious and the people were at peace; thus government and its transforming influence reached their utmost…

text:
隆矣非建官得人抑何以致是哉成王訓官首
舉此以為言意蓋曰唐虞之建官也百揆四岳
總於内矣州牧侯伯總於外矣則體統之不紊
治効不因之而可見乎是故推行于天下有庶
政也官使失敘政斯龐矣夫惟建官之有要也
則德業成于明良之會而事功奮于俊乂之登
以庶績則咸熈而之綱之紀當其可而不乖也
以九功則惟敘而有倫有要順其軌而不亂也
蓋官緣政而立則政以官而乂巨細畢舉曾有
===

職民斯艱矣夫惟建官之有要也則政敷于庶
明之勵翼澤究于羣后之恊心言乎黎民則於

生養遂而倫理明也蓋官為民而設則民以官
而安遠近丕式曾有一夫之不獲哉是則觀治
化之隆可以見聖世建官之効即建官之効可
以徵聖世立制之善成王舉是以訓官可謂深

punctuated: 隆矣，非建官得人，抑何以致是哉？成王訓官，首舉此以為言，意蓋曰：唐虞之建官也，百揆四岳總於内矣，州牧侯伯總於外矣，則體統之不紊，治効不因之而可見乎？是故推行于天下，有庶政也。官使失敘，政斯龐矣。夫惟建官之有要也，則德業成于明良之會，而事功奮于俊乂之登。以庶績則咸熈，而之綱之紀，當其可而不乖也；以九功則惟敘，而有倫有要，順其軌而不亂也。蓋官緣政而立，則政以官而乂，巨細畢舉，曾有一事之弗理哉？布列于天下，有萬國也。官守失職，民斯艱矣。夫惟建官之有要也，則政敷于庶明之勵翼，澤究于羣后之恊心。言乎黎民，則於變矣，道德一而風俗同也；言乎四方，則風動矣，生養遂而倫理明也。蓋官為民而設，則民以官而安，遠近丕式，曾有一夫之不獲哉？是則觀治化之隆，可以見聖世建官之効；即建官之効，可以徵聖世立制之善。成王舉是以訓官，可謂深知為治之體者歟！大抵帝王之制，因時損益而
translation_en:
…its highest flourishing. Had offices not been established and filled with the right men, how could this have been achieved? In instructing his officials, King Cheng began by citing this example. His meaning was, in effect: When offices were established under Tang and Yu, the Director of the Hundred Affairs and the Four Mountains coordinated affairs within the central government, while regional governors and the lords of the domains coordinated affairs outside it. With the hierarchy thus free from confusion, were not the achievements of government evident as a result?

Thus, there are the manifold affairs of government to be carried out throughout the realm. If the employment of officials loses its proper order, government becomes confused. Only because the establishment of offices had its guiding principles could virtuous accomplishments be achieved through the meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers, and practical achievements advance through the promotion of outstanding men. As for the many undertakings, all flourished: their ordering and regulation [?] were appropriate and without deviation. As for the nine accomplishments, all were properly arranged: each had its place and guiding principle, following its proper course without disorder. Offices are established to meet the needs of government, and government is consequently brought into order through officials. Matters great and small were all attended to: was there even a single affair left unmanaged?

There are the myriad states arrayed throughout the realm. If officials fail in their responsibilities, the people suffer hardship. Only because the establishment of offices had its guiding principles could government be extended through the diligent assistance of the many enlightened men, and its beneficence reach everywhere through the united efforts of the assembled lords. Speaking of the common people, they were transformed: moral principles became unified and customs became alike. Speaking of the four quarters, they responded as if moved by the wind: the people's livelihood and sustenance were secured, and the principles of human relationships made clear. Offices are established for the people, and the people consequently attain peace through officials. Those far and near alike followed the model: was there even a single person who failed to find his proper place?

Thus, by observing the flourishing of government and moral transformation, one can see the effectiveness of establishing offices in the age of the sages; and from the effectiveness of those offices, one can attest to the excellence of the institutions established in that age. In citing this to instruct his officials, King Cheng may indeed be said to have deeply understood the essential structure of good government! Generally, the institutions of emperors and kings are reduced or augmented according to the times, and …

…what matters is that they be appropriate. Thus, in establishing offices, a hundred could suffice under Tang and Yu, while twice that number could suffice under Xia and Shang: the circumstances of their times differed. Yet their effectiveness was neither greater under Tang and Yu nor less under Xia and Shang, because the Way by which they achieved good government was the same. Therefore, those who skillfully emulate antiquity follow its underlying intention; some differences in their actual arrangements are permissible. To disregard that intention and cling narrowly to its outward traces, yet seek to bring about the government of the former kings—how difficult that would be!

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
占德以成也公子之德之善斯其為治之瑞矣
乎詩人之意若曰觀化者莫先於家而稽瑞者
莫大於德吾嘗近觀公子而遠取於物矣今夫
物莫不有趾也而麟之趾則獨異焉其動也順
無胥戕也其履也和不相害也是豈其趾之獨
仁哉性成于天夫固良能之著耳夫人莫不有
子也而公之子則振振焉寬裕溫柔而宅心也
仁示人以可樂也子諒易直而居德也厚示人
以可親也抑豈公子之獨異哉性安于習夫固
===
家庭之化耳吁嗟公子之德如是而謂其瑞之
非麟可乎盖言乎其位之所在則本支雖殊皆
行有家國之寄而言乎其德之所在則繼承有
賴已具夫平治之資麟固足以徵乎治而以公
子之仁達之則奕世之人心可結也國之興固
不必外求之麟矣瑞固有以稽于麟而由公子
之厚言之則異時之國脉可培也麟之瑞已不
必遠求之郊矣是盖天地有至粹而麟得之以
為瑞者德也聖人有至教而公子化之以合瑞

punctuated: 占德以成也。公子之德之善，斯其為治之瑞矣乎！詩人之意若曰：觀化者莫先於家，而稽瑞者莫大於德。吾嘗近觀公子，而遠取於物矣。今夫物莫不有趾也，而麟之趾則獨異焉。其動也順，無胥戕也；其履也和，不相害也。是豈其趾之獨仁哉？性成于天，夫固良能之著耳。夫人莫不有子也，而公之子則振振焉。寬裕溫柔，而宅心也仁，示人以可樂也；子諒易直，而居德也厚，示人以可親也。抑豈公子之獨異哉？性安于習，夫固家庭之化耳。吁嗟！公子之德如是，而謂其瑞之非麟可乎？盖言乎其位之所在，則本支雖殊，皆行有家國之寄；而言乎其德之所在，則繼承有賴，已具夫平治之資。麟固足以徵乎治，而以公子之仁達之，則奕世之人心可結也，國之興固不必外求之麟矣。瑞固有以稽于麟，而由公子之厚言之，則異時之國脉可培也，麟之瑞已不必遠求之郊矣。是盖天地有至粹，而麟得之以為瑞者，德也；聖人有至教，而公子化之以合瑞
translation_en:
…looks to virtue as the portent of its fulfillment. Surely the goodness of the lord’s sons is an auspicious sign of good government! The poet’s meaning is as if to say: To observe moral transformation, one must begin with the family; to assess auspicious signs, nothing matters more than virtue. I have observed the lord’s sons close at hand and sought comparisons among creatures farther afield. Now, creatures all have feet, but the feet of the qilin are uniquely different. Its movements are gentle, causing no mutual injury; its tread is harmonious, causing no mutual harm. Is it only its feet that are benevolent? Its nature is formed by Heaven: this is simply the manifestation of its innate capacities. People all have sons, but the lord’s sons are benevolent and sincere. Generous, gentle, and mild, they harbor benevolence in their hearts and show themselves worthy of affection. Loving, trustworthy, straightforward, and upright, they are substantial in virtue and show themselves approachable. Yet is this because the lord’s sons alone are exceptional? Their nature becomes settled through habitual practice: this is simply the transforming influence of the household. Ah! With virtue such as theirs, can one say that the auspicious sign they present is unlike the qilin?

For, speaking of their position, although the main and collateral branches differ, all will in due course be entrusted with households and states. Speaking of their virtue, the succession has something upon which to rely: they already possess the qualities needed to bring peace and order. The qilin can indeed attest to good government; yet if the benevolence of the lord’s sons is extended, the people’s hearts can be bound to the dynasty for generations. The state’s rise need not depend on seeking a qilin elsewhere. Auspiciousness can indeed be assessed by the qilin; yet, considering the substantial virtue of the lord’s sons, the state’s vitality can be nurtured for ages to come. There is thus no need to seek the qilin’s auspicious sign far away in the outskirts. For Heaven and Earth possess an utmost purity, and what the qilin receives from this to become an auspicious sign is virtue. The sage possesses the highest teaching, and the lord’s sons are transformed by it so as to match the auspiciousness…

translation_en:
…in matching the qilin as an auspicious sign is likewise virtue. Why, then, be constrained by distinctions of kind? In general, moral transformation begins within the family, but its consummation extends throughout the world. The virtue of King Wen and his consort reaching their sons certainly reveals the beginnings of kingly transformation. When princely sons are auspicious like the qilin, is this not sufficient to attest to the consummation of the kingly Way? Those who call this a response to “Guan-guan Cry the Ospreys” (Guanju) speak truly. Thereafter, there were successors to his enterprise such as King Wu, men of perfected virtue such as Dan, and the protective bulwarks of Cheng, Huo, Lu, Wei, Gao, Yong, Cao, and Teng. They ultimately achieved the good government celebrated in “Wild Ducks” (Fuyi) and prolonged the dynasty’s blessed tenure beyond its allotted span. Did the qilin of which the poet spoke not thus find confirmation? Therefore, those who long for the good government of “Wild Ducks” should seek it in “The Feet of the Qilin” (Linzhi); those who long for the auspicious signs of “The Feet of the Qilin” should begin with “Guan-guan Cry the Ospreys.”
Heaven protects and establishes you, granting you abundant blessings. Nothing fails to prosper; you receive Heaven’s hundred blessings. It sends down enduring good fortune upon you, as though the days were insufficient.
Ye Yinglin.

A minister wishes that his ruler may receive Heaven’s blessings in their fullness, and that Heaven may bestow them yet again.
How profound was the Zhou people’s love for their ruler! They wished him the full measure of blessings and especially desired that Heaven should renew its gifts. How utterly devoted were their sentiments! “Heaven Protects You” (Tian bao) expresses the subjects’ response to their ruler, as though saying: It is the sovereign who serves Heaven, and Heaven that cherishes virtue. In protecting and securing our ruler, does Heaven merely make its favors abundant and increase them manifold? I know that its loving intent is manifest as it looks down from above, and its benevolence in bestowing gifts is revealed in the ruler’s conduct of affairs. His thoughts seem guided, his actions assisted; all his undertakings flourish. Thus he can establish the sovereign’s supreme standard, and every affair necessarily attains complete goodness. What he embodies is trustworthy, and what he carries into effect accords with the proper order. All the institutions of government are harmonized. Thus he can accord with the sense of right in people’s hearts, and none of his actions is inappropriate. This is indeed the abiding foundation by which his luminous virtue reaches Heaven and wins its favor; the blessings that gather enable him auspiciously to receive the Supreme Lord’s gracious regard.
Yet Heaven’s dealings with the ruler do not stop there. Its favor and mandate are at their height, and it constantly cherishes and sustains him without cease. Heaven’s blessings arrive in increasing abundance, renewing its boundless gifts. There is plenitude, and there is also daily renewal. In all that Heaven bestows upon him as goodness to establish a flourishing and illustrious reign, each day reveals blessings more than sufficient. How could one say that this prosperity belongs only to the present? It can be great, and it can also endure. In all the ways Heaven brings him into accord with what is fitting, thereby creating a radiant and harmonious government, people feel only that the days are insufficient to enjoy it. How could…

日不繼於後耶？是則既善其始，而人之所以受於天者備矣；復厚其終，而天之所以降於人者久矣。保定之意，斯其至乎！抑「昭受上帝，天其申命用休」，禹之謨盖幾康弼直之應也，而詩人以托之天，何也？盖戩穀罄宜，臣子陳善之敬，而詞曰「天保」，亦欲其緣天而求之人耳。不然，則棄其在我，慮非善，動斯何以宜？而一善自挾，非吉人惟日不足之心，則亦何以祈天而永命乎？故吾於此知德福之相須，而又知古人之善頌禱類如此。

translation_en:
…would it not continue into the future [?]? Thus, when the beginning has been made good, all that enables a person to receive from Heaven is complete; when the end is further enriched, what Heaven bestows upon that person endures. Is this not the fullest expression of preserving and securing him? Yet consider: “Gloriously receive the favor of the Lord on High; Heaven will renew its mandate with blessings.” These words in the Counsels of Yu presumably describe the response to efforts toward peace and upright assistance [?]. Why, then, does the poet attribute this to Heaven? Exhaustive blessings and complete fittingness express the reverence with which ministers and sons set forth what is good. Yet the poem says, “Heaven preserves you,” also intending that one should follow Heaven back to seek the cause in human conduct. Otherwise, if one abandons what lies within oneself and one’s deliberations are not good, how can one’s actions be fitting? And if one prides oneself on a single good deed, lacking the disposition of the good person who finds each day insufficient for doing good, how can one pray to Heaven and perpetuate the mandate? From this I understand that virtue and blessings depend upon one another, and also that the ancients’ skill in composing praises and prayers generally took this form.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The duke joined men of Qi and men of Song in relieving Zheng.” Twenty-eighth year of Duke Zhuang.

Yang Shoulu.

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
春秋善霸者節兵恤患而安攘之事見矣此齊
桓救鄭制楚之始春秋予之幸中國之有霸也
自昔子元謀先於窺鄭假意於襲讎而鄭自此
受伐使桓非主霸則楚孰與却鄭將焉依幸而
齊桓始霸志圖安攘思楚之當制也而門庭之
冦是禦懷鄭之始附也而簡書之義是勤師非
厚集不恃衆以為武而折楚勢以先聲義存拯
溺首同盟以從事而紓鄭患於已困使純門之
師夜遁而楚幕已遷桐丘之奔得免而鄭懸以
===
解則所以消楚人之雄視以遺鄭人之安者桓
其有功哉噫內政作而軍制明桓之所以經營
於國者凡以制楚也此其見之行事乎他日陘
亭召陵之役繼此而為之者也兩鄄會而人心
屬列國之所以推戴齊桓者恃以安靖也此其
驗諸霸事乎他日兵車衣裳之會由此而為之
者也不然則外無以攘內無以安而何取於宗
齊哉故書救鄭者善之也其稱人者將卑師少
也先齊於宋者以主兵也而桓公攘夷狄安中
