《春秋》善霸者節兵恤患，而安攘之事見矣。此齊桓救鄭制楚之始，《春秋》予之，幸中國之有霸也。自昔子元謀先於窺鄭，假意於襲讎，而鄭自此受伐。使桓非主霸，則楚孰與却，鄭將焉依？幸而齊桓始霸，志圖安攘，思楚之當制也，而門庭之冦是禦；懷鄭之始附也，而簡書之義是勤。師非厚集，不恃衆以為武，而折楚勢以先聲；義存拯溺，首同盟以從事，而紓鄭患於已困。使純門之師夜遁，而楚幕已遷；桐丘之奔得免，而鄭懸以解。則所以消楚人之雄視，以遺鄭人之安者，桓其有功哉！
噫！內政作而軍制明，桓之所以經營於國者，凡以制楚也，此其見之行事乎？他日陘亭、召陵之役，繼此而為之者也。兩鄄會而人心屬，列國之所以推戴齊桓者，恃以安靖也，此其驗諸霸事乎？他日兵車、衣裳之會，由此而為之者也。不然，則外無以攘，內無以安，而何取於宗齊哉？故書救鄭者，善之也。其稱人者，將卑師少也。先齊於宋者，以主兵也。而桓公攘夷狄、安中
translation_en:
The Spring and Autumn Annals approves of a hegemon who exercises restraint in deploying troops and brings relief to those in distress; here his work of securing the states within and repelling threats from without becomes apparent. This was the beginning of Duke Huan of Qi’s efforts to rescue Zheng and check Chu. The Spring and Autumn Annals commends him, deeming it fortunate that the central states had a hegemon. Earlier, Ziyuan’s designs had first been directed toward Zheng, under the pretext of attacking an enemy, and Zheng consequently suffered invasion. Had Duke Huan not assumed leadership as hegemon, who would have repelled Chu, and to whom could Zheng have turned? Fortunately, Duke Huan of Qi was beginning his hegemony and aspired to secure the states within and repel threats from without. Mindful that Chu must be checked, he resisted the invaders at the very gates; concerned for Zheng, which had only just pledged allegiance, he diligently fulfilled the obligations conveyed in the written summons for aid. His army was no great concentration of troops: he did not rely on numbers for military strength, but broke Chu’s momentum through the advance report of his approach. His righteous purpose was to rescue those drowning in distress: he led his fellow covenant members into action and relieved Zheng’s troubles when it was already hard pressed. He caused the army at Chunmen to flee by night, with Chu’s tents already removed; flight to Tongqiu was averted, and Zheng was delivered from its agonizing predicament. In quelling Chu’s overbearing ambitions and securing peace for the people of Zheng, did Duke Huan not render a great service!
Ah! Domestic administration was established and the military organization made clear: all that Duke Huan undertook within his state was directed toward checking Chu. Was this not its manifestation in action? The later campaigns at Xingting and Shaoling followed upon this undertaking. With the two meetings at Juan, the hearts of the people turned toward him. The various states acclaimed Duke Huan of Qi because they relied on him to secure peace. Was this not borne out in his conduct as hegemon? The later assemblies of war chariots and of rulers in ceremonial robes arose from this beginning. Otherwise, if he could neither repel threats from without nor secure peace within, what reason would there have been to acknowledge Qi’s leadership? Thus, the record’s wording, “rescued Zheng,” expresses approval. Its designation of the participants as “men” indicates that their commanders were of low rank and their forces small. title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
國之事見矣是則桓之救鄭以制楚也制楚以
安鄭一鄭安而諸夏有賴矣桓之功可少哉雖
然可幸也猶可慮也何也蓋楚之禍蔓延上國
微桓則江漢諸姬盡之矣然王迹熄而霸興夷
之所以乘夏也故齊桓始霸而楚亦浸強終春
秋之世五霸迭興而楚常與中國抗衡固天下
之大勢也故曰五霸齊桓為盛而又曰三王罪

國之事見矣。是則桓之救鄭，以制楚也；制楚以安鄭，一鄭安而諸夏有賴矣。桓之功可少哉？雖然，可幸也，猶可慮也。何也？蓋楚之禍蔓延上國，微桓則江漢諸姬盡之矣。然王迹熄而霸興，夷之所以乘夏也。故齊桓始霸，而楚亦浸強。終春秋之世，五霸迭興，而楚常與中國抗衡，固天下之大勢也。故曰：「五霸齊桓為盛。」而又曰：「三王罪人。」蓋微意也。

translation_en:
…the central states thus becomes apparent. Duke Huan’s rescue of Zheng was therefore intended to check Chu; checking Chu would secure Zheng, and with Zheng alone secured, all the Xia states had something on which to rely. Could Duke Huan’s achievement be considered small? Nevertheless, while there was cause for relief, there was still cause for concern. Why? Chu’s depredations were spreading through the central states. Without Duke Huan, the Ji-surnamed states along the Jiang and Han rivers would all have been extinguished. Yet the disappearance of the royal legacy and the rise of hegemonic power were what enabled the Yi to encroach upon the Xia. Thus, as Duke Huan of Qi first established his hegemony, Chu too gradually grew strong. Throughout the Spring and Autumn period, the Five Hegemons arose in succession, yet Chu continually rivaled the central states: this was indeed the prevailing configuration of power in the realm. Hence the saying, “Among the Five Hegemons, Duke Huan of Qi was the greatest,” but also, “Offenders against the Three Kings.” There is a subtle meaning here.
Jisun Su met with the Marquis of Jin, the Earl of Zheng, and men of Qi, Song, Wei, and Zhu at Xingqiu. 〔Eighth year of Duke Xiang〕 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the xinsi day, Bao joined the great officers of the feudal lords in making a covenant at Song. 〔Twenty-seventh year of Duke Xiang〕
Peng Fan

text:
之大故也聖人能不為世道慮乎且邢丘之會
晉悼修文襄之業改命朝聘之數使諸侯之大
夫聽命焉孰不曰儉而有禮眾之所安也豈知
君臣之分等於冠屨而政柄不可一日下移也
况伯命維新又列國所由以一觀聽者乃曰重
煩諸侯而使大夫是使列國之君不自為政而
國之利器舉以示人矣則凡居然在會者得自
列於五等之尊而積微以著又安知有君耶後
此溴梁之會諸侯皆在而大夫獨盟禮樂征伐
===
不自諸侯而政自大夫出矣謂非此會為之作
俑乎故大夫稱人貶之也宋之盟向戌倡弭兵
之說子木起凌駕之謀使晉楚之從交見焉孰
不曰務德無爭盟之善者也豈知華夷之辨嚴
於否泰而大防不可一日决也况楚氛益熾又
中國所視以為向背者乃曰狎主夏盟而與同
好是使蠻夷之君爭長先歃而國之冠裳儕於
異類矣則凡俛焉從事者皆知有兩大之勢而
末流一逞又安知有伯耶後此于申之會大合

之大故也。聖人能不為世道慮乎？且邢丘之會，晉悼修文襄之業，改命朝聘之數，使諸侯之大夫聽命焉。孰不曰儉而有禮，眾之所安也？豈知君臣之分等於冠屨，而政柄不可一日下移也？况伯命維新，又列國所由以一觀聽者，乃曰重煩諸侯而使大夫，是使列國之君不自為政，而國之利器舉以示人矣。則凡居然在會者，得自列於五等之尊，而積微以著，又安知有君耶？後此溴梁之會，諸侯皆在而大夫獨盟，禮樂征伐不自諸侯，而政自大夫出矣。謂非此會為之作俑乎？故大夫稱人，貶之也。

宋之盟，向戌倡弭兵之說，子木起凌駕之謀，使晉楚之從交見焉。孰不曰務德無爭，盟之善者也？豈知華夷之辨嚴於否泰，而大防不可一日决也？况楚氛益熾，又中國所視以為向背者，乃曰狎主夏盟而與同好，是使蠻夷之君爭長先歃，而國之冠裳儕於異類矣。則凡俛焉從事者，皆知有兩大之勢，而末流一逞，又安知有伯耶？後此于申之會，大合
translation_en:
…the momentous issues involved. Could the Sage fail to be concerned for the course of the world? At the meeting at Xingqiu, Duke Dao of Jin carried forward the accomplishments of Dukes Wen and Xiang, issued revised commands concerning the frequency of court visits and diplomatic missions, and had the grandees of the regional lords receive his orders. Who would not call this economical yet ritually proper, an arrangement acceptable to all? Yet how could they realize that the distinction between ruler and minister is like that between cap and shoes, and that the control of government must not pass downward for even a day? Moreover, the hegemon’s mandate had just been renewed: this was an occasion on which the various states would take their common bearings. Yet he declared that he was reluctant to trouble the regional lords and had them send their grandees instead. This caused the rulers of the various states to cease conducting government themselves and exposed to others the potent instruments of state. Thus all those grandees who sat complacently at the meeting could rank themselves among the honored holders of the five noble ranks. As small encroachments accumulated into manifest usurpation, how could they any longer recognize their rulers? Subsequently, at the meeting at Juliang, the regional lords were all present, but the grandees alone entered into the covenant. Rites, music, punitive expeditions, and warfare no longer proceeded from the regional lords; government issued from the grandees. Can one say that the earlier meeting did not set this precedent? Thus the grandees are designated merely as “men”: this disparages them.

At the covenant at Song, Xiang Xu advocated the cessation of warfare, while Zimu devised a plan to gain ascendancy, requiring the adherents of Jin and Chu to pay visits to both powers. Who would not say that this was a good covenant, devoted to virtue and free of contention? Yet how could they realize that the distinction between the Chinese and the barbarians must be guarded as strictly as that between Obstruction and Peace, and that this great barrier must not be breached for even a day? Moreover, Chu’s threatening power was growing ever stronger, and the central states looked to this occasion to decide their allegiance. Yet it was proposed that Jin and Chu should preside alternately over the covenants of the Xia states and share in friendly relations. This allowed a barbarian ruler to contend for precedence and be first to smear his lips with sacrificial blood, placing the capped and robed dignitaries of the states on a level with those of an alien kind. Thus all who bowed submissively to the arrangement recognized the power of two great states. Once its eventual consequences ran unchecked, how could they any longer recognize a hegemon? 諸侯而列卿獻禮伐吳滅賴雄長天下而霸不
自中國出矣謂非此盟為之濫觴乎故再言宋
者貶之也噫一會盟之間而君臣強弱夷夏盛

translation_en:
…the regional lords, while the ranked ministers presented ceremonial offerings. Chu attacked Wu and destroyed Lai, asserting supremacy throughout the realm; hegemony no longer arose from the Central States. Can one deny that this covenant was its fountainhead? Thus, the repeated mention of Song expresses condemnation. Alas! Within a single covenant meeting lay the turning points determining the strength and weakness of rulers and ministers and the flourishing and decline of the barbarians and the Xia. When the Sage edited the Classic, he could not but grieve deeply at this point.

Yet when Duke Dao held the hegemony, Wei Jiang and Zhi Ying gave him substantial assistance. Thus the achievement of the three campaigns lay in restraining Chu. At the meeting at Xingqiu, his government practiced accommodation: could he really have been remiss in caring for those within his own domain? Duke Ping’s achievements fell short of Duke Dao’s, while Zhao Wu and the others shortsightedly attended only to the immediate moment, hoping for a precarious peace. They consequently allowed the barbarians to preside over the covenants, and from this time Jin could no longer lead the regional lords. Hence the saying: “The covenant at Song was the consequence of Zhao Wu’s laxity.”

Book of Rites
“The Son of Heaven takes virtue as his carriage and music as his charioteer; the regional lords associate with one another through ritual propriety; the grandees order their ranks by established rules; the servicemen assess one another through trustworthiness; and the common people sustain one another through harmony. This is the flourishing of all under Heaven.”
Hu Zhengmeng

text:
考試官學士孫批〔辭氣典雅〕
上下各由於道治之至盛也蓋天下之治本於
道也天子脩道於上而臣民率道於下其盛治
何以加哉此之謂天下之大順也且夫自其情
而精之者德也自其身而推之者順也以德而
達之順豈惟家國之肥已乎即天下言之天子
為天下尊百官萬民所仰望而率由焉者也今
則仁義端儀刑之本而其體也正凡以持載四
海者皆德之用也德非車乎温文豫推行之利
===
而其動也和凡以統馭萬事者皆樂之理也樂
非御乎由是而諸侯朝聘有時盡其禮而不敢
失焉由是而大夫上下有分遵其法而不敢踰
焉忠信行於庶士而相要以有成者皆持循乎
此者也和睦行於百姓而相守以不變者皆敦
篤乎此者也此則為分不同同歸於道為道不
同同歸於治實理有以萃其渙而君臣上下皆
聯屬於一身大化有以統其同而元氣精神自
充滿於天下以一人和於朝也以眾人和於家

Examiner Sun, Academician, comments: 〔The diction and tone are refined and elegant.〕

When those above and below each follow the Way, government reaches its greatest flourishing. For the governance of all under Heaven is rooted in the Way. When the Son of Heaven cultivates the Way above and his subjects follow it below, how could such flourishing government be surpassed? This is what is called the great concord of all under Heaven. Now, to refine one’s feelings is virtue; to extend outward from one’s own person is concord. By means of virtue, one attains concord: could the resulting flourishing be confined to the family and the state? Consider all under Heaven. The Son of Heaven occupies its most honored position; the hundred officials and the myriad people look up to him and follow his example. Now benevolence and righteousness rectify the foundation of his exemplary conduct, and his essential constitution is upright. All that sustains and bears up the realm is the working of virtue. Is virtue not his carriage? Gentleness, refinement, and joyful ease facilitate its implementation [?], and his actions are harmonious. All that governs and directs the myriad affairs accords with the principles of music. Is music not his charioteer?

Thus the feudal lords hold court audiences and exchange missions at their appointed times, fulfilling their ritual obligations without daring to neglect them. Thus the great officers observe distinctions between higher and lower ranks, obeying their rules without daring to transgress them. Loyalty and trustworthiness prevail among the many gentlemen, who hold one another to their commitments and bring them to fulfillment: all adhere to this. Harmony and amity prevail among the common people, who sustain one another without wavering: all earnestly uphold this.

Their allotted roles differ, yet all converge upon the Way; their ways of proceeding differ, yet all converge upon good government. Substantive principle gathers together what is dispersed, so that ruler and ministers, high and low, are joined as one body. The great transforming influence unifies what they share, so that primal vitality and spiritual energy naturally fill all under Heaven. Through the one man there is harmony at court; through the multitude there is harmony within families …

text:
禮樂通乎造化則精粗之體備矣而人道因以
統於是其用顧不大哉今夫窮本知變著誠去
僞固知禮樂之可以治情也而不知其體之所
由來者大矣彼天地之情貞觀而不忒禮樂則
以俲焉象其質而具故有秩也象其氣而作故
不乖也效法有定而動靜之道形矣神明之德
微妙而難求禮樂為能達焉主於辨者通乎其
散殊也主於和者通乎其合同也機緘相孚而
仁義之理著矣夫其氣之屈而具於地神之下
===

者氣之伸而行於天神之上也惟樂俲而達之
以率乎神若有抑之而使降者則禮樂不專於
器也而包含者已運乎天地之精天地不秘其
道也而流行者皆寓於象數之末其疑是精粗

乎父子焉愛不至於流而以天屬者固由之以

Through them, the human Way is brought into unity: is their efficacy not indeed great? Now, by tracing things to their roots and understanding change, making sincerity manifest and eliminating falsity, one certainly recognizes that ritual and music can govern the emotions. Yet one fails to recognize the greatness of the source from which their substance derives. The true workings of Heaven and Earth display constancy without deviation, and ritual and music take them as their model. Ritual takes form by imitating their substance and therefore possesses order; music arises by imitating their vital energy and therefore is free of discord. With established models to follow, the Way of movement and stillness takes shape. The potency of spiritual illumination is subtle and difficult to fathom, yet ritual and music can give it expression. That which chiefly distinguishes accords with its differentiation into separate forms; that which chiefly harmonizes accords with its coming together in unity. Their inner workings correspond, and the principles of benevolence and righteousness become manifest. When vital energy contracts and takes form below, among the spirits of Earth, ritual alone models and gives expression to it, providing a dwelling for the departed spirits, as though stirring them and causing them to rise. When vital energy expands and moves above, among the spirits of Heaven, music alone models and gives expression to it, leading the spirits, as though pressing them down and causing them to descend. Thus ritual and music are not confined to material implements: what they encompass already sets in motion the essence of Heaven and Earth. Nor do Heaven and Earth conceal their Way: all that flows forth from them is lodged in the outward particulars of images and numbers. Is this perhaps the substance in both its subtle and its gross aspects [?]? Thus ritual and music bring their entirety into play, exercising their functions of unifying what is alike and distinguishing what differs. Hence the ordering of human relationships extends throughout its full scope, while the regulated expressions of utmost affection and utmost reverence do not exceed their proper bounds. …those joined through human relationships likewise rely on it to set their respective ranks aright. Thus, by observing the relationships they govern, one can understand the functions of ritual and music. How could the claim that these are made manifest and removed [?], and understood by exhaustive inquiry, be false? Yet the functions of ritual and music are vast. Carried to their fullest extent, they unite all within the seas, regulate the myriad affairs, and bring the people into affectionate accord. How could their scope be measured? All the more naturally do they govern the relationships between father and son, ruler and minister. If one can take reverence as the guiding principle to embody their order, and discern unity to establish their harmony, then ground oneself in Heaven and Earth to perfect their institutions, one can employ ritual and music well. If one does not understand their essential nature but seeks them merely in sounds and ceremonial observances, it is no wonder that harmony and order become obscured and the way of human relationships readily falls into decay. What fault lies with ritual and music? Thus the gentleman must exercise care.

text:
出詞亦古雅其深造而有得者歟允宜首薦
考試官學士張批就題立論而切近精實意自
無窮錄此將以變天下文之不根於理者
考試官學士孫批講聖人合天道處極精切且
文勢開闔辭氣高古真大手筆也是豈淺學可到哉
天人之際其性命之原也察於性命之辨而後
可與語天人之道矣夫原於天者之謂命賦於
人者之謂性性與命一也其有不同者在天在
人之分也聖人之與眾人亦一也而有不同者
===
其所以察於性命之辨者之異也天能以其性
命于人而不能使人之必盡其性聖人能以其
性合於天而天不能以其命私於聖人此性命
之辨也孟子曰聖人之於天道命也有性焉君
子不謂命也夫聖人亦豈能外天之命以為性
也而必曰不謂命者聖人盡其性而不委於命
之謂也今夫天以陰陽五行化生萬物其流行
賦予莫不有命也人函天地之氣以生降衷秉
彞亦莫不有性也惟莫不有命也是故仁之於

The juncture of Heaven and humanity is the source of human nature and Heaven’s decree. Only after discerning the distinction between nature and decree can one be engaged in discussion of the Way of Heaven and humanity. What originates in Heaven is called decree; what is endowed in human beings is called nature. Nature and decree are one. Any difference between them lies in the distinction between their residing in Heaven and in human beings. Sages and ordinary people are likewise one; any difference between them lies in how they discern the distinction between nature and decree. Heaven can confer its nature upon human beings, but cannot ensure that they fully realize their nature. The sage can bring his nature into accord with Heaven, but Heaven cannot favor the sage with its decree. This is the distinction between nature and decree. Mencius says: “The sage’s relation to the Way of Heaven is a matter of decree, yet nature is involved; the gentleman does not call it decree.” Could the sage establish his nature apart from Heaven’s decree? The insistence on saying that he “does not call it decree” means that the sage fully realizes his nature rather than leaving matters to decree. title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
父子也義之於君臣也禮之於賓主也知之於
賢否也一也無有乎弗具無有乎弗同無有乎
或擇於人者也惟莫不有性也是故父子之仁
也君臣之義也賓主之禮也賢否之知也一也
所不慮而知所不學而能所不能解於其心者
也天無所擇於人也而或有弗存焉有弗同焉
人所不能解於其心也而或有不知不能焉非
性命之殊者然也不知盡其性之在我而徒委
之天者衆人也聖人則以其性之在我者而盡
===
由之而命不與焉是故與衆人異也惟衆人不
知其性之在我而弗之盡也是故於父子而仁
之有弗至焉於君臣而義之有弗盡焉於賓主
而禮之有弗恭焉於賢否而知之有弗哲焉惟
聖人以其性之在我而盡由之也是故均仁也
而父子之相愛者無弗至也均義也而君臣之
相與者無弗盡也均禮也而賓主之相接者無
弗恭也均知也而賢否之相知者無弗哲也人
見其仁之無弗至也義之無弗盡也禮知之無

父子也，義之於君臣也，禮之於賓主也，知之於賢否也，一也，無有乎弗具，無有乎弗同，無有乎或擇於人者也。惟莫不有性也，是故父子之仁也，君臣之義也，賓主之禮也，賢否之知也，一也，所不慮而知，所不學而能，所不能解於其心者也。天無所擇於人也，而或有弗存焉，有弗同焉；人所不能解於其心也，而或有不知不能焉，非性命之殊者然也。不知盡其性之在我而徒委之天者，衆人也；聖人則以其性之在我者而盡由之，而命不與焉，是故與衆人異也。

惟衆人不知其性之在我而弗之盡也，是故於父子而仁之有弗至焉，於君臣而義之有弗盡焉，於賓主而禮之有弗恭焉，於賢否而知之有弗哲焉。惟聖人以其性之在我而盡由之也，是故均仁也，而父子之相愛者無弗至也；均義也，而君臣之相與者無弗盡也；均禮也，而賓主之相接者無弗恭也；均知也，而賢否之相知者無弗哲也。人見其仁之無弗至也，義之無弗盡也，禮知之無
translation_en:
…between father and son, righteousness between ruler and minister, ritual propriety between guest and host, and wisdom in discerning the worthy from the unworthy: these are alike in all. None lacks them, none differs in possessing them, and no preference is shown among people. Since none is without an inherent nature, benevolence between father and son, righteousness between ruler and minister, ritual propriety between guest and host, and wisdom in discerning the worthy from the unworthy are likewise common to all. These are what people know without deliberation and can do without learning, and what they cannot cast out of their hearts. Heaven shows no preference among people, yet some fail to preserve these qualities or manifest them equally. People cannot cast these qualities out of their hearts, yet some fail to know or exercise them. This is not the result of differences in their inherent nature or Heaven’s decree. Ordinary people do not understand that fulfilling their inherent nature lies within themselves, and merely leave it to Heaven. The sage, however, fully follows the inherent nature that lies within himself, without allowing Heaven’s decree to enter into the matter. Thus he differs from ordinary people.

Because ordinary people do not understand that their inherent nature lies within themselves and fail to fulfill it, their benevolence between father and son may fall short of its utmost extent; their righteousness between ruler and minister may remain unfulfilled; their ritual propriety between guest and host may lack reverence; and their wisdom in discerning the worthy from the unworthy may lack clear judgment. Because the sage fully follows the inherent nature that lies within himself, though his benevolence is the same, the mutual love between father and son invariably reaches its utmost extent; though his righteousness is the same, ruler and minister invariably fulfill their obligations to one another; though his ritual propriety is the same, guest and host invariably treat one another reverently; and though his wisdom is the same, his discernment of the worthy and unworthy invariably shows clear judgment. People see that his benevolence invariably reaches its utmost extent, that his righteousness is invariably fulfilled, and that his ritual propriety and wisdom never…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
弗恭且哲也而曰聖人之於人異也天之私于
聖人者獨厚也亦不思之甚矣夫聖人之性亦
眾人之性也其由乎父子君臣賓主賢否之類
者亦猶夫眾人也然而仁之有至弗至焉義之
有盡弗盡焉禮之有恭弗恭焉知之有哲弗哲
焉者盡性與不盡性之異也惟聖人之盡其性
也然後能以其性而盡人之性也夫盡人之性
亦聖人之所以自盡其性也何者天不能使人
必盡其性而其裁成輔相之責不能不賴於聖
===
人而聖人亦有不能辭其責於天者是故聖人
之性盡矣而人之性有未盡焉則聖人之於天
道亦容有間而聖人之性未盡也是故吾仁矣
而天下之為父子者有弗親焉則聖人之仁未
盡也吾義矣而天下之為君臣者有弗義焉則
聖人之義未盡也吾禮矣知矣而天下之為賓
主賢否者有弗恭且哲焉則聖人之禮知未盡
也聖人於是乎有敦睦之愛焉有都俞之敬焉

translation_en: …never lacking in reverence and discernment, and say: “The sage differs from other people; Heaven has shown him uniquely generous favor.” How utterly thoughtless this is! The sage’s nature is also the nature of ordinary people. His conduct in relations between fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, hosts and guests, and the worthy and unworthy is likewise that of ordinary people. Yet whether benevolence reaches its fullest extent, righteousness is fully realized, ritual propriety displays reverence, and wisdom displays discernment depends on the difference between fully realizing one’s nature and failing to do so. Only after the sage fully realizes his own nature can he, through that nature, fully realize the nature of others. Fully realizing the nature of others is also how the sage fully realizes his own nature. Why is this? Heaven cannot ensure that people fully realize their nature, and so must rely upon the sage to undertake the responsibility of shaping things to completion and assisting them. The sage, in turn, cannot decline this responsibility toward Heaven. Thus, even if the sage’s nature has been fully realized, if the nature of others remains unrealized, there may still be a gap between the sage and the Way of Heaven, and his own nature remains incompletely realized. Thus, though I am benevolent, if fathers and sons anywhere under Heaven lack affection for one another, the sage’s benevolence remains incompletely realized. Though I am righteous, if rulers and ministers anywhere under Heaven lack righteousness, the sage’s righteousness remains incompletely realized. Though I possess ritual propriety and wisdom, if hosts and guests anywhere under Heaven lack reverence, or discernment is lacking concerning the worthy and unworthy, the sage’s ritual propriety and wisdom remain incompletely realized. Accordingly, the sage displays love that strengthens harmonious relations, reverence expressed in exchanges of assent and approval, governance through □□ deference [?], and discernment in knowing people—all in order to shape things to completion and assist them…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
成己成物以求盡乎其性也求盡乎性所以求
盡乎天也至於天下之事其勢之所窮而不能
不變者聖人亦惟以性之所不變者以濟其變
是故有禪授焉有征伐焉有竊負而逃焉有四
凶之誅焉常之所在則以其性而為經變之所
在則以其性而為權然變者事也不變者性也
惟不變故能盡變不變性也盡變亦性也凡以
裁成輔相成己成物以求盡乎其性也求盡乎
性所以求盡乎天也嗚呼聖人盡性之功至此
===
而後與天道為一而命之在天者則將制而用
之而天亦不能違之矣夫聖人能制天之命而
用之而天亦不能違焉者非天不違於聖人也

…perfecting oneself and bringing other beings to fulfillment, in order to realize one’s nature fully. Seeking fully to realize one’s nature is the means of seeking fully to realize Heaven. As for affairs in the world whose circumstances reach an impasse and must change, the sage likewise uses only what is unchanging in human nature to bring those changes to a successful conclusion. Thus there is abdication and transfer of the throne; there are punitive campaigns; there is secretly carrying [one’s father] on one’s back and fleeing; and there is the punishment of the Four Evildoers. In ordinary circumstances, the sage takes his nature as the constant standard; in exceptional circumstances, he takes his nature as the basis for discretionary judgment. Yet what changes is affairs; what does not change is human nature. Precisely because it does not change, it can respond fully to change. What is unchanging is human nature; what responds fully to change is also human nature. All this serves to shape and assist the processes of Heaven and Earth, perfecting oneself and bringing other beings to fulfillment, in order to realize one’s nature fully. Seeking fully to realize one’s nature is the means of seeking fully to realize Heaven.

Ah! Only when the sage’s work of fully realizing his nature reaches this point does he become one with the Way of Heaven. He can then regulate and employ the destiny that rests with Heaven, and even Heaven cannot oppose him. Now, when the sage can regulate and employ Heaven’s decree, and even Heaven cannot oppose him, it is not that Heaven refrains from opposing the sage: it is that the sage fully realizes his Way and does not oppose Heaven. Nor is Heaven’s decree actually controlled by the sage: rather, the sage fully realizes his nature and thereby establishes Heaven’s decree. Thus, if he strengthens the foundations and is sparing in expenditure, Heaven cannot impoverish him; if provision for sustenance is complete and action is timely, Heaven cannot afflict him with sickness; if he cultivates the Way without wavering, Heaven cannot bring him harm. This is what is meant by uniting with Heaven through human effort, without leaving matters to Heaven; establishing destiny through righteousness, without surrendering to destiny. title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
奉天時天且弗違而況於人乎況於鬼神乎言
有以制之矣由是而觀則人之所以合乎天者
顧可求之乎性分之外哉昔者堯舜禹湯文武
之數聖人者其得於天命之備也而詩書所稱
則惟曰惟時惟幾曰顧諟曰純亦不已曰建其
有極噫此數聖人者之所以得乎天者也苟時
幾之不察顧諟之不常純德之或雜而皇極弗
建焉則此數聖人者亦惡在其能天哉傳曰大
天而思之孰與物畜而制之從天而頌之孰與
===
制天之命而用之盖察乎性命之辨矣雖然孟
子學於子思者也子思之言曰天命之謂性而
孟子則曰有性焉君子不謂命也何哉盖性也
命也一也子思之言性也懼人之不知其原於
天也而似是之非得以亂之故稱天焉孟子之
言性也懼人之惑於命而不知其性之在我也不
故曰君子不謂命也是故由子思之言可以知
性而幻妄之說廢矣由孟子之言可以盡性而
矯誣之論息矣聖賢之言不同而同於衛道之

奉天時，天且弗違，而況於人乎？況於鬼神乎？言有以制之矣。由是而觀，則人之所以合乎天者，顧可求之乎性分之外哉？昔者堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之數聖人者，其得於天命之備也，而詩書所稱，則惟曰「惟時惟幾」，曰「顧諟」，曰「純亦不已」，曰「建其有極」。噫！此數聖人者之所以得乎天者也。苟時幾之不察，顧諟之不常，純德之或雜，而皇極弗建焉，則此數聖人者亦惡在其能天哉？傳曰：「大天而思之，孰與物畜而制之？從天而頌之，孰與制天之命而用之？」盖察乎性命之辨矣。

雖然，孟子學於子思者也。子思之言曰：「天命之謂性。」而孟子則曰：「有性焉，君子不謂命也。」何哉？盖性也，命也，一也。子思之言性也，懼人之不知其原於天也，而似是之非得以亂之，故稱天焉。孟子之言性也，懼人之惑於命而不知其性之在我也不。故曰：「君子不謂命也。」是故由子思之言，可以知性，而幻妄之說廢矣；由孟子之言，可以盡性，而矯誣之論息矣。聖賢之言不同，而同於衛道之
translation_en:
…accord with Heaven’s seasons. If even Heaven does not oppose him, how much less will human beings, or ghosts and spirits?” This means that there is a means of directing it. Viewed in this light, could the means by which human beings accord with Heaven possibly be sought outside their allotted nature? The sages of old—Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu—fully received Heaven’s endowment. Yet what the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents praise in them is simply this: “Attend to the times and the incipient signs”; “Keep it constantly in view”; “In purity, likewise, never cease”; and “Establish the supreme standard.” Ah! These were the means by which those sages attained accord with Heaven. Had they failed to discern the times and incipient signs, failed to maintain constant watchfulness, allowed their pure virtue to become mixed, or failed to establish the august standard, wherein could even these sages have shown their capacity to accord with Heaven? The transmitted text says: “Rather than exalt Heaven and ponder it, would it not be better to nurture it as a thing and direct it? Rather than follow Heaven and praise it, would it not be better to direct Heaven’s mandate and put it to use?” This surely shows discernment of the distinction between nature and destiny.

Nevertheless, Mengzi studied under Zisi. Zisi said, “What Heaven ordains is called nature,” whereas Mengzi said, “Nature is involved in these things, but the gentleman does not call them destiny.” Why is this? Nature and destiny are one. In speaking of nature, Zisi feared that people would not understand its origin in Heaven, allowing plausible falsehoods to confuse it; hence he invoked Heaven. In speaking of nature, Mengzi feared that people would become confused about destiny and fail to understand that their nature lies within themselves [?]. Hence he said, “The gentleman does not call them destiny.” Thus, through Zisi’s words one can understand nature, and fanciful, delusive teachings are rejected; through Mengzi’s words one can fully realize one’s nature, and misleading, false arguments are silenced. The words of sages and worthies differ, yet they are alike in their intention to defend the Way…

…as minister during the restoration, also submitted itemized reports on troops and provisions along the frontiers. Pei Yanling served as Salt and Finance Commissioner, yet no one could ascertain the purported surpluses; Li Jifu compiled the Record of the Yuanhe Era, encompassing matters great and small. In our dynasty, during the Jingde and Huangyou eras and down through the Zhiping and Xining eras, records were invariably kept to regulate state finances. Spanning more than eighty years from beginning to end, these sometimes enable us, living in the present, to understand the past. However many changes occurred in the intervening years, those who follow can rely on these records to examine similarities through differences. Yet governance has its declines and revivals, and affairs undergo many reductions and additions. Practices long observed may no longer accord with the original ordinances; what is transmitted to posterity should therefore take the form of a completed book.

I humbly reflect that I have been fortunate to serve, despite my shortcomings, in the Ministry of Revenue, and have long enjoyed imperial favor in performing my official duties. Unworthily entrusted with the great financial reckoning, I am ashamed to lack comprehensive ability. Although I have exhausted my efforts, my achievements have shown no particular distinction. I have nevertheless pursued inquiries widely, never allowing my resolve to slacken. Accordingly, I have collected old documents dating from the Yuanfeng era onward, to supplement the gaps in what Han Jiang had recorded. Through my recent examination of these materials, I have gained a thorough understanding of the precedents established by our imperial ancestors.

At the dynasty’s founding in the Jianlong era, the various circuits were divided among contending powers. 英祖懷勵精之志而大業未終
神考奮彊富之謨而新法則過善變通者隨時
而已大有爲者惟聖能之玆盖伏遇
===
恭己愛人憂民節用凡令之未便者
無不釋去於事之當急者即見舉行問疾
苦於閭閻民莫不悅賜節孝以粟帛人知
有親
德意已洽於衆心財計尚軫乎
宸慮謂冊籍浩瀚者莫能勾檢而簿書散漫者
豈免遺亡況世有遠近之殊政有弛張之
異匪加裒集曷可簡稽乃下
詔於戶曹俾增修其舊貫顧慙淺陋莫副詳延
punctuated:
咸平、景德之盛，號稱太平，而岱封郊賚之頻，類多糜費。雖仁皇以清儉息事，適西戎之竊發無時，民已疲而賦則愈繁，寇既平而兵不復汰。加以宗子蕃衍，兼之官吏冗浮，遂令費而無經，豈復生之有道？英祖懷勵精之志，而大業未終；神考奮彊富之謨，而新法貝過。善變通者，隨時而已；大有為者，惟聖能之。
兹蓋伏遇〇〇〇〇，恭已愛人，憂民節用。凡令之未便者，無不釋去；於事之當急者，即見舉行。問疾苦於閻閭，民莫不悅；賜節孝以粟帛，人知有親。德意已洽於衆心，財計尚軫乎宸慮。謂冊籍浩瀚者莫能勾檢，而簿書散漫者豈免遺亡？况世有遠近之殊，政有弛張之異，匪加裒集，曷可簡稽？乃下詔於戸曹，俾增修其舊貫。顧慙淺陋，莫副詳延。
translation_en:
…The flourishing Xianping and Jingde eras were acclaimed as an age of great peace, yet the frequent Feng sacrifices at Mount Tai and distributions of rewards at the suburban sacrifices generally entailed great extravagance. Although Emperor Renzong sought to quiet affairs through simplicity and frugality, the western Rong launched incursions at unpredictable times. The people were already exhausted, yet taxation grew ever heavier; the invaders had been pacified, yet the troops were no longer reduced. Moreover, the imperial clansmen multiplied, while officials became excessively numerous. Consequently, expenditure lacked any fixed bounds: how could there still be a proper way to generate wealth? Emperor Yingzong aspired to vigorous governance, but his great undertaking remained unfinished. Emperor Shenzong vigorously pursued plans for strength and prosperity, but his New Policies brought errors [?]. Those skilled in adapting institutions simply respond to the times; only a sage can accomplish great things.
Now we humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], who conducts himself reverently and loves others, cares for the people and economizes on expenditure. Every ordinance that proves inconvenient is abolished, and every matter requiring urgent attention is promptly undertaken. You inquire into suffering among the common people, and all are pleased; you bestow grain and silk upon those distinguished for chastity and filial piety, and people learn to cherish their parents. Your benevolent intentions have already won the hearts of the multitude, yet financial planning still weighs upon Your Majesty’s thoughts. You observe that the records are so voluminous that they cannot be checked, while registers and documents lie scattered—how could they escape loss? Moreover, periods differ in their remoteness from the present, and administration varies in its relaxation and tightening. Unless these materials are collected, how can they readily be examined? You therefore issued an edict to the revenue authorities, directing them to expand and revise the existing compilation. Yet I am ashamed of my shallow learning and cannot live up to the discerning invitation extended to me…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
屢彌歲年僅成篇帙取元豐八年之多者
為準掲司農五事之重者為綱曰收支曰
民賦部居彪列曰課入曰儲運科指昄分
他若經費之簡繁必詳出納之慎忽列以
通表總大畧於各卷之端約以成規注細
目於分條之下若夫內外之登耗法令之
峻遲以及兵食之盈虛商貨之通滯在一
時所行者粗已究其抏敝非三司所領者
乃以繫之私藏盖法久而通勢窮必極即
===
目之所覩亦心之可憂夷虜未賓金繒之
征求不絕水旱繼至田野之僵仆相仍餉
輸半藉於末鹽賑發每需於內帑四事失
理三冗莫除供額歲益加多財用日惟不
足膏脂之朘削易竭元氣之虛憊難培中
原之瘡痏靡甦萑苻之逋亡可慮自非得
更化之善何以為裕後之謀顧
國之所調度者盡載此編而財之在官民者
止有此數明徵可見休戚攸關匪以徒備

punctuated:
屢彌歲年，僅成篇帙。取元豐八年之多者為準，掲司農五事之重者為綱：曰收支，曰民賦，部居彪列；曰課入，曰儲運，科指昄分。他若經費之簡繁，必詳出納之慎忽。列以通表，總大畧於各卷之端；約以成規，注細目於分條之下。若夫內外之登耗，法令之峻遲，以及兵食之盈虛，商貨之通滯，在一時所行者，粗已究其抏敝；非三司所領者，乃以繫之私藏。盖法久而通，勢窮必極，即目之所覩，亦心之可憂。
夷虜未賓，金繒之征求不絕；水旱繼至，田野之僵仆相仍。餉輸半藉於末鹽，賑發每需於內帑。四事失理，三冗莫除。供額歲益加多，財用日惟不足。膏脂之朘削易竭，元氣之虛憊難培。中原之瘡痏靡甦，萑苻之逋亡可慮。自非得更化之善，何以為裕後之謀？顧國之所調度者，盡載此編，而財之在官民者，止有此數。明徵可見，休戚攸關，匪以徒備
translation_en:
…Only after years had repeatedly passed was the work finally compiled into volumes. Taking the larger figures of the eighth year of Yuanfeng as the benchmark, we established the five principal concerns of the Court of Imperial Granaries as its organizing framework: receipts and expenditures, and taxes on the people, arranged distinctly by category; revenue collections, and storage and transport, with their categories and purport broadly distinguished [?]. As for other matters, such as the complexity or simplicity of regular expenditures, we invariably detailed the care or negligence attending receipts and disbursements. Comprehensive tables summarize the main outlines at the beginning of each volume; established rules are presented concisely, with particulars noted under individual headings. As for increases and losses within and outside the capital, the severity or laxity of laws and ordinances, the abundance or shortage of military provisions, and the free circulation or obstruction of merchandise, we have broadly investigated the depletion and deterioration arising from practices of the time. Matters outside the jurisdiction of the Three Fiscal Agencies have been appended under the privy treasury. Laws long in force undergo adaptation, and circumstances pushed to exhaustion necessarily reach their limit. What meets the eye is also cause for anxiety in the heart.
The foreign peoples have not submitted, and their demands for gold and silk never cease. Floods and droughts arrive in succession, and people continually collapse in the fields. Deliveries of military provisions depend in large part on salt commerce [?], while relief disbursements repeatedly require funds from the inner treasury. The four affairs are mismanaged, and the three forms of redundancy remain uneliminated. Required contributions grow greater each year, while available funds become daily less adequate. The people's substance, whittled away by exactions, is easily exhausted; their depleted vitality is difficult to restore. The wounds of the Central Plain have not healed, and fugitives taking refuge among brigands are a cause for concern. Unless sound reforms can be achieved, how can we devise a plan to leave ample resources to posterity? All that the state allocates and disburses is recorded in this compilation, yet the wealth held by officials and people amounts only to these sums. The clear evidence is there to see, and well-being and distress hinge upon it. This is not merely intended to furnish…

translation_en:
…regulations, but also to assist in governance. I humbly hope that Your Majesty will read it during the second watch of the night, taking warning from past events; if its measures are put into practice for several years, beneficial results may perhaps be expected. Examine where imbalances and abuses lie, so as to devise remedies; judge the relative urgency of affairs, so as to determine the order in which measures should be undertaken. From the court throughout the realm, from the palace to the government offices, let all observe frugality to curb extravagance: poverty may then be transformed into wealth. Below, this will secure the livelihood of the common people throughout the ordered realm; above, it will prolong without limit the blessings of the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain. Your servant, gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your sagely Majesty, is overcome with fervent feeling and trembling awe. I respectfully submit this memorial together with the accompanying work for Your Majesty’s attention.

皇上大孝之至、獨得之見，遠符武王。子能鋪張揚厲之，其亦善鳴國家之盛者乎！

同考試官檢討王批：我皇上明堂大典，上媲成周，真曠世之舉。子能敷揚盛美，而於我皇考佑啓之仁、皇上繼述之孝，條叙明切，可以使天下誦而傳之。多士之良也，是宜首擢。

同考試官編修高批：我皇上肇舉明堂大典，媲美成周，此作揄揚殆盡。子其式觀聖制而能言其大者與！

同考試官編修趙批：述時稱二義，以揄揚我皇上推天崇親、與有周並美之極，非近代儒者之論可及。佳士！佳士！

考試官學士張批：宗祀明堂，乃武王、周公義起之禮，以尊文王者。孔子於《孝經》特發明之，後儒率不知此，漫無定說。我
translation_en:
…His Majesty’s utmost filial devotion and uniquely attained insight accord with King Wu across the ages. You have elaborated upon and glorified these qualities: are you not one who ably proclaims the flourishing of the state?

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Examining Editor: His Majesty’s great ceremony in the Hall of Light rivals that of the Zhou at its height—a truly unparalleled undertaking. You have expounded its splendid virtues and clearly and precisely set forth the benevolence of our late imperial father in protecting and guiding his successor, and His Majesty’s filial devotion in carrying on his father’s work. This deserves to be recited and transmitted throughout the realm. You are an outstanding man among the many candidates and ought rightly to be selected first.

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Compiler: His Majesty has inaugurated the great ceremony in the Hall of Light, matching the splendor of the Zhou at its height. This composition praises it almost exhaustively. Surely you have taken the imperial writings as your model and have thus been able to express their great import!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Compiler: You expound the two principles of timeliness and fitting measure, thereby praising to the utmost His Majesty’s honoring of Heaven and exaltation of his father, achievements equal in splendor to those of the Zhou. The arguments of Confucian scholars of recent ages cannot approach this. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Comment by Examiner Zhang, Academician: The ancestral sacrifice in the Hall of Light was a rite instituted by King Wu and the Duke of Zhou on grounds of righteousness to honor King Wen. Confucius specially elucidated it in the Classic of Filial Piety. Later Confucian scholars have generally failed to understand this and have offered no settled explanation. Our…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
皇上嚴父之孝比于武王我
皇考配天之德比于文王實足當之而
或問一篇又推見大義以决千古之疑者子敷敭殆盡可稱佳士矣
考試官學士孫批
明堂大典我
皇上超出千古之見盡倫盡制比隆成周子能敬述而揚厲之蓋沐浴
聖化而有得者允稱佳士春闈首薦舍子其誰
對曰禮之興也莫貴於時莫大於稱二者
備矣是謂大順大順禮之極致也夫有天
===
下之大位者謂之時具天下之大德者謂
之稱行是二者而宜之者之謂義明其義
之盡以斷天下之疑以立萬世之典者之
謂聖數者皆備以考三王而不謬以俟百
世而不惑者之謂大順為禮之極致也是
道也有天地以来惟武王能行之惟孔子
能明之兼武王孔子之道而備美極盛孰
有過於
今日者哉我

===

之稱行是二者而宜之者之謂義明其義
之盡以斷天下之疑以立萬世之典者之
謂聖數者皆備以考三王而不謬以俟百

道也有天地以來惟武王能行之惟孔子
能明之兼武王孔子之道而備美極盛孰
有過於
今日者哉我
punctuated:
皇上嚴父之孝比于武王，我皇考配天之德比于文王，實足當之。而《或問》一篇，又推見大義，以决千古之疑者。子敷敭殆盡，可稱佳士矣。
考試官學士孫批：明堂大典，我皇上超出千古之見，盡倫盡制，比隆成周。子能敬述而揚厲之，蓋沐浴聖化而有得者，允稱佳士。春闈首薦，舍子其誰？
對曰：禮之興也，莫貴於時，莫大於稱。二者備矣，是謂大順。大順，禮之極致也。夫有天下之大位者，謂之時；具天下之大德者，謂之稱；行是二者而宜之者之謂義；明其義之盡，以斷天下之疑，以立萬世之典者之謂聖。數者皆備，以考三王而不謬，以俟百世而不惑者之謂大順，為禮之極致也。是道也，有天地以来，惟武王能行之，惟孔子能明之。兼武王、孔子之道，而備美極盛，孰有過於今日者哉？我
translation_en:
…His Majesty’s filial devotion in honoring his father compares with that of King Wu, and our deceased imperial father’s virtue, which qualifies him to be associated with Heaven in sacrifice, compares with that of King Wen. They truly merit these comparisons. Moreover, the essay Questions and Answers (Huowen) brings the great underlying principles to light, resolving doubts that have persisted through the ages. You have expounded and exalted these principles almost exhaustively and may indeed be called an outstanding scholar.

Comment by Examiner Sun, Academician: In the great ceremony of the Hall of Enlightenment, His Majesty has shown insight surpassing that of all previous ages, fulfilling human relationships and ritual institutions to the utmost and matching the glory of the accomplished Zhou. You have reverently recounted and extolled this achievement. Evidently, you have benefited from immersion in the sage ruler’s transforming influence and truly deserve to be called an outstanding scholar. Who but you should receive the first recommendation in the spring Metropolitan Examination?

In reply: In the institution of ritual, nothing is more precious than timeliness, and nothing greater than fitness. When both are present, this is called perfect accord. Perfect accord is the highest realization of ritual. To occupy the supreme position in the world is what is meant by timeliness; to possess the greatest virtue in the world is what is meant by fitness. To put these two into practice appropriately is what is meant by righteousness. Fully to illuminate this righteousness, thereby settling the doubts of the world and establishing authoritative rites for all ages, is what is meant by sageliness. When all these qualities are present, so that one may test them against the Three Kings without error and await the sages of a hundred generations hence without misgiving, this is called perfect accord, the highest realization of ritual. Since Heaven and Earth first existed, only King Wu could put this Way into practice, and only Confucius could illuminate it. In uniting the Way of King Wu and Confucius, with complete excellence and supreme splendor, what age could surpass the present? Our …

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
皇上秉生知之資撫制作之權光承
天序立天下之大位非所謂時乎我
皇考睿宗皇帝躬修德讓克配于
天聖功昭赫繫遹駿之望篤生
聖嗣啓受命之原非所謂稱乎以天下之大德
當天下之大位奉嚴父之文舉
大享之典而協乎人心當乎天理非所謂行而
宜之之義乎往者戊戌之歲大議初下羣
論籍籍禮臣皇懼莫知定擬我
===
皇上親御宸翰作為或問反覆千餘言
妙悟英斷微詞奧旨炳然懸之日月與六經昭
映信非虛矣嘗仰而誦之見其折羣疑以
孔子之言論隆祖以近親之非憲成形一
本之義準成周宗祀之典明周武君臣之
分定百世宗祧之法別祖功宗德之異凡
若此者真有以超百王之見而斷千古不決
之疑非天下之至聖其孰能與於此哉由是
大典昭於一代天下臣民曉然知

punctuated: 皇上秉生知之資，撫制作之權，光承天序，立天下之大位，非所謂時乎？我皇考睿宗皇帝躬修德讓，克配于天，聖功昭赫，繫遹駿之望，篤生聖嗣，啓受命之原，非所謂稱乎？以天下之大德，當天下之大位，奉嚴父之文，舉大享之典，而協乎人心，當乎天理，非所謂行而宜之之義乎？往者戊戌之歲，大議初下，羣論籍籍，禮臣皇懼，莫知定擬。我皇上親御宸翰，作為《或問》，反覆千餘言，妙悟英斷，微詞奧旨，炳然懸之日月，與六經昭映，信非虛矣！嘗仰而誦之，見其折羣疑以孔子之言，論隆祖以近親之非，憲成形一本之義，準成周宗祀之典，明周武君臣之分，定百世宗祧之法，別祖功宗德之異。凡若此者，真有以超百王之見，而斷千古不決之疑，非天下之至聖，其孰能與於此哉？由是大典昭於一代，天下臣民曉然知
translation_en:
…His Majesty possesses the endowment of innate understanding and holds the authority to establish institutions and rites. Gloriously inheriting Heaven’s succession, he occupies the highest position under Heaven. Is this not what is meant by timeliness? Our late imperial father, Emperor Ruizong, personally cultivated virtue and deference and was worthy to be paired with Heaven. His sagely achievements shone brilliantly, sustaining hopes of illustrious greatness; he begot a sagely heir and opened the way for the reception of the Mandate. Is this not what is meant by fitness? With the greatest virtue under Heaven, His Majesty occupies the highest position under Heaven, observes the forms for honoring his father, and performs the great sacrificial ceremony, thereby according with human hearts and conforming to Heaven’s principle. Is this not what is meant by righteousness—carrying these things out fittingly?

Formerly, in the wuxu year [1538], when the great deliberation was first referred to the officials, conflicting opinions abounded. The officials responsible for ritual were alarmed and did not know how to formulate a settled proposal. His Majesty personally took up the imperial brush and composed Questions and Answers (Huowen), examining the matter repeatedly in more than a thousand words. Its marvelous insight and discerning judgments, its subtle expressions and profound import, were displayed as brilliantly as the sun and moon, shining together with the Six Classics. This is assuredly no empty claim! I have reverently read it aloud and seen how it resolves the many doubts through Confucius’s words; discusses the error of exalting an ancestor on account of close kinship; sets forth the principle of a single origin [?]; takes as its standard the Zhou dynasty’s canonical sacrifice to an imperial father as Heaven’s correlate; clarifies the distinction between ruler and subject in the case of King Wu of Zhou; establishes rules for ancestral temples for a hundred generations; and distinguishes the honoring of a founding ancestor for achievement from the honoring of a later ancestor for virtue. All such judgments truly surpass the understanding of a hundred kings and settle doubts unresolved through the ages. Who but the greatest sage under Heaven could attain this?

Thus the great rite was made manifest in this dynasty, and officials and common people throughout the realm clearly understood…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
天子之孝可通于神明加于百姓刑于四海施
于萬世盖自成周以還越二千年而再見
其盛也兹非所謂大順而為禮之極致也
乎然此義自周以来鮮克知之徒察於制
度之細而靡究於義理之原紛紛之議而
不可為訓久矣愚嘗聞之禮曰義者禮之
實也協於義而協則禮雖先王未有可以
義起也又曰其數易陳也其義難明也故
不知義者不可以言禮秦漢而下舉其數
===
而失其義者不能更僕數也是故有一殿
有五室有九室十二室有四堂十二堂之
異有配以始祖有配以祖考有三君並配
侑有祖宗迭配有主於嚴父而一世迭配
之殊蔡邕鄭玄桓譚之所紀述聶崇義李
謐王炎李覯之所考究何其紛紛也裴頠
歐陽修之論制殆庶幾近之乎太始永平
顯慶之所經營杜鴻漸王涯孫抃司馬光
王安石陳與義之所論辨何其紛紛也胡

punctuated:
天子之孝可通于神明，加于百姓，刑于四海，施于萬世。盖自成周以還，越二千年而再見其盛也。兹非所謂大順而為禮之極致也乎？然此義自周以来，鮮克知之，徒察於制度之細，而靡究於義理之原，紛紛之議而不可為訓久矣。

愚嘗聞之，《禮》曰：「義者，禮之實也。」協於義而協，則禮雖先王未有，可以義起也。又曰：「其數易陳也，其義難明也。」故不知義者，不可以言禮。秦漢而下，舉其數而失其義者，不能更僕數也。是故有一殿，有五室，有九室、十二室，有四堂、十二堂之異；有配以始祖，有配以祖考，有三君並配侑，有祖宗迭配，有主於嚴父而一世迭配之殊。蔡邕、鄭玄、桓譚之所紀述，聶崇義、李謐、王炎、李覯之所考究，何其紛紛也！裴頠、歐陽修之論制，殆庶幾近之乎？太始、永平、顯慶之所經營，杜鴻漸、王涯、孫抃、司馬光、王安石、陳與義之所論辨，何其紛紛也！胡
translation_en:
…the Son of Heaven’s filial devotion can reach the spirits, extend to the common people, serve as a model throughout the Four Seas, and benefit ten thousand generations. More than two thousand years after the consummate Zhou order, its splendor has appeared again. Is this not what is called supreme concord, the highest realization of ritual? Yet since the Zhou, few have understood this meaning. They have merely scrutinized the details of institutions without investigating the source of their underlying principles. Their conflicting discussions have long been unfit to serve as authoritative guidance.

I have heard it said in the Book of Rites: “Rightness is the substance of ritual.” When it accords with rightness and is harmonious [?], a rite may be instituted on the basis of rightness even if the former kings never practiced it. It also says: “Its particulars are easy to set forth; its meaning is difficult to elucidate.” Thus those who do not understand rightness cannot discuss ritual. Since the Qin and Han, those who have enumerated its particulars while losing its meaning have been too numerous to count, even with successive attendants taking turns at the task. Hence the divergent arrangements: one hall; five chambers; nine or twelve chambers; four or twelve halls. There have likewise been differences in whom to associate with the deity in sacrifice: the founding ancestor; ancestors and deceased fathers; three rulers jointly; ancestors alternating; or, taking the honoring of one’s father as the governing principle, a different father in each successive generation. How bewilderingly various are the accounts of Cai Yong, Zheng Xuan, and Huan Tan, and the investigations of Nie Chongyi, Li Mi, Wang Yan, and Li Gou! Perhaps the discussions of institutional arrangements by Pei Wei and Ouyang Xiu came close to the truth? How bewilderingly various are the undertakings of the Taishi, Yongping, and Xianqing eras, and the arguments of Du Hongjian, Wang Ya, Sun Bian, Sima Guang, Wang Anshi, and Chen Yuyi! Hu…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
寅錢公輔之論義殆庶幾近之乎然皆未
有持時與稱二者相值之說卓然見武王
周公制禮崇親之心于千載之上者也是
聖人之道待人而明若斯之難也嗚呼此
豈可與寡聞淺見者道哉盖嘗論之明堂
之制猶可畧也其義則難明也是武王周
公以義起焉者也盖武王周公之意以為
郊以享帝廟以享親天人之道備矣惟我
文王備聖人之至德是天命之所與也使
===
終同羣廟則何以嚴親躋以配郊則嫌于
並祖故以義起設為明堂以隆專祀而推
尊于主宰之神是尊文王之至也夫尊文
王者主于尊德也非武王周公之獨私于
親也不然則舜可為矣而不為禹湯可為
矣而亦不為三聖人者愛親之心豈與武
周異哉時可得為而親之德未能配天而
不愧則雖聖人未敢先天以有為也此稱
之為難之說也武王周公之意又以為迎

之爲難之說也武王周公之意又以爲迎
punctuated: 寅、錢公輔之論義，殆庶幾近之乎？然皆未有持時與稱二者相值之說，卓然見武王、周公制禮崇親之心于千載之上者也。是聖人之道待人而明，若斯之難也。嗚呼！此豈可與寡聞淺見者道哉？盖嘗論之：明堂之制猶可畧也，其義則難明也，是武王、周公以義起焉者也。盖武王、周公之意以為：郊以享帝，廟以享親，天人之道備矣。惟我文王備聖人之至德，是天命之所與也。使終同羣廟，則何以嚴親？躋以配郊，則嫌于並祖。故以義起，設為明堂，以隆專祀，而推尊于主宰之神，是尊文王之至也。夫尊文王者，主于尊德也，非武王、周公之獨私于親也。不然，則舜可為矣而不為，禹、湯可為矣而亦不為。三聖人者愛親之心，豈與武、周異哉？時可得為，而親之德未能配天而不愧，則雖聖人未敢先天以有為也。此稱之為難之說也。武王、周公之意又以為迎
translation_en:
… might Hu Yin and Qian Gongfu’s discussions of its meaning have come close to the truth? Yet none advanced an explanation showing how timeliness and fittingness must coincide, thereby discerning clearly, across a thousand years, the intentions of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou in establishing rites to exalt their parent. Such is the difficulty of making the Way of the sages clear: it must await someone capable of elucidating it. Alas! How could this be discussed with those of scant learning and shallow understanding?

I have considered the matter thus: the institutional arrangements of the Hall of Enlightenment may be treated briefly, but its underlying meaning is difficult to elucidate. This was something King Wu and the Duke of Zhou instituted on grounds of righteousness. Their thinking was that the suburban sacrifice served to offer worship to the Supreme Lord, and the ancestral temple to offer worship to one’s parents; thus the ways of Heaven and humanity were fully provided for. Yet our King Wen possessed the supreme virtue of a sage, and Heaven’s mandate had been bestowed upon him. If he were forever treated like those worshipped in the other ancestral temples, how would this give their parent due reverence? If they elevated him to share in the suburban sacrifice, they risked seeming to place him on an equal footing with the founding ancestor. Accordingly, on grounds of righteousness, they established the Hall of Enlightenment to honour him with a dedicated sacrifice and exalt him as the companion of the deity who rules over all. This was the utmost honour they could accord King Wen.

Honouring King Wen was chiefly a matter of honouring virtue; it was not merely King Wu and the Duke of Zhou showing partiality toward their own parent. Otherwise, Shun could have done this, yet did not; Yu and Tang could have done it, yet likewise did not. Could these three sages have differed from King Wu and the Duke of Zhou in their love for their parents? Even when the circumstances permitted such action, if a parent’s virtue was not such that he could worthily be associated with Heaven, then even a sage would not dare act in advance of Heaven. This explains why fittingness is difficult to achieve. King Wu and the Duke of Zhou further thought that welcoming …

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
至大報四序禘嘗誠孝之心達矣惟此明
堂但以崇文考之德出于二禮之外者也
如四序並舉則近于瀆禮之為煩或歲首
一行則失于取義之無謂故以義起擇于
季秋以行大享而著本于成形之義是親
文王之至也夫親文王亦主于嚴德也非
武王周公之可得公于人者也不然則成
王之世未聞拘嚴父之說而祀武王也康
王之世未聞泥成形之義而祀成王也是
===
二聖人者其愛親之心豈獨厚於人哉親
德旣盛而又適丁乎應天之時故特舉嚴
父之典而不讓所謂聖人奉天之時也此
時之為貴之說也故知時之為貴也則明
堂之祀非有天下者不可得為也知稱之
為難也則嚴父之典非有天下者之皆得
為也故曰二者備矣是謂大順孔子曰則
周公其人所謂以義起者豈不信然哉是
知虞夏之際協諸義不協而止者也漢晉

punctuated: 至、大報、四序禘嘗，誠孝之心達矣。惟此明堂，但以崇文考之德，出于二禮之外者也。如四序並舉，則近于瀆禮之為煩；或歲首一行，則失于取義之無謂。故以義起，擇于季秋以行大享，而著本于成形之義，是親文王之至也。夫親文王，亦主于嚴德也，非武王周公之可得公于人者也。不然，則成王之世，未聞拘嚴父之說而祀武王也；康王之世，未聞泥成形之義而祀成王也。是二聖人者，其愛親之心豈獨厚於人哉？親德旣盛，而又適丁乎應天之時，故特舉嚴父之典而不讓，所謂聖人奉天之時也。此時之為貴之說也。故知時之為貴也，則明堂之祀，非有天下者不可得為也；知稱之為難也，則嚴父之典，非有天下者之皆得為也。故曰：「二者備矣，是謂大順。」孔子曰：「則周公其人。」所謂以義起者，豈不信然哉？是知虞夏之際，協諸義，不協而止者也；漢晉
translation_en:
…the rites welcoming the solstice, the great sacrifice of requital, and the di and chang ancestral sacrifices of the four seasons fully express sincere filial devotion. Only this rite in the Hall of Light serves specifically to exalt the virtue of their cultured father, standing apart from the two categories of rites. If it were performed in all four seasons, its frequency would verge on profaning ritual; if performed once at the beginning of the year, its choice of timing would lack a meaningful rationale. Thus, instituting it on grounds of righteousness, they chose the last month of autumn for the great sacrifice, grounding it in the significance of things attaining their completed forms. This was the utmost expression of affection for King Wen. Affection for King Wen likewise centered on reverence for his virtue; it was not something that King Wu and the Duke of Zhou could make a general practice for everyone. Otherwise, why do we never hear that, in King Cheng’s reign, he adhered rigidly to the doctrine of revering one’s father and sacrificed to King Wu, or that, in King Kang’s reign, he clung to the significance of completed forms and sacrificed to King Cheng? Could these two sages alone have loved their parents more deeply than others? Their father’s virtue was abundant, and they also happened to encounter the proper time for responding to Heaven. They therefore undertook the exceptional rite of revering their father without declining the responsibility. This is what is meant by the sage’s observing Heaven’s timing. This explains why proper timing is precious.

Thus, once we understand why proper timing is precious, we see that the sacrifice in the Hall of Light can be performed only by one who possesses all under Heaven. Once we understand why being worthy of it is difficult, we see that the rite of revering one’s father cannot be performed by everyone who possesses all under Heaven. Hence the saying: “When both are present, this is called the great accord.” Confucius said: “The Duke of Zhou was such a man.” Is this not indeed what is meant by instituting a rite on grounds of righteousness? From this we know that, in the time of Yu and Xia, rites were measured against righteousness, and when they did not accord with it, they were abandoned; Han and Jin…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
之後協諸義不協而不止者也孰有若我
皇上修禮嚴親于武王有光者乎又孰有若我
皇考凝德對天于文王有光者乎夫文王之德
詩書所稱備矣我
皇考之德則載于史氏之書藏于金匱之祕非
疏遠草茅之臣所得睹識也往者
皇上推崇
徽號以對
皇天懸諸日月之上叅于兩儀之間則嘗彷彿
===
窺其似矣請得而鋪張之乎是故論太極

…after the Han and Jin, they tested their actions against righteousness, yet did not desist when they failed to accord with it. Who has equaled our Emperor in perfecting the rites and honoring his father, bringing added glory to King Wu? And who has equaled our Emperor’s deceased father in bringing his virtue to completion and responding to Heaven, bringing added glory to King Wen? The virtue of King Wen is fully praised in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. The virtue of our Emperor’s deceased father, however, is recorded in the historians’ writings and preserved among the confidential records in the golden coffer. It is not something that a humble servant, remote from court and living in obscurity, could see and comprehend. Formerly, when our Emperor exalted his father’s honorific title in response to August Heaven, raising it above the sun and moon and setting it alongside Heaven and Earth, I caught, as it were, a faint glimpse of his likeness. May I be permitted to expound upon it?

Thus, he discussed the Supreme Ultimate and traced the ordering of the Five Phases; when praying during drought, he took responsibility for the Five Affairs of personal conduct. This is called knowing Heaven. In cultivating himself and regulating his household, he progressively put into practice the way of illuminating virtue and bringing harmony to his lineage. In pursuing learning and investigating principle, his love of goodness and fondness for antiquity were such that each day seemed insufficient. This is called holding fast to the Way. He extended compassionate care and broadly distributed relief and loans: this was the generosity that does not act rashly [?]. He was circumspect in his tastes and preferences and solemn in his dignified bearing: this was the reverence of continuously brightening virtue. His admonition against becoming engrossed in objects and his designation of “Pure Unity”—were these not what is meant by purity achieved through carving and polishing? His exceptional acuity, his understanding of the subtle and elucidation of the hidden—were these not what is meant by sagacity requiring no remonstrance? text:
于忠孝因洪範作威福之語而訓講臣以
謹侯度因陽春臺之遊而作賦以警流連
與不聞亦式作易思懼者何殊是謂之恭
因玉器之售而佩象箸之戒因蜀錦之獻
而思女工之勞衣止浣濯曰吾將慎乃儉
德惟懷永圖也居憚營造曰吾將服寵爲
美安民爲樂也與卑服即康功田功者何
異是謂之儉以言其敬則飭社稷山川之
祀釋放心操存之旨闡苞桑之戒發凝命
===
之義與翼翼之心同一揆矣以言其文則
證道于經取材于史詩文以發其藻思謨
訓以立其章程與丕顯之謨無二致矣以
言乎其獻也則聰明睿智足以有臨包十
德之全備衆美之會而卓然爲至德之匹
也此之謂盛德此之謂配
天而不愧然竊聞天下學士大夫之論以爲
皇考雖未得大位實受命之主也故

于忠孝。因洪範作威福之語，而訓講臣以謹侯度；因陽春臺之遊，而作賦以警流連，與不聞亦式、作易思懼者何殊？是謂之恭。因玉器之售，而佩象箸之戒；因蜀錦之獻，而思女工之勞。衣止浣濯，曰：「吾將慎乃儉德，惟懷永圖也。」居憚營造，曰：「吾將服寵爲美，安民爲樂也。」與卑服、即康功田功者何異？是謂之儉。以言其敬，則飭社稷山川之祀，釋放心操存之旨，闡苞桑之戒，發凝命之義，與翼翼之心同一揆矣。以言其文，則證道于經，取材于史，詩文以發其藻思，謨訓以立其章程，與丕顯之謨無二致矣。以言乎其獻也，則聰明睿智足以有臨，包十德之全，備衆美之會，而卓然爲至德之匹也。此之謂盛德，此之謂配天而不愧。

…in loyalty and filial devotion. Taking up the words in the Great Plan concerning the exercise of authority and the bestowal of blessings, he admonished his lecturer to observe carefully the standards governing a prince. After an excursion to Yangchun Terrace, he composed a rhapsody to warn against lingering over pleasure. How did this differ from being exemplary even where one is not heard, or from thinking apprehensively when undertaking something easy? This is what is called reverence. When jade objects were offered for sale, he took to heart the warning of the ivory chopsticks; when brocade from Shu was presented, he reflected on the toil of the women who wove it. For clothing, he contented himself with garments that had been washed, saying, “I shall carefully uphold that virtue of frugality, keeping lasting plans in mind.” In his dwelling, he shrank from undertaking construction, saying, “I shall regard the honors bestowed upon me as my adornment, and the peace of the people as my delight.” How did this differ from wearing humble clothes and devoting oneself to the work of securing the people's welfare and cultivating the fields? This is what is called frugality. As for his respectfulness, he put in order the sacrifices to the altars of soil and grain and to the mountains and rivers; explained the meaning of recovering the wandering mind and holding it fast; expounded the warning about securing oneself as firmly as a clump of mulberry roots; and elucidated the meaning of making Heaven's mandate secure. These accorded with the same principle as a reverently vigilant heart. As for his literary cultivation, he verified the Way through the Classics and drew material from the histories. In poetry and prose he expressed his richly wrought thoughts, and through counsels and admonitions he established his rules and standards. These were entirely consonant with the illustrious counsels of antiquity. As for his worthiness, his perceptiveness, understanding, sagacity, and wisdom sufficed to exercise authority. He embraced all ten virtues in their completeness and united every excellence, standing forth as a match for the highest virtue. This is what is called abundant virtue; this is what is called being worthy to stand beside Heaven without shame.
Yet I have humbly heard the scholars and officials of the realm argue that, although Your Majesty's deceased father never attained the imperial throne, he was truly a ruler who received Heaven's mandate. translation_en:
…Our August Emperor succeeded to the imperial line, assumed its charge, and brought about a restoration. His lofty, magnificent enterprise is indeed the enterprise of his imperial father. Tracing it to its very roots, we find that it assuredly has its source. May I expound and extol it?

Thus, the imperial father once argued that appointing chief ministers depended above all on finding the right men. Our August Emperor grasped this principle and carefully selected his chief advisers, so that all under Heaven enjoy the benefits of obtaining worthy men. His father once argued that establishing offices was of the utmost importance. Our August Emperor grasped this principle and welcomed counsel widely, so that those serving as his ears and eyes possess impartial clarity and discernment. His father once lamented the harm caused by surveillance officials, prefects, and magistrates; accordingly, our August Emperor scrutinized officials’ administration that harassed the people [?]. His father once laid down provisions for pitying widows and caring for orphans; accordingly, our August Emperor’s beneficence in relieving the poor and treating the sick became comprehensive.

In writing a preface on external medicine, his father recognized that foreign aggression must be resisted; hence our August Emperor harbors the righteous resolve to scourge the Di barbarians and plow up their courts. In discussing cities, his father explained that strategically advantageous terrain must be secured; hence our August Emperor exercises care over the offices guarding the realm’s strategic approaches and gateways [?]. In burning incense, his father thought of burning southernwood in sacrifice; when presented with brocade, he thought of plain cloth and silk. Hence our August Emperor personally practices frugality to lead his subordinates. In observing pines, his father thought of seeking talented men; in observing angling, he thought of raising recluses to office. Hence…

punctuated:
皇上拊髀以思賢。諸若此者，未易縷舉。此之謂大業，此之謂嚴親而有光。是知嚴親而有光者，得乎天位之時也；配天而不愧者，本乎親德之稱也。故曰：「二者備矣，是謂大順。」大順，禮之極致也，是曠百世而一逢之會也。
雖然，嘗讀《我將》之詩，而思武王、周公憂勤畏天敬祖之心矣。所以教其子孫以為君、為父、為臣、為子之道者，無巳也。故能祈天永命，而歷服最久，非偶然哉！我皇上肇明大典，適曠百世一逢之會，遡二千年並周之美。嚴親以天，推天崇親，所欲垂示聖子
translation_en:
…Your Majesty slaps your thigh in longing for worthy men. Such instances cannot readily be enumerated in detail. This is what is meant by a great undertaking; this is what is meant by honoring one’s parent and bringing him glory. Thus we know that honoring one’s parent and bringing him glory depends upon the occasion of attaining the heavenly throne, while associating him with Heaven without shame rests upon the commensurate virtue of that parent. Hence it is said: “When both are fulfilled, this is called supreme accord.” Supreme accord is the highest attainment of ritual: an occasion encountered but once in a hundred generations.
Nevertheless, I have read the ode “I Bring My Offerings” (Wo Jiang) and reflected upon the anxious diligence with which King Wu and the Duke of Zhou revered Heaven and honored their ancestors. There was no end to their instruction of their descendants in the ways of being a ruler, a father, a minister, and a son. Thus they could pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate, and their dynasty’s tenure was the longest. Surely this was no accident! Our Emperor has inaugurated and made manifest the great rite, meeting an occasion encountered but once in a hundred generations and reaching back two thousand years to equal the excellence of Zhou. He honors his parent through Heaven and extends the reverence due to Heaven to exalt his parent, wishing thereby to transmit instruction to his sage sons…

第二問
楊守魯
同考試官主事李批：「述形勢以見我祖宗創定之難，陳時事以為聖天子保守之助，足占忠悃。」

考試官學士張批：「備述祖宗創造之勞，讀之可惕然深省也。保大思艱之道，獨歸諸兵民，可謂知其要矣。取子非特以文詞而已。」
考試官學士孫批：
translation_en:
…and divine grandsons, through the virtues of benevolence, filial piety, reverence, and kindness, and the proper ways of ruler, father, son, and minister, so as to perpetuate blessings without limit—could this be all? Among the ministers who uphold civil virtue and render illustrious assistance, there must be those who can extend the principle of setting an example and inspiring trust, examine ritual and unify virtue, put laws in order and benefit the people, and thereby regulate all under Heaven. Thus they will respond worthily to our sagacious sovereign, like the great ministers of Zhou. How fortunate I, in my ignorance, am to witness this flourishing age in person!
Second Policy Question
Yang Shoulu
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Secretary: “He describes the strategic circumstances to show the difficulties our imperial ancestors faced in founding and establishing the dynasty, and discusses current affairs to assist our sage Son of Heaven in preserving it. title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
祖宗創造鴻業
神謨廟筭子能一二道之末復於
聖天子保大思艱之道懇切至當于胷中之抱負奇氣豈可以不盡言邪
帝王之有天下也有攻取之形勢有保守
之規模故形勢者得失之機也規模者理
亂之畧也察其機者合而不離知其畧者
要而有常其道一也我
太祖高皇帝自南而取北
成祖文皇帝自北而取南形勢規模在古無配
===
聖子
神孫繼繼承承循其規模之大以益固其形勢
之強猗與盛矣學者近依傳聞烏能道其
萬一請陳固陋昔周先王盖積數百年之
基至武王而有天下周公陳其事著于大
武之舞至孔子論樂繹其義而後知周公
之意在教其子孫不忘其祖立業之艱難
也今欲稱說
皇祖經綸草昧之槩以為

祖宗創造鴻業，神謨廟筭，子能一二道之。末復於聖天子保大思艱之道，懇切至當。于胷中之抱負奇氣，豈可以不盡言邪？

帝王之有天下也，有攻取之形勢，有保守之規模。故形勢者，得失之機也；規模者，理亂之畧也。察其機者，合而不離；知其畧者，要而有常。其道一也。我太祖高皇帝自南而取北，成祖文皇帝自北而取南，形勢規模，在古無配。聖子神孫，繼繼承承，循其規模之大，以益固其形勢之強，猗與盛矣！學者近依傳聞，烏能道其萬一？請陳固陋。昔周先王，盖積數百年之基，至武王而有天下。周公陳其事，著于大武之舞。至孔子論樂，繹其義，而後知周公之意，在教其子孫不忘其祖立業之艱難也。今欲稱說皇祖經綸草昧之槩，以為
translation_en:
You have been able to recount some of the divine designs and court deliberations through which our imperial ancestors founded their magnificent enterprise. At the end, your discussion of how the sagely Son of Heaven should preserve its greatness and reflect upon its founding hardships is earnest and entirely fitting. How could you leave unexpressed any of the aspirations and extraordinary spirit within your breast?

When emperors and kings possess All under Heaven, they have strategic configurations for conquest and institutional frameworks for preservation. Strategic configurations are thus the pivot of gain and loss; institutional frameworks are the plans upon which order and disorder depend. Those who discern that pivot bring things together without allowing them to come apart; those who understand those plans grasp the essentials and maintain constancy. Their Way is one. Our Emperor Taizu Gao proceeded from the south to conquer the north; Emperor Chengzu Wen proceeded from the north to conquer the south. Their strategic configurations and institutional frameworks had no equal in antiquity. Their sagely sons and divine grandsons succeeded them generation after generation, following the grandeur of their institutional frameworks to consolidate still further the strength of their strategic position. Ah, how glorious! How could a scholar, relying merely on transmitted reports, recount even one ten-thousandth of this? Allow me to present my limited understanding. The former kings of Zhou accumulated a foundation over several hundred years, until King Wu came to possess All under Heaven. The Duke of Zhou set forth their deeds and embodied them in the dance of Great Martial Achievement (Dawu). Only when Confucius discussed music and elucidated its meaning did it become clear that the Duke of Zhou intended to teach their descendants never to forget the hardships through which their ancestors had founded their enterprise. Now I wish to recount in outline how our imperial ancestors brought order to an age of turmoil, so as to provide…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
聖天子保大思艱之助儻亦孔氏之意乎嘗考
高皇帝提劔而起於濠也自濠徂滁自滁徂和
脫難孫崖艤舟巢湖取太平入集慶其經
始審顧雖遷豳治岐不足以喻其勞也是
時漢強於西吳富於東國珍之詐友定之
堅伺於南王宣之逼擴廓之眾壓於北此
固得失之機而攻取之會也嗚呼非天下
至明不足以辨此
聖祖於是通淮北之使而羈海上之志也置嶺
===
表之師而防二敵之合也故設鐵橋以挫
上流之鋒守長興以塞隙窺之竇而二敵
離矣鄱陽之戰繫垓下之𧴀葑門之虜傳
泜水之檄而四方懼矣由是大業始固而
天誅可北嚮焉故右取山東以扼其吭左
據潼關以斷其臂中臨洺莫則勢孤援絕
而穢胡不支西掃雲代則破竹建瓴而餘
燼自滅此所以成混一之勢之大略也
成祖文皇帝之平内難聲罪而奮於燕也平九

成祖文皇帝之平內難聲罪而奮於燕也平九
punctuated:
聖天子保大思艱之助，儻亦孔氏之意乎？嘗考高皇帝提劔而起於濠也，自濠徂滁，自滁徂和，脫難孫崖，艤舟巢湖，取太平，入集慶，其經始審顧，雖遷豳治岐，不足以喻其勞也。是時漢強於西，吳富於東，國珍之詐、友定之堅，伺於南；王宣之逼、擴廓之眾，壓於北。此固得失之機，而攻取之會也。嗚呼！非天下至明，不足以辨此。聖祖於是通淮北之使，而羈海上之志也；置嶺表之師，而防二敵之合也。故設鐵橋以挫上流之鋒，守長興以塞隙窺之竇，而二敵離矣。鄱陽之戰，繫垓下之𧴀；葑門之虜，傳泜水之檄，而四方懼矣。由是大業始固，而天誅可北嚮焉。故右取山東以扼其吭，左據潼關以斷其臂，中臨洺莫，則勢孤援絕，而穢胡不支；西掃雲代，則破竹建瓴，而餘燼自滅。此所以成混一之勢之大略也。
成祖文皇帝之平内難，聲罪而奮於燕也，平九
translation_en:
…to help the sagely Son of Heaven preserve his great dominion and reflect upon the hardships of its founding—might this also accord with Confucius’s intent? I have examined how Emperor Gao rose at Hao, sword in hand. From Hao he went to Chu, and from Chu to He; he escaped danger at Sunya [?], moored his boats on Lake Chao, took Taiping, and entered Jiqing. So painstaking were his initial undertakings and careful deliberations that even the Zhou ancestors’ migration to Bin and establishment at Qi cannot adequately convey his labors. At that time, Han was powerful in the west and Wu wealthy in the east. The cunning Guozhen and the steadfast Youding lay watching in the south; the menace of Wang Xuan and the hosts of Kuokuo bore down from the north. This was indeed a moment upon which success or failure turned, and an opportunity for attack and conquest. Alas! Only someone of the utmost discernment under Heaven could have understood this.
The sagely founder therefore exchanged envoys with Huaibei, keeping the ambitions of the maritime power in check; he stationed troops beyond the southern mountain ranges to prevent his two enemies from joining forces. Thus he established an iron bridge to blunt the thrust from upstream and held Changxing to close the opening through which an enemy might exploit a weakness; the two enemies were thereby kept apart. The battle of Poyang bound the fierce beast of Gaixia [?]; the capture at Fengmen sent forth a proclamation like that at the Zhi River, and all quarters trembled. With this, the great enterprise became secure, and Heaven’s punitive campaign could turn northward. On the right he took Shandong to grip the enemy’s throat; on the left he occupied Tongguan to sever its arm. His advance through the center upon Ming and Mo left the enemy isolated and cut off from assistance, so that the vile northern barbarians could not hold out. Sweeping westward through Yun and Dai, he advanced as easily as splitting bamboo and with the force of water poured from a roof; the surviving embers died out of themselves. Such was the broad outline of how he achieved the strategic ascendancy that brought unification.
When Emperor Wen, Chengzu, quelled the internal troubles, he proclaimed his opponents’ crimes and rose in arms in Yan. He pacified Jiu…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
門以張六師據居庸而取懷來娄桑疾馳
不及掩耳滹沱先聲易於摧朽其决策一
怒雖破尋虜離不足以喻其勇也是時大
寧勁兵未至而遼東有肘腋之虞真定之
捷方新而河間逼門庭之寇此固得失之
機而竒正之辨也嗚呼非天下至明不足
以察此
聖祖於是殲鄭壩之老師而疲紫荆之惰氣也
急松關之脫兎而修東隅之草具也故斧
===
===
鉞之帥視如兒戲矣釋遼東之獲將而勞
勉慰藉之有加揮戈之氣天下震恐矣聞
大同之伺擾而投袂赴援之恐後由是根
本無虞而大斾始南征焉至其制敵也合
能分之逸能勞之獨往獨來而盛李吳平
之將不知其所攻飽能饑之治能亂之為
主為客而魏冀齊魯之邦不知其所守此
所以成靖難之功之大畧也盖嘗合而論
其世矣當漢之索戰也吳人不能趨捲甲

門以張六師據居庸而取懷來輿桑疾馳
不及掩耳滹沱先聲易於摧朽其決策一

以察此

急松關之脫免而修東隅之草具也故斧
===
鉞之師視如兒戲矣釋遼東之獲將而勞
勉慰藉之有加揮戈之氣天下震恐矣聞
大同之伺擾而投袂赴援之恐後由是根
本無虞而大旆始南征焉至其制敵也合
能分之逸能勞之獨往獨來而盛李吳平
之將不知其所攻飽能饑之治能亂之為
主為客而魏冀齊魯之邦不知其所守此
所以成靖難之功之大畧也蓋嘗合而論
其世矣當漢之索戰也吳人不能踰捲甲
punctuated:
門，以張六師；據居庸而取懷來，娄桑疾馳，不及掩耳；滹沱先聲，易於摧朽。其决策一怒，雖破尋虜離，不足以喻其勇也。是時，大寧勁兵未至，而遼東有肘腋之虞；真定之捷方新，而河間逼門庭之寇。此固得失之機，而竒正之辨也。嗚呼！非天下至明，不足以察此。
聖祖於是殲鄭壩之老師，而疲紫荆之惰氣也；急松關之脫兎，而修東隅之草具也。故斧鉞之帥，視如兒戲矣。釋遼東之獲將，而勞勉慰藉之有加，揮戈之氣，天下震恐矣。聞大同之伺擾，而投袂赴援之恐後。由是根本無虞，而大斾始南征焉。至其制敵也，合能分之，逸能勞之，獨往獨來，而盛李吳平之將不知其所攻；飽能饑之，治能亂之，為主為客，而魏冀齊魯之邦不知其所守。此所以成靖難之功之大畧也。盖嘗合而論其世矣：當漢之索戰也，吳人不能趨捲甲
translation_en:
…men [completing Jiumen], thereby deploying the six armies. He secured Juyong and took Huailai; at Lousang he galloped forward so swiftly that there was no time even to cover one’s ears. At the Hutuo River, his reputation preceded him, making victory easier than crushing rotten wood. Such was his resolve when roused to anger that even defeating Xun and capturing Li [?] would not suffice as a comparison for his valor. At this time, the crack troops from Daning had not yet arrived, and Liaodong posed a danger close at hand. The victory at Zhending was still fresh, yet at Hejian enemy forces pressed upon his very doorstep. These were indeed the critical junctures determining success or failure, and the occasions for distinguishing extraordinary from orthodox tactics. Alas! Only someone of the greatest discernment under Heaven could perceive this.
The Sacred Progenitor thereupon annihilated the weary army at Zhengba and further exhausted the flagging spirit of the forces at Zijing. He pressed the enemy at Songguan with the speed of an escaping hare and prepared makeshift provisions in the east [?]. Thus he regarded commanders wielding the battle-axe of authority as mere children at play. He released the general captured from Liaodong, treating him with exceptional encouragement and consolation. The martial spirit with which he brandished his spear made all under Heaven tremble. Hearing that forces at Datong were watching for an opportunity to harass him, he shook out his sleeves and hastened to their relief, fearing he might arrive too late. With his base thus secure, his great standard at last advanced southward.
As for his mastery of the enemy: when they were united, he could divide them; when rested, he could tire them. He came and went entirely at his own discretion, so that the generals Sheng, Li, Wu, and Ping did not know where he would attack. When the enemy were well fed, he could starve them; when orderly, he could throw them into confusion. Acting now as host and now as guest, he left the lands of Wei, Ji, Qi, and Lu uncertain where to defend. Such, in broad outline, were the means by which he accomplished the Pacification of the Troubles.
I have considered these eras together. When Han sought battle, the men of Wu could not hasten forward with their armor rolled up…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
之功吳之被圍也中原不能收漁人之利
定德相據而我處其中終不得成其掎角
之勢遼濟聲援而我頓其下卒不得遂
其衡决之圖若是者非敵之盡愚也亦由
伐謀之術有奪其氣先人之智有奪其心
焉故也是知取南取北雖有形勢之殊至
其固根本之地爭要害之利擇常勝之筭
批瑕釁之動規模則一而已雖然此猶自
我
===
聖祖攻取形勢之中求之而見其規模自具如
此至其
統一之後立綱陳紀設官分職經野體國備
邊養民節目無不悉而體統無不全所謂
保守之規模者窮年不能述其美矣今我
聖天子據
成祖之形勢以撫域中守
太祖之規模以保弘業譬之握紫杓以酌寒暑
而無不順也持平衡以權輕重而無不當

定德相據而我處其中終不得成其犄角
之勢遼濟聲援而我頓其下卒不得遂
其衡決之圖若是者非敵之盡愚也亦由

焉故也是知取南取北雖有形勢之殊至
其固根本之地爭要害之利擇常勝之筭

聖祖攻取形勢之中求之而見其規模自具如
此至其
統一之後立綱陳紀設官分職經野體國備
邊養民節目無不悉而體統無不全所謂
保守之規模者窮年不能述其美矣今我
聖天子據
成祖之形勢以撫域中守
太祖之規模以保弘業譬之握紫杓以酌寒暑
而無不順也持平衡以權輕重而無不當
punctuated:
之功。吳之被圍也，中原不能收漁人之利。定德相據，而我處其中，終不得成其掎角之勢；遼濟聲援，而我頓其下，卒不得遂其衡决之圖。若是者，非敵之盡愚也，亦由伐謀之術有奪其氣，先人之智有奪其心焉故也。是知取南取北，雖有形勢之殊，至其固根本之地，爭要害之利，擇常勝之筭，批瑕釁之動，規模則一而已。雖然，此猶自我聖祖攻取形勢之中求之，而見其規模自具如此。至其統一之後，立綱陳紀，設官分職，經野體國，備邊養民，節目無不悉，而體統無不全。所謂保守之規模者，窮年不能述其美矣。
今我聖天子據成祖之形勢以撫域中，守太祖之規模以保弘業，譬之握紫杓以酌寒暑而無不順也，持平衡以權輕重而無不當
translation_en:
…the success of a rapid march. When Wu was besieged, the Central Plain could not reap the fisherman’s profit from others’ conflict. Ding and De held positions in mutual support [?], while our ruler occupied the space between them; in the end, they could not establish a coordinated pincer movement. Liao and Ji offered each other support [?], while our ruler encamped beneath their positions; ultimately, they could not carry out their plan to break through. Such outcomes did not mean that the enemies were all foolish. Rather, his skill in defeating their plans robbed them of their spirit, and his wisdom in anticipating others robbed them of their resolve. Thus we know that, although conquering the south and conquering the north involved different strategic circumstances, the overall design was the same: securing the heartland, contending for the advantages of strategic positions, choosing calculations that assured repeated victory, and striking at weaknesses and openings. Yet this is still only what we discern by examining the strategic circumstances of our sagely ancestors’ conquests: their overall design was already complete in this way. After unification, they established guiding principles and ordered regulations, created offices and assigned duties, laid out the countryside and organized the state, prepared the frontier defenses and nurtured the people. No detail went unaddressed, and the institutional framework was complete in every respect. As for what is called the design for preserving and defending the realm, an entire year would not suffice to recount its merits.
Now our sagely Son of Heaven relies upon the strategic position established by Chengzu to bring peace to the realm, and upholds Taizu’s overall design to preserve the great imperial enterprise. It is like grasping the celestial Dipper to regulate cold and heat, so that everything follows its proper course, or holding a level balance to weigh the light and the heavy, so that every assessment is fitting…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
也要無旁落不周之處偏勝不舉之劑明
矣而執事猶有擇言之義敢不盡其愚甞
試論之天下之勢一也方其始取之也則
以察其形勢為要而規模之所自出及其
終保之也則以守其規模為重而形勢之
所由固是故觀于我
高皇取北之勢則勝國之失可為永鑒者矣觀
于我
文皇取南之勢則金陵謀臣之失可為永鑒者
===

translation_en:
… indeed. Clearly, then, there is no point at which authority slips away or provision falls short, nor any measure that favors one side excessively or leaves something unaddressed. Yet you, honored examiners, still have a duty to select worthy counsel. How could I dare not fully offer my humble thoughts? Let me attempt to discuss this. The strategic circumstances of the realm form a single whole. When first acquiring it, the essential task is to examine its configuration and strategic advantages: from these the framework of government emerges. When subsequently preserving it, the chief concern is to maintain that framework: through this its configuration and strategic advantages are secured. Thus, if we consider the strategic circumstances in which our Emperor Gao took the north, the failures of the preceding dynasty can serve as an everlasting warning. If we consider those in which our Emperor Wen took the south, the failures of the advisers at Jinling can likewise serve as an everlasting warning.
The failure of the preceding dynasty lay in its condition of disintegration, like collapsing earth and shattered tiles, which no one remedied: this was its partition among rival strongmen. Its origin lay in failing to cherish the people. The failure at Jinling lay in its exposure to attack from behind and seizure by the throat, against which no one could defend it: this was the loss of all its strategic strongholds. Its origin lay in failing to train its troops. Thus, the severe punishment of corrupt and cruel officials at the beginning of the Hongwu reign was intended to improve the people's livelihood and foster conditions of utmost security throughout the realm. The vigorous mobilization of armies to seek out the northern enemy at the beginning of the Yongle reign was intended to invigorate the troops and establish a position of utmost strength throughout the realm. Here, indeed, the broad outlines of the sagely ancestors' methods for preserving good government can be discerned. Formerly, …

皇上加惠元元責守令宣化之不至大恩也怒
邊帥之不武繫頸轅門而笞之大威也此
其握機御遠與
聖祖同也今天下全勢未損萬分之一也而縉
紳大夫諰諰然有厝火於薪之憂豈非居
安思危恐於艱大之寄猶有遺慮也哉漢
臣有曰民有七亡而無一得欲望國安誠
難民有七死而無一生欲望刑措誠難此
非守令貪殘化理之所致耶是故當無事
===
時明其政刑以養民培根本之業何憚而
不為也宋臣有曰三弊因循於上則百務
弛慢廢壞於下故雖有兵將財用與禦戎
之策可任之臣而皆不得其用此非未思
其術之過耶是故當無事時振其紀綱以
練兵謹要害之固何憚而不為也且今東
南民力竭矣猶可言也而
畿輔之民使空其杼軸何也西北戎馬敝矣
猶可言也而
