身之道養乎天下也夫其身
之道誠養乎天下而後可爲
國之味不然其有能味者乎
===
是故國以士爲味士以道爲
味而後明盛之理可從致矣
昔者伊尹之於湯也思說以
堯舜之味而高宗之於傅說
亦惟曰爾惟麴糱惟鹽梅斯
二者非所謂天下之至味者
乎商道之盛至今猶耿光者
punctuated:
蘄以其士之道養乎天下也。夫其士之道誠養乎天下，而後可爲民之味；不然，其有味之者乎？士之自擇也，蘄以其身之道養乎天下也。夫其身之道誠養乎天下，而後可爲國之味；不然，其有能味者乎？是故國以士爲味，士以道爲味，而後明盛之理可從致矣。
昔者伊尹之於湯也，思說以堯舜之味；而高宗之於傅說，亦惟曰：「爾惟麴糵，惟鹽梅。」斯二者，非所謂天下之至味者乎？商道之盛，至今猶耿光者，
translation_en:
…seeks to nourish all under Heaven through the Way embodied by its scholars. Only when the Way embodied by those scholars truly nourishes all under Heaven can it become a savor for the people; otherwise, would anyone savor it? Scholars, in choosing for themselves, seek to nourish all under Heaven through the Way embodied in their own persons. Only when the Way embodied in their persons truly nourishes all under Heaven can it become a savor for the state; otherwise, could anyone savor it? Thus the state takes scholars as its savor, and scholars take the Way as their savor; only then can enlightened and flourishing government be attained.
In former times, Yi Yin sought to persuade Tang with the savor of Yao and Shun; and Gaozong likewise said to Fu Yue: “You are the yeast and malt, the salt and plums.” Were these two men not what might be called the finest savors under Heaven? That the flourishing Way of Shang still shines brightly to this day…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
其有以致之矣爾多士以丁
未進其亦慎擇所爲味如商
之二臣以惠天下之養以仰
對
聖天子明盛之理則唯亦有聞於
無窮哉臣治不佞辱
詔從大夫之後與校試之責焉敬
===
以是申告之末簡
掌翰林院事通議大夫吏部
左侍郎兼翰林院學士張治
謹序

其有以致之矣爾多士以丁
未進其亦愼擇所爲味如商
之二臣以惠天下之養以仰
對
聖天子明盛之理則唯亦有聞於
無窮哉〔臣治〕不佞辱
詔從大夫之後與校試之責焉敬
===
以是申告之末簡
掌翰林院事通議大夫吏部
左侍郎兼翰林院學士張〔治〕
謹序
punctuated:
其有以致之矣。爾多士以丁未進，其亦慎擇所爲味，如商之二臣，以惠天下之養，以仰對聖天子明盛之理，則唯亦有聞於無窮哉！臣治不佞，辱詔從大夫之後，與校試之責焉，敬以是申告之末簡。
掌翰林院事、通議大夫、吏部左侍郎兼翰林院學士張治謹序。
translation_en:
…there was indeed a means by which this was achieved. You many scholars who advance in this dingwei year [1547] should likewise carefully choose what you take as your savor. Emulate the two ministers of Shang, benefiting the nourishment of all under Heaven and thereby answering the enlightened and flourishing governance of the sagely Son of Heaven above. Then surely your fame, too, may endure without end!
Your servant Zhi, untalented as I am, was honored with an imperial command to follow in the ranks of the great officers and share responsibility for evaluating the examination papers. I respectfully reiterate this admonition to you on this final leaf.
Preface respectfully composed by Zhang Zhi, in charge of the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Left Vice Minister of Personnel and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.

嘉靖二十有六載，是爲丁未。天子朝羣后，來萬邦。萬邦之士與計偕者四千三百人有竒，景附闕下，願爲帝臣，求試于有司。春二月，禮部尚書臣費寀、侍郎臣許成名、臣崔桐以聞。上命學士臣承恩、臣治往主試事。同考則侍讀臣朴，編修臣璣、臣貞吉、臣晟、臣訥、臣儀、臣景淳、臣樹聲，檢討臣材、臣以勤、臣𤩽，都給事中臣大同、臣綸、
translation_en:
Preface to the Metropolitan Examination Record

The twenty-sixth year of Jiajing was the dingwei year. The Son of Heaven received the assembled lords in audience and drew the myriad realms to his court. Scholars from the myriad realms who accompanied the tribute missions numbered more than four thousand three hundred. They gathered beneath the palace gates, cleaving to the throne like shadows, wishing to become the Emperor’s servants and seeking examination by the responsible authorities. In the second month of spring, your servants Fei Cai, Minister of Rites, and Xu Chengming and Cui Tong, Vice Ministers, reported this to the throne. His Majesty commanded your servants Cheng’en and Zhi, Academicians, to take charge of the examination. The Associate Examiners were your servants Pu, Reader; Ji, Zhenji, Sheng, Ne, Yi, Jingchun, and Shusheng, Compilers; Cai, Yiqin, and Xian (𤩽) [?], Examining Editors; and Datong and Lun, Chief Supervising Secretaries, …

臣海隅側陋，遭逢聖明，備位宫長，不能竭忠殫力，報塞萬分之一，夙夜兢惕，私心惓惓。圖惟薦賢舉能，倣古上臣事君以人之義，迺今躬親
translation_en:
…Right Supervising Secretary, your servant Yunyan; Acting Bureau Director, your servant Feng; and Secretaries, your servants Shichun and Weiyue. The examination was overseen by the Censors, your servants Shou and Chuxiu. They and all the other functionaries were carefully selected to fill their posts. We reverently carried out the illustrious command, pledging ourselves to diligent service. We examined the candidates in three sessions and, respectfully following the imperial decision, selected three hundred successful candidates. Established precedent calls for a record, setting down their names and those of their compositions worthy of transmission, to be presented to the throne. Your servant Cheng’en respectfully supplies this preface at its beginning.
Your servant, an obscure and humble man from a remote coastal region, has had the good fortune to live under Your Majesty’s sagacious rule and to occupy the post of head of the Household Administration. Unable, even by exhausting my loyalty and strength, to repay one ten-thousandth of this favor, I am apprehensive morning and night, my heart filled with earnest devotion. I have sought to recommend the worthy and promote the capable, emulating the principle by which eminent ministers of antiquity served their sovereigns by providing them with men. Now I personally undertake…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
其任臣幸甚幸甚先是嘉靖
辛卯臣嘗典試南畿後六年
典試
京畿獲觀文於兩都人士及茲
夫合天下士試之獲盡觀四
方之文殊狀異態隋珠和璧
競爽並耀讜論嘉猷層見疊
===
出究天人之原恢皇王之緒
明道德之歸探性情之秘文
有經緯之方武有戡定之畧
錯綜六藝揮霍百家若覽職
貢方物畢陳筐篚稠疊玉帛
紛錯若閱輿圖都邑具列名
山大川棊布星羅昭然指掌
alt_text:
其任臣幸甚幸甚先是嘉靖
辛卯臣嘗與試南畿後六年
與試
京畿獲觀文於兩都人士及茲
夫合天下士試之獲盡觀四
方之文殊狀異態隋珠和璧
競爽並耀讜論嘉猷層見疊
===
出究天人之原恢皇王之緒
明道德之歸探性情之秘文
有經緯之方武有戡定之畧
錯綜六藝揮霍百家若覽職
貢方物畢陳筐篚稠疊玉帛
紛錯若閱輿圖都邑具列名
山大川棊布星羅昭然指掌
punctuated: 其任，臣幸甚，幸甚！先是，嘉靖辛卯，臣嘗典試南畿，後六年，典試京畿，獲觀文於兩都人士。及茲夫合天下士試之，獲盡觀四方之文，殊狀異態，隋珠和璧，競爽並耀；讜論嘉猷，層見疊出。究天人之原，恢皇王之緒，明道德之歸，探性情之秘。文有經緯之方，武有戡定之畧，錯綜六藝，揮霍百家。若覽職貢，方物畢陳，筐篚稠疊，玉帛紛錯；若閱輿圖，都邑具列，名山大川，棊布星羅，昭然指掌
translation_en: …this responsibility: your servant is most fortunate, most fortunate! Previously, in the xinmao year of Jiajing [1531], I presided over the examination in the Southern Metropolitan Region; six years later, I presided over the examination in the Northern Metropolitan Region. Thus I had the opportunity to read the writings of scholars from the two metropolitan regions. Now, with scholars from throughout the realm gathered for examination, I have been able to survey fully the writings of the four quarters. In their diverse forms and varied styles, they are like the pearl of Sui and the jade disc of He, vying in brilliance and shining together; forthright arguments and excellent counsels emerge in constant succession. They investigate the origins of Heaven and humanity, extend the legacy of the august sovereigns and kings, elucidate the ultimate purport of the Way and virtue, and explore the mysteries of human nature and feeling. In civil affairs, they offer methods for ordering the realm; in military affairs, strategies for subduing disorder and securing peace. They interweave the Six Classics and range freely through the Hundred Schools. It is like inspecting tribute offerings: local products are displayed in their entirety, baskets piled thickly upon one another, jade and silk arrayed in profusion. It is like examining a map: capitals and cities are all set out, famous mountains and great rivers distributed like pieces on a game board or stars in the sky, as plainly visible as upon one’s palm…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
也天下之大觀備矣臣觀萬
國之會朝也分封而别壤殊
途而異轍及其戾止不敢後
先者大一統也羣士之敷言
也人殊其才性異其尚及其
合并莫敢異致者會
皇極也同文同軌之治猗歟盛哉
===
臣惟天下之生久矣宇宙貞
元之會唐虞三代以来僅僅
可數也是故至治之世不可
屢值
明聖之主能幾遇哉我
太祖高皇帝應
天受命驅逐胡虜而有天下正乾
alt_text:
也天下之大觀備矣臣觀萬
國之會朝也分封而別壤殊
途而異轍及其戾止不敢後
先者大一統也羣士之數言
也人殊其才性異其尚及其
合并莫敢異致者會
皇極也同文同軌之治猗歟盛哉
===
臣惟天下之生久矣宇宙貞
元之會唐虞三代以來僅僅
可數也是故至治之世不可
屢值
明聖之主能幾遇哉我
太祖高皇帝應
天受命驅逐胡虜而有天下正乾
punctuated:
也，天下之大觀備矣。臣觀萬國之會朝也，分封而别壤，殊途而異轍，及其戾止，不敢後先者，大一統也。羣士之敷言也，人殊其才，性異其尚，及其合并，莫敢異致者，會皇極也。同文同軌之治，猗歟盛哉！
臣惟天下之生久矣，宇宙貞元之會，唐虞三代以来，僅僅可數也。是故至治之世，不可屢值；明聖之主，能幾遇哉？我太祖高皇帝應天受命，驅逐胡虜而有天下，正乾
translation_en:
… Thus the grand spectacle of all under Heaven is complete. Your servant observes that when the myriad states assemble at court, their enfeoffed territories are distinct, and their routes and tracks differ; yet when they arrive, none dares come early or late, for they honor the great unity. When the assembled scholars expound their views, each differs in talent, and their dispositions incline them toward different preferences; yet when their views are brought together, none dares aim at a different end, for all converge upon the sovereign’s supreme standard. A realm governed with a common script and uniform carriage tracks—ah, how flourishing!
Your servant reflects that life under Heaven has endured a long time. Since the ages of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, the occasions when the cosmos has passed from completion into renewal can scarcely be counted more than a few times. Thus an age of consummate governance is seldom encountered; how often can one meet an enlightened and sage ruler? Our Emperor Taizu Gao responded to Heaven and received its mandate, drove out the northern barbarians, took possession of all under Heaven, and set right Heaven …

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
坤之大統昭日月之重明豐
功偉烈超出千古
聖子
神孫繩繩繼繼百八十年于茲矣
我
皇上
天縱
===
聖神誕膺
寶曆深仁厚澤丕冒遐邇際天
所覆極地所載莫不顒顒然
向風承德一統之治
皇極之行愈隆愈盛固其所哉然
則士生
今日豈非千載而一時也夫太

我皇上，天縱聖神，誕膺寶曆，深仁厚澤，丕冒遐邇。際天所覆，極地所載，莫不顒顒然向風承德。一統之治，皇極之行，愈隆愈盛，固其所哉！然則士生今日，豈非千載而一時也？夫太
translation_en:
…and Earth’s great succession, manifesting the renewed radiance of sun and moon. His abundant achievements and mighty deeds surpassed all antiquity. Sagely sons and divine grandsons have continued the succession without interruption, for one hundred and eighty years down to the present.
Our Emperor, endowed by Heaven with sagely and divine qualities, has gloriously assumed the imperial mandate. His profound benevolence and generous beneficence amply embrace those far and near. Throughout all that Heaven covers and Earth sustains, none fail to look reverently toward his influence and receive his virtue. That unified rule and the implementation of the August Ultimate should grow ever more exalted and flourishing is surely fitting! Thus, for scholars to be born in this day—is this not an opportunity occurring but once in a thousand years? Now, great…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
平之業以人而致亦以人而
守
國家求賢是急登進諸士將何
爲也臣用敢告曰
祖宗豐芑作養之仁
皇上禮樂陶鎔之化諸士漸被乆
矣茲當脫迹巖穴感奮風雲
===
致身之始其將何居夫士莫
先尚志而審所効法臣聞虞
有九官周有十人皆聖賢之
選也諸士能紹其芳躅矣乎
諸士實生虞周之時非是則
何式主司非是亦莫敢以告
先資自獻諸士則既已自許

punctuated: 平之業，以人而致，亦以人而守。國家求賢是急，登進諸士，將何爲也？臣用敢告曰：「祖宗豐芑作養之仁，皇上禮樂陶鎔之化，諸士漸被乆矣。茲當脫迹巖穴，感奮風雲，致身之始，其將何居？夫士莫先尚志，而審所効法。臣聞虞有九官，周有十人，皆聖賢之選也。諸士能紹其芳躅矣乎？諸士實生虞周之時，非是則何式？主司非是亦莫敢以告。先資自獻，諸士則既已自許
translation_en: …the enterprise of peace is achieved through men and is also preserved through men. The state makes seeking worthy men its urgent concern. To what end does it advance you gentlemen? Your servant therefore ventures to declare: “You gentlemen have long benefited from the ancestral emperors’ benevolent nurture of talent, like the cultivation of luxuriant millet, and from His Majesty’s transforming influence, which molds men through rites and music. Now, as you emerge from secluded retreats among cliffs and caves, stirred by this auspicious convergence of circumstances, and begin to enter public service, what position will you take? For a scholar, nothing comes before setting his aspirations high and carefully considering whom to emulate. Your servant has heard that Yu had nine officials and Zhou had ten men, all chosen from among sages and worthies. Can you gentlemen follow in their illustrious footsteps? You indeed live in an age like that of Yu and Zhou. Whom else, then, should you take as models? Nor would those presiding over the examination dare offer you any other counsel. In your earlier presentation of yourselves [?], you gentlemen have already pledged yourselves…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
矣許而弗克終主司者之所
懼也諸士念哉爲人臣而享
有祿位邦家之基生民之命
社稷之寄諸士與有關矣無負爾
所學無忝爾所舉無棄爾今
日之言慎乃恒德敬爾官守
陳力宣猷以弼
===
至治衍
宗社億萬年無疆之休主司有厚
望焉諸士尚其懋哉臣不佞
頃奉
明詔仰見
皇上慎重賢科務期得人至意惕
然恐不勝任諸士式克念爾

頃奉
明詔仰見
皇上愼重賢科務期得人至意惕
然恐不勝任諸士式克念爾
punctuated: 矣。許而弗克終，主司者之所懼也。諸士念哉！爲人臣而享有祿位，邦家之基、生民之命、社稷之寄，諸士與有關矣。無負爾所學，無忝爾所舉，無棄爾今日之言。慎乃恒德，敬爾官守，陳力宣猷，以弼至治，衍宗社億萬年無疆之休。主司有厚望焉，諸士尚其懋哉！臣不佞，頃奉明詔，仰見皇上慎重賢科、務期得人至意，惕然恐不勝任。諸士式克念爾
translation_en: …have already made this commitment. To commit yourselves yet fail to carry it through is what those presiding over the examination fear. Consider this, gentlemen! As servants of the ruler enjoying stipends and rank, you have a part in the foundations of the state, the lives of the people, and the charge of safeguarding the altars of soil and grain. Do not betray what you have learned, disgrace your selection, or abandon the words you have spoken today. Maintain constancy in virtue, attend reverently to your official duties, exert your strength, and carry forward sound plans, thereby assisting in the attainment of perfect government and extending the boundless blessings of the imperial ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain for countless millions of years. Those presiding over the examination have great expectations of you. Strive diligently, gentlemen! Your servant, lacking in ability, recently received the enlightened edict and perceived with reverence His Majesty’s earnest intention to treat this examination for worthy men with the utmost care and ensure that suitable men are obtained. In trepidation, I fear that I may not be equal to the task. Gentlemen, may you bear in mind your…

text:

法承

translation_en:
…the admonitions of your chief examiners, then perhaps we, your servants, may in some small measure discharge our responsibility to uphold the law and carry out the commands.
This preface is respectfully composed by Sun Cheng’en, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, Administrator for Assisting Governance, Grand Master for Proper Counsel, and Left Vice Minister of Personnel, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Twenty-sixth Year of Jiajing (1547)

Officials in Charge of the Examination:

Fei Cai, Grand Master for Assistance in Governance, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Rites concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zihe; he was from Yanshan County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the xinwei year (1511).

Xu Chengming, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites. His courtesy name was Siren; he was from Liaocheng County, Shandong, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Examiners:

Sun Cheng'en, in charge of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent, with the honorary ranks of Administrator for Assistance in Governance (zizhi yin) and Grand Master for Proper Counsel, and Left Vice Minister of Personnel concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhenfu; he was from Huating County in the directly administered metropolitan region, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Zhang Zhi, in charge of the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, and Right Vice Minister of Personnel concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Wenbang; he was from Chaling Subprefecture, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Associate Examiners:

Guo Pu, Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhifu; he was from Anyang County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Li Ji, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman of the Literary Service (wenlin lang). His courtesy name was Bangzai; he was from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Zhao Zhenji, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman of the Literary Service. His courtesy name was Mengjing; he was from Neijiang County, Sichuan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Pan Sheng, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman of the Literary Service. His courtesy name was Siming; he was from Xinchang County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Yan Ne, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman of the Literary Service. His courtesy name was Minqing; he was registered in Wu County in the directly administered metropolitan region and was a native of Changshu County. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Gao Yi, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman of the Literary Service. His courtesy name was Zixiang; he was from Qiantang County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Qu Jingchun, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman of the Literary Service. His courtesy name was Shidao; he was from Changshu County in the directly administered metropolitan region, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiachen year (1544).

Lin Shusheng, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman of the Literary Service. His courtesy name was Yuji; he was from Huating County in the directly administered metropolitan region, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Wang Cai, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman for Summoned Service (zhengshi lang). His courtesy name was Zinan; he was from Xincheng County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Chen Yiqin, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the honorary rank of Gentleman for Summoned Service. His courtesy name was Yifu; he was from Nanchong County, Sichuan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

translation_en:
Chao Zao, Hanlin Academy Examining Editor, held the rank of Gentleman for Promoting Service. His courtesy name was Junshi; he was from Kaizhou, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Zheng Datong was Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel. His courtesy name was Jiewu; he was from Putian County, Fujian, and was a metropolitan graduate of the year transcribed as “sichou” [?; probably jichou, 1529].

Li Lun, Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Rites, held the rank of Gentleman for Rendering Service. His courtesy name was Deyan; he was registered in Huai'an Guard under the Wanquan Regional Military Commission and was a native of Yingshang County, Zhili. He was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year (1538).

He Yunyan, Right Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Works, held the rank of Gentleman for Promoting Service. His courtesy name was Shibin; he was from Fenshui County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Chen Feng, a Principal Secretary acting as Director of the Guangxi Bureau in the Ministry of Justice, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. His courtesy name was Yubo; he was registered in the Nanjing Rear Guard of the Reserve and was a native of Jinhua County, Zhejiang. He was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year (1535).

Li Shichun, Principal Secretary of the Bureau of Personnel in the Ministry of Personnel, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. His courtesy name was Yiyuan; he was from Guangzhou, Henan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year (1538).

Wu Weiyue, Principal Secretary of the Jiangxi Bureau in the Ministry of Justice, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. His courtesy name was Junbo; he was from Xiaofeng County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year (1538).

Examination Monitoring Officials:

Huang Shou, Investigating Censor for the Shandong Circuit, held the rank of Gentleman for Serving Literature. His courtesy name was Gongpei; he was from the Ningxia Central Garrison Guard, Shaanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the year transcribed as “sichou” [?; probably jichou, 1529].

Chen Chuxiu, Investigating Censor for the Shandong Circuit, held the rank of Gentleman for Serving Literature. His courtesy name was Shunbi; he was from Nan'an County, Fujian, and was a metropolitan graduate of the renchen year (1532).

Proctors:

Li Chong, Principal Secretary of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. His courtesy name was Rucheng; he was from Jingyang County, Shaanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year (1538).

Zhang Huan, Principal Secretary of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the rank of Gentleman for Straightforward Service. His courtesy name was Maoshi; he was registered in Changzhou County, Zhili, and was a native of Wu County. He was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year (1538).

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Wu Chun, a Vice Director acting as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the rank of Grand Master for Upright Service. His courtesy name was Yirong; he was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year (1538).

Yuan Gun, a Principal Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the rank of Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. His courtesy name was Buzhi; he was from Wu County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year (1538).

Officials Responsible for Collecting and Keeping Examination Scripts:

Li Cong, a Central Secretariat Drafter, held the rank of Gentleman for Promoting Service. His courtesy name was Zhongying; he was from Renqiu County, Zhili, and was a student admitted by virtue of his family's official status.

Yingfeng (𨾏應鳳; surname reading uncertain [?]) was Right Case Reviewer in the Right Office of the Court of Judicial Review [?]. His courtesy name was Dahe; he was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and was a Confucian scholar.

Officials Receiving Examination Scripts

Lao Zhang, Vice Prefect of Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi, had the courtesy name Jingcai. He was from Chongde County, Zhejiang, and was a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the gengwu year.

Qian Qi, Assistant Prefect of Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, had the courtesy name Zijing. He was registered with the Imperial Medical Institute, was originally from Wu County in the directly administered metropolitan region (Zhili), and was a tribute scholar of the jiawu year.

Zhao Wen, Assistant Prefect of Ningguo Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Zhong’an. He was from Huo Subprefecture, Shanxi, and was a National University student.

Cai Jida, Magistrate of Shanyang County in Huai’an Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Wangzhi. He was from Tong’an County, Fujian, and was a tribute scholar of the dingyou year.

Officials Sealing Candidates’ Identifying Information

Zhang Ji, Supernumerary Vice Prefect of Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Shiwei. He belonged to the official register of Yunnan Right Guard and was a tribute scholar of the renwu year.

Wang Jiao, Assistant Prefect of Yuezhou Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Jingfu. He was from Qinghe County, Zhili, and was a National University student.

Li Can, Magistrate of Wanzai County in Yuanzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, had the courtesy name Yingming. He was from Changzhou County, Zhili, and was a tribute scholar of the wuzi year.

Gong Shu, Magistrate of Xiangshan County in Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, had the courtesy name Jindao. He was from Changzhou County, Zhili, and was a tribute scholar of the jiawu year.

Transcription Officials

Zhou Han, Prefectural Judge of Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Xuanzhang. He was from Shenze County, Zhili, and was a tribute scholar of the xinmao year.

Luo Hong, Magistrate of Su Subprefecture in Fengyang Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Chongdao. He was from Cixi County, Zhejiang, and was a tribute scholar of the wuzi year.

Luo Yingshi, Magistrate of Nanxi County in Xuzhou Prefecture, Sichuan, had the courtesy name Daozhong. He was from Yunnan Right Guard and was a tribute scholar of the jiawu year.

Xu Wenxian, Magistrate of Jianshi County in Kuizhou Prefecture, Sichuan, had the courtesy name Liyuan. He was from Changzhou County, Zhili, and was a National University student.

Proofreading Officials

Guo Xi, Assistant Prefect of Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, had the courtesy name Xinqing. He was from Feixiang County, Zhili, and was a tribute scholar of the xinmao year.

Long Yun, Magistrate of Gong’an County, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Bocong. He was from Lingui County, Guangxi, and was a tribute student of the wuzi year.

Wang Rui, Magistrate of Heshui County, Qingyang Prefecture, Shaanxi, had the courtesy name Deyuan. He was from Xiangfu County, Henan, and was a tribute student of the wuzi year.

Ye Zhenheng, Magistrate of Qian’an County, Yongping Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Mengyuan. His household was registered with a battalion of the Guangning Central Garrison Guard; he was originally from Yongchuan County, Sichuan, and was a tribute student of the gengzi year.

Patrol and Gate Supervision Officials

Hu Lian, General of Manifest Valor (Zhaoyong jiangjun) and Guard Commander of the Ninghai Guard, Shandong, had the courtesy name Ruqi. He was from Guangzhou Subprefecture, Henan.

Li Xigeng, General of Manifest Might (Mingwei jiangjun) and Assistant Commander of the Jining Guard, Shandong, had the courtesy name Tangbin. He was from Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture.

Wu Liangchen, General of Manifest Might and Assistant Commander of the Huaiqing Guard, Henan, had the courtesy name Yuanzhong. He was from Tongcheng County, Zhili.

Zhang Dong, General of Manifest Might and Assistant Commander of the Laizhou Guard, Shandong, had the courtesy name Chaozhu. He was from Nanchang County, Jiangxi.

Zhang Rujiao, General of Manifest Might and Assistant Commander of the Lingshan Guard, Shandong, had the courtesy name Ziming. He was from Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture.

Liu Tian’en, General of Manifest Might and Assistant Commander of the Yizhen Guard, Zhili, had the courtesy name Junchong. He was from Taizhou Subprefecture, Zhili.

Provisioning Officials

Liu Wenguang was an Office Manager acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Catering in the Ministry of Rites. His courtesy name was Zishi; he was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute student of the wuzi year.

Li Guoji, Gentleman for Fostering Virtue (Chengde lang) and Assistant Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Zhengzhi. He was from Ningdu County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute student of the renwu year.

Li Anguo, Gentleman of Scholarly Excellence (Wenlin lang) and Vice Magistrate of Wanping County, Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Dingzhi. He was from Tongzhou Subprefecture, Zhili, and was a student of the Imperial Academy.

Wang Shishen, Gentleman of Scholarly Excellence and Vice Magistrate of Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Daoxian. He was from Yancheng County, Henan, and was a student of the Imperial Academy.

Wang Zhongjie, Gentleman of Scholarly Excellence and Vice Magistrate of Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Yongzhen. He was from Ninghai County, Zhejiang, and was a student of the Imperial Academy.

Mo Zijing, Gentleman of Scholarly Excellence and Vice Magistrate of Wanping County, Shuntian Prefecture, had the courtesy name Xiren. He was from She County, Zhili, and was a student of the Imperial Academy.

四書
固天縱之將聖又多能也
中也者天下之大本也和也者天下之達
道也致中和天地位焉萬物育焉
禹思天下有溺者由己溺之也稷思天下
有饑者由己饑之也是以如是其急也

君子黃中通理正位居體美在其中而暢
===

節亨剛柔分而剛得中

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

固天縱之將聖，又多能也。

中也者，天下之大本也；和也者，天下之達道也。致中和，天地位焉，萬物育焉。

禹思天下有溺者，由己溺之也；稷思天下有饑者，由己饑之也，是以如是其急也。

易

君子黃中通理，正位居體，美在其中，而暢於四支，發於事業，美之至也。

節，亨。剛柔分，而剛得中。

聖人以此齋戒，以神明其德夫！

和順於道德，而理於義；窮理盡性，以至於命。

書

安汝止，惟幾惟康。其弼直，惟動丕應，徯志。

以昭受上帝，天其申命用休。

厥田惟中下，厥賦貞，作十有三載乃同。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Surely Heaven has endowed him with the qualities of a sage, and he also possesses many abilities.”

“Equilibrium is the great foundation of all under Heaven; harmony is the universally followed Way of all under Heaven. When equilibrium and harmony are fully realized, Heaven and Earth take their proper places, and the myriad things flourish.”

“Yu thought that if anyone under Heaven drowned, it was as though he himself had drowned that person; Ji thought that if anyone under Heaven went hungry, it was as though he himself had caused that person’s hunger. That is why they were so urgent in their efforts.”

Book of Changes (Yijing)

“The gentleman embodies the yellow of the center and comprehends the underlying patterns; he occupies his proper position and abides in his essential form. Beauty resides within him, extends through his four limbs, and manifests itself in his undertakings. This is beauty at its utmost.”

“Restraint: success. The firm and yielding lines are apportioned, and the firm obtains the central position.”

“By this the sage purifies himself and observes abstinence, thereby making his virtue spiritually luminous!”

“They accord harmoniously with the Way and its virtue, and are ordered according to rightness. They investigate principle to its utmost and fully realize their nature, thereby attaining an understanding of Heaven’s mandate.”

Book of Documents (Shujing)

“Rest securely in your proper place; attend to the first signs of events and to tranquility. Let those who assist you be upright; then whenever you act, all will respond abundantly, awaiting your intentions.”

“Thereby gloriously receive the favor of the Lord on High; Heaven will renew its mandate with blessings.”

“Its fields were of the lower-middle grade, and its tax assessment was fixed. Only after thirteen years of work did it become equal to the others.”

意如、叔弓、仲孫貜帥師伐莒。〔昭公十年〕
禮記
天子以德為車，以樂為御；諸侯以禮相與，大夫以法相序，士以信相考，百姓以睦相守，天下之肥也。
升中于天，而鳳皇降，龜龍假；饗帝于郊，而風雨節，寒暑時。
禮樂偩天地之情，達神明之德，降興上下之神，而凝是精粗之體，領父子君臣之節。
君子敬則用祭器，是以不廢日月，不違龜筮，以敬事其君長，是以上不瀆於民，下不褻於上。
第貳塲
論
聖人之於天道。
詔誥表〔內科一道〕

translation_en:
… Yiru, Shu Gong, and Zhongsun Jue led an army to attack Ju. 〔Tenth year of Duke Zhao.〕
Book of Rites
The Son of Heaven takes virtue as his carriage and music as his charioteer. The feudal lords deal with one another through ritual propriety; the great officers establish their relative order through rules; the gentlemen assess one another through trustworthiness; and the common people sustain one another through harmony. This is the flourishing of All under Heaven.
When completed achievements are reported to Heaven, phoenixes descend, and turtles and dragons arrive. When the Supreme Lord is offered sacrifice in the suburban rite, wind and rain are measured, and cold and heat come in their proper seasons.
Rites and music accord with the inherent nature of Heaven and Earth, communicate the potency of spiritual powers, bring down and raise up the spirits above and below, give stable form to both the subtle and the gross, and govern the proper relationships between father and son, ruler and minister.
When the gentleman acts with reverence, he uses sacrificial vessels. Thus he does not neglect the appointed days and months or disregard divination by turtle shell and milfoil, and he serves his ruler and superiors with reverence. Consequently, those above do not treat the people disrespectfully, and those below do not show disrespect toward those above.
Second Session
Discourse
The sage in relation to the Way of Heaven.
Edicts, Proclamations, and Memorials 〔One question in this category [?].〕

Five legal judgments: recommending and appointing officials and clerks with past offenses; determining household status by the registers; offering sacrifices to deities included in the sacrificial canon; requesting military supplies at the frontier; arranging joint hearings of lawsuits involving military personnel and civilians.
Third Session
Five Policy Questions
Question: Confucius said that the modifications to Zhou ritual could be known even a hundred generations hence. Ritual is therefore the instrument by which sage kings receive Heaven’s unfolding mandate and govern the world. Over the course of a hundred generations, Heaven must bring forth sages and wise men who personally undertake transmission and creation, further refining and embellishing ritual. Thus it gradually flourishes and becomes more fully elucidated, so that its influence can extend without limit. title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
本歟爾諸士究心理學是必有折衷前
聞以是正諸家之說者幸究言之毋自
諉曰尊所聞也
問儒者抱業求自見於世其於當時之務
未有不究心者試舉近日
廷謨之大者二事與多士商之
國家財賦倚於東南轉漕山東入于通惠歲
輸大司農者四百萬石此
祖宗定制也頃以災歉之故稍從折變邊圉告
===
棘間亦藉為餽給然
國儲則漸損矣
皇上責成計部必全復舊徵誠治安之長策也
而或者則慮應邊之不裕或謂諸邊餽
給原不資於太倉或又謂邊郡逋負之
久凶饉之傷而調募之衆多非取助于
太倉不可然歟否歟茲欲使內儲不移
外餉恒足其策安在歟
國家邊防重於西北慎守東勝達于黑山阻

國儲則漸損矣
皇上責成計部必全復舊徵誠治安之長策也
而或者則慮邊之不裕或謂諸邊餽
給原不慮於太倉或又謂邊郡逋負之
久凶饉之偏而調募之衆多非取助於
太倉卒可熟歟否歟茲欲使內儲不移
外餉恒足其策安在歟
國家邊防重於西北慎守東勝達于黑山阻
punctuated:
本歟？爾諸士究心理學，是必有折衷前聞，以是正諸家之說者，幸究言之，毋自諉曰：「尊所聞也。」
問：儒者抱業求自見於世，其於當時之務，未有不究心者。試舉近日廷謨之大者二事，與多士商之。國家財賦倚於東南，轉漕山東，入于通惠，歲輸大司農者四百萬石，此祖宗定制也。頃以災歉之故，稍從折變；邊圉告棘，間亦藉為餽給，然國儲則漸損矣。皇上責成計部，必全復舊徵，誠治安之長策也。而或者則慮應邊之不裕，或謂諸邊餽給原不資於太倉，或又謂邊郡逋負之久、凶饉之傷，而調募之衆多，非取助于太倉不可。然歟？否歟？茲欲使內儲不移，外餉恒足，其策安在歟？國家邊防重於西北，慎守東勝，達于黑山，阻
translation_en:
…the root? You scholars have devoted yourselves to the learning of principle; surely you have weighed what you have previously learned and thereby corrected the teachings of the various schools. Please discuss this fully, without excusing yourselves by saying, “We revere what we have been taught.”
Question: Confucian scholars, possessing scholarly attainments and seeking to make themselves known in the world, invariably devote thought to the affairs of their time. Let us take two major matters recently deliberated at court and discuss them with you scholars.
The state's fiscal revenues depend upon the southeast. Grain is transported through Shandong into the Tonghui Canal, with four million shi delivered annually to the Grand Minister of Agriculture. This is the established system of our imperial ancestors. Recently, because of disasters and poor harvests, some payments have been permitted in commuted form. When urgent trouble arose on the frontiers, these revenues were also occasionally drawn upon to supply them. The state's reserves, however, have gradually diminished. His Majesty has charged the Ministry of Revenue with fully restoring the former levies: this is indeed a long-term policy for orderly and peaceful government. Yet some fear that provision for the frontiers will be insufficient. Some say that frontier supplies originally did not depend on the Court of the Imperial Granaries; others say that, with the frontier prefectures long in arrears, suffering from famine, and having so many troops transferred and recruited there, assistance from the Court of the Imperial Granaries is indispensable. Is this so or not? What policy would now keep the internal reserves from being diverted while ensuring that supplies for the troops beyond are always sufficient?
The state's frontier defenses are concentrated in the northwest, with Dongsheng closely guarded and extending to Heishan, relying on … as a barrier.

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
其故何歟夫當時之將若魏尚李廣耿
恭段熲張奐皇甫規之徒特一太守刺
史校尉之任耳而震懾強虜坐制諸羌
今大將擁旄憲臣開府而虜騎長驅狼
奔豕突往歲喋血于太原繼又鳴鏑於
宣府繼又飲馬於涇原矣懸軍深入兵
家所忌彼獨不畏者何歟且宣元之世
而叩關納欵稽顙稱臣遣子入侍今以
聖治之隆
===
聖化之遠而夷情反覆變詐不常假市貢為窺
伺之計譯番文無真正之言花當則脅
求添貢把兒孫則深入虜掠今諸番先
期擾動糜費廩餼邊臣不能阻回至煩
朝廷切責此其悖慢甚矣豈天厚其毒而潰
之歟將佑啟
神功駿烈以成中興之盛也諸士子藏器待時
久矣行將與謀帷幄之中其何以佐修
攘之計乎願試陳之以觀濟時之畧

聖化之遠而夷情反覆變詐不常假市貢爲窺

求添貢把兒孫則深入虜掠今諸番先
期擾動糜費廩餼邊臣不能阻回至煩
朝廷切責此其悖慢甚矣豈天厚其毒而潰
之歟將佑啓
神功駿烈以成中興之盛也諸士子蘊器待時
久矣行將與謀帷幄之中其何以佐修
攘之計乎願試陳之以觀濟時之畧
punctuated: 其故何歟？夫當時之將，若魏尚、李廣、耿恭、段熲、張奐、皇甫規之徒，特一太守、刺史、校尉之任耳，而震懾強虜，坐制諸羌。今大將擁旄，憲臣開府，而虜騎長驅，狼奔豕突。往歲喋血于太原，繼又鳴鏑於宣府，繼又飲馬於涇原矣。懸軍深入，兵家所忌，彼獨不畏者何歟？且宣元之世，而叩關納欵，稽顙稱臣，遣子入侍。今以聖治之隆、聖化之遠，而夷情反覆，變詐不常，假市貢為窺伺之計，譯番文無真正之言。花當則脅求添貢，把兒孫則深入虜掠。今諸番先期擾動，糜費廩餼，邊臣不能阻回，至煩朝廷切責，此其悖慢甚矣！豈天厚其毒而潰之歟？將佑啟神功駿烈，以成中興之盛也？諸士子藏器待時久矣，行將與謀帷幄之中，其何以佐修攘之計乎？願試陳之，以觀濟時之畧。
translation_en:
… What accounts for this? The generals of those times—men such as Wei Shang, Li Guang, Geng Gong, Duan Jiong, Zhang Huan, and Huangfu Gui—held only the posts of governor, regional inspector, or commandant. Yet they struck terror into powerful enemies and kept the various Qiang peoples under control with ease. Today, great generals bear command banners and censorial officials establish headquarters, yet enemy cavalry ride deep into our territory, rushing like wolves and charging like boars. In past years they shed blood at Taiyuan; next they sounded their whistling arrows at Xuanfu; then they watered their horses at Jingyuan. To advance deep into hostile territory with an isolated army is something military strategists warn against. Why do these enemies alone have no fear of it?

Moreover, in the reigns of Emperors Xuan and Yuan of the Han, they came to the frontier gates to offer submission, knocked their foreheads upon the ground and acknowledged themselves as subjects, and sent their sons to attend at court. Today, despite the flourishing of sagely government and the far-reaching influence of sagely transformation, the foreigners are fickle in their intentions and endlessly change their deceptions. They use trade and tribute as a pretext for spying upon us, and translations of their writings contain no truthful words. Huadang uses threats to demand permission to bring additional tribute, while Ba’ersun penetrates deep into our territory to take captives and plunder. Now the various foreign groups cause disturbances before the appointed time and squander provisions. Frontier officials cannot turn them back, so that the court has had to issue stern reprimands. Their defiance and insolence are indeed extreme! Is Heaven allowing their wickedness to grow so as to bring about their ruin? Or will it lend its aid and open the way for divine achievements and magnificent deeds, bringing a glorious dynastic restoration to fruition?

You candidates have long kept your abilities in reserve, awaiting your opportunity. Soon you will take part in deliberations within the command tent. How will you assist in planning measures to strengthen internal government and repel external foes? Set forth your views, so that we may assess your strategies for meeting the needs of the times.

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Surely Heaven has endowed him to be a great sage; he also has many abilities.”

Qin Liang

Associate Examiner Zheng, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “The two words ‘endowed’ and ‘also’ are particularly difficult to expound. A dry treatment fails to convey their meaning fully; a rambling one loses relevance. This essay is concise in expression yet complete in meaning, distinguishing it from the work of the other candidates. Include it.”

Associate Examiner Chao, Examining Editor, comments: “The argument is precise, and its exposition of principle complete and pure. It sufficiently demonstrates learning with a firm foundation. Include it.”

Associate Examiner Pan, Compiler, comments: “It ably brings out Zigong’s meaning, while its diction and style possess an antique elegance. This is surely the work of someone who has studied deeply and attained understanding.”

Associate Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Refined in thought and elegant in expression, this is among the finest essays on the meaning of the Analects. It should be included as a model.”

Examiner Zhang, Academician, comments: “Its explanation of sagehood and of having many abilities is clear and exhaustive.”

Examiner Sun, Academician, comments: “The exposition is precise and thorough.”

The worthy man explains that the Way of the sage reaches to Heaven and cannot be apprehended through limited understanding. For the Way of the sage is the Way of Heaven. To regard having many abilities as constituting sagehood is itself evidence of limited understanding. Is this not why Zigong, in addressing the Grand Steward, spoke of Heaven’s endowment? title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
曰天之於人也有所厚有所不厚斯人之於天
也有所能有所不能何則流行賦予聖人之於
人同類也而知愚賢不肖之等異焉惟聖人則
以其身而立天地民物之極聰明睿智自生民
以来未之或盛者殆非人所能與蓋天縱之以
聖而聖人之所不能違焉者矣降衷秉彝聖人
之性與人同也而仁知百姓之見拘焉惟聖人
則以其心而體天地萬物之理生知安行其至
神之妙不可以名者有非人所能及蓋聖人不
===
自限於天而天亦不能為之限焉者矣是故自
其大者觀之聖則無所不能然不知渾然全體
之中自具夫泛應曲當之用才全德備不可以
偏長目也夫所謂多能者乃其事之餘耳豈足
以盡聖道之全哉自其小者觀之多能亦可以
言聖然不知一才一藝之美不可語天道精微
之極聖神功化殆難以方所求也夫所謂聖者
一以貫之者耳又何止於多能之小哉蓋聖者
道之至而天所成也謂夫子為聖者似足以知

punctuated: 曰：「天之於人也，有所厚，有所不厚；斯人之於天也，有所能，有所不能。何則？流行賦予，聖人之於人，同類也，而知愚賢不肖之等異焉。惟聖人則以其身而立天地民物之極，聰明睿智，自生民以来未之或盛者，殆非人所能與。蓋天縱之以聖，而聖人之所不能違焉者矣。降衷秉彝，聖人之性與人同也，而仁知百姓之見拘焉。惟聖人則以其心而體天地萬物之理，生知安行，其至神之妙不可以名者，有非人所能及。蓋聖人不自限於天，而天亦不能為之限焉者矣。是故自其大者觀之，聖則無所不能，然不知渾然全體之中，自具夫泛應曲當之用。才全德備，不可以偏長目也。夫所謂多能者，乃其事之餘耳，豈足以盡聖道之全哉？自其小者觀之，多能亦可以言聖，然不知一才一藝之美，不可語天道精微之極。聖神功化，殆難以方所求也。夫所謂聖者，一以貫之者耳，又何止於多能之小哉？蓋聖者，道之至而天所成也。謂夫子為聖者，似足以知
translation_en:
…was as follows: “Heaven endows some people generously and others less generously; accordingly, people have things they can and cannot do by virtue of Heaven’s endowment. Why is this? In the flowing forth and bestowal of that endowment, the sage belongs to the same kind as other people, yet distinctions arise between the wise and foolish, the worthy and unworthy. Only the sage, through his own person, establishes the ultimate standard for Heaven and Earth, the people and all things. His perceptiveness and sagely wisdom, unsurpassed since humankind first came into being, are surely beyond what others can match. Heaven has indeed granted him sagehood without restraint, and this is something that even the sage cannot contravene. In receiving the inner moral norm bestowed by Heaven and holding to the constant principles, the sage’s nature is the same as that of others; yet the benevolent, the wise, and the common people are confined by their respective perceptions. Only the sage, through his mind, embodies the principles of Heaven and Earth and the myriad things. He knows them from birth and puts them into practice with ease; the ineffable subtlety of his supremely numinous capacity lies beyond others’ reach. The sage does not confine himself within limits attributed to Heaven, nor can Heaven impose limits upon him.

“Thus, viewed in its greater aspect, sagehood entails being capable of everything. Yet people fail to understand that within its integrated wholeness there inherently resides the capacity to respond to all circumstances and deal fittingly with every particular. Complete in talent and fully endowed with virtue, the sage cannot be characterized by a single special proficiency. What is called versatility is merely incidental to his undertakings: how could it encompass the whole of the sagely Way? Viewed in its lesser aspect, versatility, too, may be used to speak of sagehood. Yet people fail to understand that excellence in a single talent or art cannot express the utmost subtlety of Heaven’s Way. The transformative achievements of the sage’s numinous power can scarcely be sought within fixed bounds. What is called sagehood is simply having one principle running through everything. How could it be confined to the lesser matter of versatility? Sagehood is indeed the culmination of the Way, brought to completion by Heaven. To call the Master a sage would seem sufficient to understand…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
心此作以心字立說發出聖人精蘊必邃於
心學者
同考試官編修李批詞理俱到而大本達道
位育處尤發揮透徹可以占所養矣
考試官學士張批是知心學者之語
考試官學士孫批體認精審
中庸言道具於人之心盡其心則盡道矣盖心
統乎道合天地萬物而一者也能盡其心則位
育之功至矣夫豈待於外哉子思之意曰天下
===
無心外之道君子有盡心之學今夫人之一心
以其體之本然而無所偏倚者之謂中是中也
即天所命於人以為性寂然不動而喜怒哀樂
之機已根於此所以涵天地萬物之理於靜虛
者也盖無一理之不具故不待於外而無所不
備矣非天下之大本乎以其用之自然而無所
乖戾者之謂和是和也即人所率於性而為道
隨感而應通天下古今之人而無或不同所以
循天地萬物之情而順動者也盖無一物之不

For the heart-mind embraces the Way, uniting Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things into one. If one can fully realize one’s heart-mind, the achievement of bringing Heaven and Earth into their proper positions and nurturing the myriad things will reach its culmination. How could this depend on anything external? Consider the single heart-mind of a human being. Its substance, in its original condition, without deviation or inclination, is called equilibrium. This equilibrium is precisely what Heaven confers upon human beings as their nature. Still and unmoving, it already contains the roots from which pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy arise. It is that whereby the principles of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are encompassed in stillness and emptiness. Since there is no principle it does not possess, it depends on nothing external and lacks nothing. Is this not the great foundation of all under Heaven? text:
得故不假於人而無所不周矣非天下之達道
乎夫道之具於人心其體用如此君子於此誠
能存戒懼於不睹不聞之時約而至於至靜之
中不使有一毫之偏倚則極其中而大本立矣
辨善惡於隱微幽獨之地精而至於應物之處
不使有一毫之差謬則極其和而大用行矣由
是吾心之中即天地之中吾心既不違於中則
天地亦不能違吾心而有所不位矣陰陽動靜
各止其所殆與心而同其神乎萬物之和即吾
===
心之和和既極於吾心則萬物亦不能違吾心
而有所不育矣懽忻交通充塞無間殆與心而
一其化乎蓋至是而體道之功無以加矣然皆
始於心焉向使須臾之不敬一念之未純則與
天地不相似而萬物且違之矣况得而位育之
哉此君子所以貴有盡心之學也雖然堯舜之
道亦不過此危微精一之訓萬世治天下之法
也後世心學不明去道益遠而唐虞之化不復
見者豈不可深慨哉此子思所以憂天下而作

Such are the substance and functioning of the Way inherent in the human heart. If the gentleman can truly preserve vigilance and apprehension when nothing is seen or heard, gathering himself inward until he reaches utter stillness and permitting not the slightest deviation or bias, then he brings his equilibrium to its utmost and establishes the great foundation. If he distinguishes good from evil in what is hidden and subtle, in solitude unseen by others, refining his discernment through to his responses to things and permitting not the slightest error, then he brings his harmony to its utmost and puts its great functioning into practice. Thus, the equilibrium of my heart is the equilibrium of Heaven and Earth. Once my heart does not depart from equilibrium, Heaven and Earth likewise cannot depart from my heart and leave anything out of its proper place. Once harmony reaches its utmost in my heart, the myriad things likewise cannot depart from my heart and leave anything unnurtured. Joyful communion pervades everything without a gap: do they not indeed become one with the heart in their transforming activity? At this point, the achievement of embodying the Way can advance no further; yet it all begins in the heart. Were there even a moment’s lack of reverence or a single thought not wholly pure, one would no longer accord with Heaven and Earth, and the myriad things would turn away. …examining the suitability of the uplands and lowlands and distinguishing the properties of the five grains, he labored urgently, intent only on bringing the people into a condition of adequate food and warmth before he would rest. Since Ji felt concern for the hunger of all under Heaven as though he himself were hungry, he could not but relieve their suffering from famine. The reason for passing his gate three times without entering was that Yu and Ji truly wished to devote themselves to all under Heaven. How could they have delighted in exhausting themselves? Alas! Heaven brings forth sages and worthies for the people's sake; thus their hearts never forget the people under Heaven, even for a single day. Yet their circumstances differ, and when they cannot fulfill their love for the people, they can only find joy within themselves. Thus Master Yan's joy was not joy in forgetting all under Heaven: he had no other course. In saying that Yu, Ji, and Yan Hui followed the same Way, Mengzi deeply lamented Yan Hui's unfulfilled aspirations. Was this not also Mengzi lamenting his own aspirations?

考試官學士孫批說理明暢
文言於坤之六五著其內外之善而賛其合一
之盛也夫君子之道內外合一而體用無間也
積於中而發於外其斯以為盛乎文言什坤爻
六五而以君道言之若此夫黄裳者中順之象
也中順者君所具之德也以中言之不偏不倚
===
而體全於未發之前惟精惟一而迹泯於先幾
之始淵乎其凝天命而涵衆理之會通也湛乎
其行達道而具萬事之條理也有黄之象焉故
曰黄以言乎中之色也以順言之無好無惡不
恃位而居物之先不驕不亢每虛己以受人之
感退然養其至和而勢不足以汩其真也夷然
安於後動而物不足以亂其守也有裳之象焉
故曰裳以言乎下之飾也夫中順雖有內外之
殊而其道則無二致盖中所以立順之體而順

He is discerning and single-minded, and all traces disappear at the very inception, before the first stirrings. How profound his consolidation of Heaven’s mandate and his embrace of the convergence and interconnection of all principles! title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
不可惡矣義者道德之散見以為用者也易則
隨其事物之宜而揆以中正之則凡所以辨是
非之等以明得失之報者雜而不越也開而當
名也盖言天下之至動而不可亂矣夫易所謂
極體用之全者盖如此由是天下之理其散殊
者雖至萬也莫不於易而窮之以幽明之故則
察以晝夜之道則知而天地萬物無復遁情焉
人物之性其賦予者至不一也莫不於易而盡
之知之無不明處之無不當而裁成品節各適
===
其道焉然命者又理與性之所從出也理無不
窮則易之所以通知而無外者盖與流行不已
之真机渾融矣形下者其形上之體乎性無不
盡則易之所以曲成而不遺者盖與太極無妄
之化相流通矣至變者其至神之用乎夫易所
謂貫顯微之妙者盖如此由是而觀則天道非
易不能明易非聖人不能作天也易也聖人也
夫何間然哉抑論之易者人之心也人不能皆
聖人故聖人作易以告之使由是皆得其心焉

punctuated:
不可惡矣。義者，道德之散見以為用者也。易則隨其事物之宜，而揆以中正之則，凡所以辨是非之等，以明得失之報者，雜而不越也，開而當名也。盖言天下之至動，而不可亂矣。夫易所謂極體用之全者，盖如此。由是，天下之理，其散殊者雖至萬也，莫不於易而窮之；以幽明之故則察，以晝夜之道則知，而天地萬物無復遁情焉。人物之性，其賦予者至不一也，莫不於易而盡之；知之無不明，處之無不當，而裁成品節，各適其道焉。
然命者，又理與性之所從出也。理無不窮，則易之所以通知而無外者，盖與流行不已之真机渾融矣。形下者，其形上之體乎？性無不盡，則易之所以曲成而不遺者，盖與太極無妄之化相流通矣。至變者，其至神之用乎？夫易所謂貫顯微之妙者，盖如此。
由是而觀，則天道非易不能明，易非聖人不能作。天也，易也，聖人也，夫何間然哉？抑論之，易者，人之心也。人不能皆聖人，故聖人作易以告之，使由是皆得其心焉
translation_en:
…yet cannot be regarded with aversion. Righteousness is the diverse manifestation of the Way and its virtue in their functioning. The Changes follows what is fitting for particular things and affairs and measures them against the standard of centrality and correctness. In distinguishing degrees of right and wrong and clarifying the consequences of success and failure, it embraces complexity without overstepping bounds and unfolds distinctions with names appropriate to them. Thus it speaks of the utmost movement under Heaven, yet cannot be thrown into disorder. Such is what is meant by saying that the Changes encompasses the fullness of substance and function. Hence, although the differentiated principles of the world number in the myriad, none fails to be fully investigated through the Changes. Through it one discerns the causes of the hidden and the manifest and understands the way of day and night; thus Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things can no longer conceal their true circumstances. Although the natures endowed upon people and things are exceedingly diverse, none fails to be fully realized through the Changes. Understanding is invariably clear, and the handling of things invariably appropriate; through shaping, completing, grading, and regulating them, each is brought into accord with its proper way.
Heaven’s mandate, however, is also that from which principle and nature issue. When no principle remains uninvestigated, the comprehensive understanding of the Changes, which leaves nothing outside its scope, is wholly fused with the true motive force that circulates without cease. Is that which lies below form not the substance of that which lies above form? When no nature remains unrealized, the Changes’ capacity to bring each thing to completion according to its particular circumstances, omitting nothing, interpenetrates the unerring transformations of the Supreme Ultimate. Is utmost change not the functioning of utmost spiritual efficacy? Such is what is meant by saying that the Changes penetrates the subtle workings of the manifest and the hidden.
Viewed in this light, the Way of Heaven cannot be made clear without the Changes, and the Changes could not have been composed without the sages. Heaven, the Changes, and the sages—what separation could there be among them? To consider the matter further, the Changes is the human heart-mind. Since people cannot all be sages, the sages composed the Changes to instruct them, so that through it all might recover their own heart-minds…

text:

閑邪以存誠順適乎道心之正主敬以直内允
孚乎天德之純存於心者欲其無邪慝焉事乃
一心之用不審于事則動之所以妄也必惟幾
以省其發而致嚴于理欲之分惟康以省其安
而深憂乎悔吝之介見於行者欲其無繆戾焉
而又左右之臣皆以正君為急繩愆糾繆非徒

punctuated: 心為萬化之原，不得其止，則心之所以危也。必閑邪以存誠，順適乎道心之正；主敬以直内，允孚乎天德之純。存於心者，欲其無邪慝焉。事乃一心之用，不審于事，則動之所以妄也。必惟幾以省其發，而致嚴于理欲之分；惟康以省其安，而深憂乎悔吝之介。見於行者，欲其無繆戾焉。而又左右之臣，皆以正君為急，繩愆糾繆，非徒美之是將也；以責難為恭，明諫顯諍，非惟善之是承也。謹位之功如此，由是徵諸庶民，則神道之感通，有以妙鼓舞之術；王猷之允塞，有以神倡率之機。將見聖人有作，而物咸覩之，推之無不準也；大君有命，而民皆宜之，動之無不化也。其心悅誠服，殆有預待乎未事之先者矣。由是質諸上帝，則冲漠無朕之理，自我信之；光明下濟之神，自我凝之。將見有道之君，足當天心之眷，有以介景福于無疆；無虞之世，自獲佑命之隆，有以錫純嘏于不替。其篤厚不忘，殆非有出于圖度之私者矣。夫下而得民，則帝位出于民
translation_en:
…the heart is the source of all transformations; if it does not attain its proper resting place, this is what makes it precarious. One must ward off evil to preserve sincerity, conforming to the rectitude of the moral mind; one must make reverence one's guiding principle to straighten the inner self, truly according with the purity of Heaven's virtue. What one preserves in the heart must be free of wickedness. Affairs are the workings of this single heart; failure to scrutinize affairs is what makes one's actions reckless. One must attend to the first stirrings, examining their emergence and strictly distinguishing principle from desire; one must attend to one's ease, examining one's repose and remaining deeply concerned about the threshold of remorse and regret. What appears in one's conduct must be free of error and perversity. Moreover, the ministers at the ruler's side must all regard correcting him as urgent. By restraining his faults and correcting his errors, they do more than merely advance his merits. They regard demanding difficult achievements of him as true respect; by openly remonstrating and forthrightly disputing, they do more than merely support his good actions.

Such is the work of attending carefully to the throne. If its effects are then tested among the common people, the sympathetic response elicited through the numinous Way makes the art of inspiring them wondrously effective; the full realization of kingly principles gives numinous efficacy to the workings of leadership. Then one will see that when the sage acts, all beings look to him: wherever his example is extended, none fails to take it as a standard. When the great ruler issues commands, the people all find them fitting: wherever he moves them, none fails to be transformed. Their heartfelt delight and sincere submission seem almost to anticipate events before they occur.

If this is then verified before the Lord on High, the principle that is silent, formless, and without trace finds its realization through me; the numinous power that shines brightly and descends to aid the world is consolidated through me. Then one will see that a ruler possessing the Way fully merits Heaven's favor and thereby receives great blessings without limit. An age free from troubles naturally obtains abundant heavenly protection and thereby receives lasting, ample blessings. Such steadfast favor, never forgotten, surely does not arise from self-interested calculation. For, below, when one wins the people, the imperial throne derives from the people's…

translation_en:
…beloved and esteemed in their hearts becomes still more secure; by gaining Heaven’s favor above, the imperial throne, cherished and protected by Heaven’s heart, becomes still more firmly established. In essence, all this results from cultivating both the inner self and outward conduct. Can the emperor fail to attend to the work of exercising care in his position? Consider further: Shun occupied the throne as a great sage—what an age that of Youyu was! Yet Yu still earnestly admonished him to exercise care in his position, invoking Heaven’s mandate and the people’s hearts as confirmation. The minister did not forget to offer loyal counsel merely because order had already been achieved; the ruler did not grow remiss in accepting good counsel merely because he was already a sage. High and low were diligent and solicitous, ruler and minister trusted one another: was this not why their harmonious, flourishing government of supreme concord stood unrivaled through the ages?

“All affairs of government are harmonious; the myriad states are at peace.”
Zhou Rudou

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Chief Supervising Secretary: “He speaks well of harmonious government and a peaceful people. Reading this feels like personally encountering the flourishing age of Tang and Yu.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Chao, Examining Editor: “Classical and weighty, without superficiality; it can serve as a model.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Pan, Compiler: “Lucid, polished, and classically elegant; it should be recorded as a model.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting: “Concise in expression and refined in meaning: an outstanding composition.”
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Academician: “His depiction of the flourishing government and transforming influence of Tang and Yu is nearly exhaustive.”
Comment by Examiner Sun, Academician: “Even and fluent, clear and pertinent.”

The worthy king cites the flourishing government and transforming influence of the age of sages to demonstrate the excellence of establishing offices. Establishing offices is the means of pursuing good government. When, in an age of sages, government is harmonious and the people are at peace, governance and transforming influence reach their utmost…

text:

總於內矣州牧侯伯總於外矣則體統之不紊
治効不因之而可見乎是故推行于天下有庶

則德業成于明良之會而事功奮于俊乂之登
以庶績則咸熈而之綱之紀當其可而不乖也

translation_en:
…height. Had offices not been established and staffed with the right men, how could this have been achieved? In instructing his officials, King Cheng began by citing this example. His meaning was surely this: when offices were established under Tang and Yu, the Director of the Hundred Affairs and the Chiefs of the Four Mountains exercised overall direction at court, while regional governors and the leaders of the feudal lords exercised overall direction beyond it. With the hierarchy thus free from disorder, would not the efficacy of government consequently become apparent?

Thus, there are the many affairs of government to be carried out throughout the realm. If the deployment of officials loses its proper order, government becomes confused. It is precisely because the establishment of offices follows essential principles that virtuous achievements are realized through the meeting of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers, and practical accomplishments flourish through the advancement of outstanding talent. As for the various undertakings, all prosper: their ordering and regulation [?] are appropriate and admit no deviation. As for the nine achievements, all are duly ordered: they have their proper relationships and governing principles, following their appointed courses without confusion. Since offices are established to meet the needs of government, government is brought into order through officials. Matters great and small are all attended to: could there ever be a single affair left unmanaged?

There are also the myriad states arrayed throughout the realm. If officials fail in the duties of their offices, the people suffer hardship. It is precisely because the establishment of offices follows essential principles that government is extended through the diligent assistance of the many enlightened men, and its beneficence reaches everywhere through the united efforts of the assembled lords. Speaking of the common people, they are transformed: moral principles become unified and customs become shared. Speaking of the four quarters, they respond as though moved by the wind: the people’s livelihood and nurture are secured, and ethical relationships are made clear. Since offices are established for the people, the people gain peace through officials. Far and near, all broadly follow the model: could there ever be a single person who failed to find his proper place?

Thus, by observing the flourishing of government and moral transformation, one can see the effectiveness of establishing offices in the age of the sages; and from that effectiveness one can verify the excellence of the institutions established in that age. By citing this example to instruct his officials, King Cheng may indeed be said to have understood profoundly the essential structure of good government! In general, the institutions of emperors and kings are reduced or augmented according to the times, and…

…what matters is their appropriateness. Thus, in the same undertaking of establishing offices, under Tang and Yu there could be only a hundred, while under Xia and Shang there could be twice that number: the circumstances of their times differed. Yet their results were neither greater under Tang and Yu nor less under Xia and Shang, because the Way by which they achieved good government was the same. title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
由德以成也公子之德之善斯其為治之瑞矣
乎詩人之意若曰觀化者莫先於家而稽瑞者
莫大於德吾嘗近觀公子而遠取於物矣今夫
物莫不有趾也而麟之趾則獨異焉其動也順
無胥戕也其履也和不相害也是豈其趾之獨
仁哉性成于天夫固良能之著耳夫人莫不有
子也而公之子則振振焉寛裕温柔而宅心也
仁示人以可樂也子諒易直而居德也厚示人
以可親也抑豈公子之獨異哉性安于習夫固
===
家庭之化耳吁嗟公子之德如是而謂其瑞之
非麟可乎盖言乎其位之所在則本支雖殊皆
行有家國之寄而言乎其德之所在則繼承有
賴已具夫平治之資麟固足以徵乎治而以公
子之仁達之則奕世之人心可結也國之興固
不必外求之麟矣瑞固有以稽于麟而由公子
之厚言之則異時之國脉可培也麟之瑞已不
必遠求之郊矣是盖天地有至粹而麟得之以
為瑞者德也聖人有至教而公子化之以合瑞

非麟可乎盖言乎其位之所在則本支雖殊皆
行有家國之寄而言乎其德之所在則繼承有
賴已具夫平治之資麟固足以徵乎治而以公
子之仁達之則奕世之人心可結也國之興固
不必外求之麟矣瑞固有以稽于麟而由公子
之厚言之則異時之國脉可培也麟之瑞已不
必遠求之郊矣是盖天地有至粹而麟得之以
爲瑞者德也聖人有至教而公子化之以合瑞
punctuated: 由德以成也。公子之德之善，斯其為治之瑞矣乎！詩人之意若曰：「觀化者莫先於家，而稽瑞者莫大於德。吾嘗近觀公子，而遠取於物矣。今夫物莫不有趾也，而麟之趾則獨異焉。其動也順，無胥戕也；其履也和，不相害也。是豈其趾之獨仁哉？性成于天，夫固良能之著耳。夫人莫不有子也，而公之子則振振焉。寛裕温柔，而宅心也仁，示人以可樂也；子諒易直，而居德也厚，示人以可親也。抑豈公子之獨異哉？性安于習，夫固家庭之化耳。吁嗟！公子之德如是，而謂其瑞之非麟可乎？盖言乎其位之所在，則本支雖殊，皆行有家國之寄；而言乎其德之所在，則繼承有賴，已具夫平治之資。麟固足以徵乎治，而以公子之仁達之，則奕世之人心可結也，國之興固不必外求之麟矣。瑞固有以稽于麟，而由公子之厚言之，則異時之國脉可培也，麟之瑞已不必遠求之郊矣。是盖天地有至粹，而麟得之以為瑞者，德也；聖人有至教，而公子化之以合瑞
translation_en:
…is achieved through virtue. Surely the goodness of the lord’s sons’ virtue is therefore an auspicious sign of good government! The poet’s meaning seems to be: “For one who observes moral transformation, nothing takes precedence over the family; for one who examines auspicious signs, nothing is greater than virtue. I have looked close at hand at the lord’s sons and drawn a comparison from creatures farther afield. Now all creatures have feet, yet the feet of the qilin are uniquely different. Its movements are gentle, without mutual injury; its tread is harmonious, doing no harm to others. Can it be that only its feet are benevolent? Its nature is formed by Heaven: this is simply the manifestation of its innate capacity for goodness. People all have sons, yet the lord’s sons are exceptionally noble. Broad-minded, generous, warm, and gentle, they are benevolent at heart and show themselves worthy of delight. Kind [?], trustworthy, amiable, and upright, they are substantial in virtue and show themselves worthy of affection. Yet can it be that the lord’s sons alone are inherently different? Their nature has become settled through habituation: this is simply the transforming influence of the household.

“Ah! Since the virtue of the lord’s sons is like this, can one say that their auspiciousness is unlike that of the qilin? Speaking of their positions, although the main line and collateral branches differ, all will bear responsibilities for the ruling house and the state. Speaking of their virtue, the succession has something to rely upon: they already possess the resources for peace and good government. The qilin certainly suffices to attest to good government; yet if the benevolence of the lord’s sons is extended, the people’s hearts can be bound to the dynasty for generations. The state’s flourishing certainly need not seek an external sign in the qilin. Auspiciousness can indeed be verified in the qilin; yet, considered in terms of the substantial virtue of the lord’s sons, the state’s future vitality can be nurtured. The auspiciousness represented by the qilin need no longer be sought far away in the countryside. Thus Heaven and Earth possess an utmost purity, and what the qilin receives from it to become an auspicious sign is virtue. The sage possesses an utmost teaching, and the lord’s sons are transformed by it so as to match the auspiciousness…

translation_en:
…with the qilin in its auspiciousness is likewise virtue. Why, then, be constrained by distinctions of kind? In general, moral transformation begins in the family, but its completion extends throughout all under Heaven. That the virtue of King Wen and his consort reached their sons certainly reveals the beginning of kingly transformation. When princely sons are as auspicious as the qilin, is this not sufficient evidence that the kingly Way has been perfected? The commentators’ assertion that this answers the poem “The Ospreys Cry” (Guan ju) is indeed true. Among his offspring, one continued his undertaking like King Wu, another perfected virtue like Dan; and as protective bulwarks there were Cheng, Huo, Lu, Wei, Gao, Yong, Cao, and Teng. They ultimately brought about the ordered rule celebrated in “Wild Ducks and Gulls” (Fu yi), and prolonged the dynasty’s blessed tenure beyond its allotted span. Does this not substantiate what the poet called the qilin? Thus, whoever longs for the ordered rule of “Wild Ducks and Gulls” should seek it in “The Qilin’s Hooves” (Lin zhi); whoever longs for the auspiciousness of “The Qilin’s Hooves” should begin with “The Ospreys Cry.”

“Heaven protects and establishes you, granting you complete prosperity. All accords with what is fitting; you receive Heaven’s hundred blessings. It sends down lasting blessings upon you, as though each day afforded insufficient time.”

Ye Yinglin 葉應麟

text:

考試官學士張批愛君之意溢於言表

人臣祝君受天福之備而又申錫之也甚矣周
人之愛君也祝以受福之備而尤欲自天申之
焉意何至哉天保臣子答君之意若曰惟辟奉
天惟天眷德天之保定我君豈惟單厚多益巳
哉吾知仁愛之意昭於降監之中而敷錫之仁
示諸行事之際思若啓而行若翼咸熙乎庶績
===
有以建維皇之極而事必盡善焉體之信則達
之順克諧乎百度有以協人心之義而動無弗
宜焉是固昭格之素有以克享乎天心而百福
之遒用以靈承乎帝眷矣然天之於君不但巳
也眷命方隆恒寵綏於不巳而天休滋至自申
錫於無疆富有也而復日新焉凡其錫之以善
而成昌明之祚者日惟見其福之有餘矣豈曰
獨盛於今耶可大也而復可久焉凡其協之於
宜以成熈皞之治者人惟見其日之不足矣豈

A minister prays that his ruler may receive Heaven’s blessings in their fullness, and that Heaven may bestow them yet again. How profound was the people of Zhou’s love for their ruler! They prayed that he might receive blessings in their fullness, and especially wished Heaven to renew them. How utterly devoted their feelings were! “Heaven Protects” (Tian bao) expresses the subjects’ response to their ruler, as though saying: The sovereign serves Heaven; Heaven cherishes virtue. In protecting and securing our ruler, does Heaven merely make him abundantly prosperous and increase his benefits? I know that its loving concern is manifest as it looks down upon him, and that its benevolent generosity appears in the conduct of his affairs. His thoughts seem guided, his actions aided; all his undertakings flourish. Thus he can establish the sovereign’s ultimate standard, and every affair attains perfect goodness. What he embodies in sincerity he expresses in accordance with the proper order; all the institutions of government are harmonized. Thus he accords with the sense of right in human hearts, and every action is fitting. This is assuredly because his enduring capacity to reach Heaven has won Heaven’s favor; the gathering of every blessing enables him auspiciously to receive the regard of the Lord on High.

Yet Heaven’s dealings with the ruler do not stop there. Its favoring mandate is flourishing, and it continually cherishes and secures him without cease. Heavenly blessings arrive in ever greater abundance, renewed without limit. Already rich in possession, he is renewed each day. Through all the good bestowed upon him to establish a flourishing and illustrious reign, each day reveals only a further abundance of blessings. How could one say that this flourishing belongs to the present alone? Capable of greatness, it is also capable of enduring. Through all that brings him into accord with what is fitting and establishes a radiant and harmonious government, people feel only that the days are insufficient. How could …

曰不繼於後耶？是則既善其始，而人之所以受於天者備矣；復厚其終，而天之所以降於人者久矣。保定之意，斯其至乎！抑「昭受上帝，天其申命用休」，禹之謨，盖幾康弼直之應也，而詩人以托之天，何也？盖戩穀罄宜，臣子陳善之敬，而詞曰「天保」，亦欲其緣天而求之人耳。不然，則棄其在我，慮非善，動斯何以宜？而一善自挾，非吉人惟日不足之心，則亦何以祈天而永命乎？故吾於此知德福之相須，而又知古人之善頌禱類如此。

translation_en:
…say that it will not continue into the future? Thus, with the beginning already made good, all that people receive from Heaven is complete; with the outcome further enriched, what Heaven bestows upon people endures. Surely this brings the meaning of protection and stability to its fullest expression! Moreover, “Receive with distinction the favor of the Lord on High, and Heaven will renew its mandate with blessings”: these words in Yu’s counsels surely describe the response to bringing affairs to peace and assisting with uprightness [?]. Why, then, does the poet attribute this to Heaven? Long life, blessings, and fitting conduct in all things are the good that ministers and sons reverently set before their superiors. Yet the poem says, “Heaven protects”: it, too, wishes people to proceed from Heaven and seek the cause in human conduct. Otherwise, if one abandons what lies within oneself and one’s deliberations are not good, how can one’s actions be fitting? And if one prides oneself on a single good deed, lacking the good person’s sense that each day affords insufficient time, how can one pray to Heaven and perpetuate the mandate? Thus, from this I understand the mutual dependence of virtue and blessings, and also understand that the ancients’ skill in praise and prayer generally took this form.

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
春秋善覇者節兵恤患而安攘之事見矣此齊
桓救鄭制楚之始春秋予之幸中國之有覇也
自昔子元謀先於窺鄭假意於襲讎而鄭自此
受伐使桓非主覇則楚孰與却鄭將焉依幸而
齊桓始覇志圖安攘思楚之當制也而門庭之
寇是禦懷鄭之始附也而簡書之義是勤師非
厚集不恃衆以為武而折楚勢以先聲義存拯
溺首同盟以從事而紓鄭患於已困使純門之
師夜遁而楚幕已遷桐丘之奔得免而鄭懸以
===
解則所以消楚人之雄視以遺鄭人之安者桓
其有功哉噫内政作而軍制明桓之所以經營
於國者凡以制楚也此其見之行事乎他日陘
亭召陵之役繼此而為之者也兩鄄會而人心
屬列國之所以推戴齊桓者恃以安靖也此其
驗諸覇事乎他日兵車衣裳之會由此而為之
者也不然則外無以攘内無以安而何取於宗
齊哉故書救鄭者善之也其稱人者將卑師少
也先齊於宋者以主兵也而桓公攘夷狄安中

齊桓始霸志圖安攘思楚之當制也而門庭之
寇是禦懷鄭之始附也而簡書之義是勤師非
厚集不恃衆以為武而折楚勢以先聲義存拯
溺首同盟以從事而紓鄭患於已困使純門之
師夜遁而楚幕已遷桐丘之奔得免而鄭懸以
===
解則所以消楚人之雄視以遺鄭人之安者桓
其有功哉噫内政作而軍制明桓之所以經營
於國者凡以制楚也此其見之行事乎他日陘
亭召陵之役繼此而為之者也兩鄄會而人心
屬列國之所以推戴齊桓者恃以安靖也此其
驗諸霸事乎他日兵車衣裳之會由此而為之
者也不然則外無以攘内無以安而何取於宗
齊哉故書救鄭者善之也其稱人者將卑師少
也先齊於宋者以主兵也而桓公攘夷狄安中
punctuated: 春秋善覇者節兵恤患，而安攘之事見矣。此齊桓救鄭制楚之始，春秋予之，幸中國之有覇也。自昔子元謀先於窺鄭，假意於襲讎，而鄭自此受伐。使桓非主覇，則楚孰與却？鄭將焉依？幸而齊桓始覇，志圖安攘，思楚之當制也，而門庭之寇是禦；懷鄭之始附也，而簡書之義是勤。師非厚集，不恃衆以為武，而折楚勢以先聲；義存拯溺，首同盟以從事，而紓鄭患於已困。使純門之師夜遁，而楚幕已遷；桐丘之奔得免，而鄭懸以解。則所以消楚人之雄視，以遺鄭人之安者，桓其有功哉！噫！内政作而軍制明，桓之所以經營於國者，凡以制楚也。此其見之行事乎？他日陘亭、召陵之役，繼此而為之者也。兩鄄會而人心屬，列國之所以推戴齊桓者，恃以安靖也。此其驗諸覇事乎？他日兵車衣裳之會，由此而為之者也。不然，則外無以攘，内無以安，而何取於宗齊哉？故書救鄭者，善之也。其稱人者，將卑師少也。先齊於宋者，以主兵也。而桓公攘夷狄安中
translation_en:
The Spring and Autumn Annals commends the hegemon for restraining his use of troops and relieving distress; his work of securing the central states and repelling external threats is thus made manifest. This was the beginning of Duke Huan of Qi’s efforts to rescue Zheng and check Chu. The Spring and Autumn Annals approves of him, deeming it fortunate that the central states had a hegemon.

Previously, Ziyuan’s designs had first turned toward an attack on Zheng, under the pretext of striking an enemy, and Zheng consequently suffered invasion. Had Duke Huan not assumed the hegemony, who would have repelled Chu? On whom could Zheng have relied? Fortunately, Duke Huan of Qi had begun his hegemony, intent on securing the central states and repelling external threats. Recognizing that Chu must be checked, he resisted the invaders at Zheng’s very gates; mindful of Zheng’s recent adherence, he diligently fulfilled the obligation to provide aid conveyed in written appeals. He did not assemble a massive army or rely on numbers for military might, but blunted Chu’s power by the advance report of his coming. Intent on rescuing those in peril, he led his allies into action and relieved Zheng’s distress when it was already hard pressed. He caused the army at Chunmen to flee by night, with Chu’s tents already removed; flight to Tongqiu was averted, and Zheng was released from its desperate plight. In curbing the men of Chu’s overbearing ambitions and bringing peace to the people of Zheng, did Duke Huan not render meritorious service?

Ah! Domestic administration was established and military organization made clear: all that Duke Huan organized within his state was directed toward checking Chu. Was this not its manifestation in action? The later campaigns at Xingting and Shaoling continued what began here. With the two meetings at Juan, men’s hearts turned toward him. The various states acclaimed Duke Huan of Qi because they relied on him for peace and security. Was this not borne out in his deeds as hegemon? The later assemblies of war chariots and of rulers in ceremonial robes proceeded from this beginning. Otherwise, if he could neither repel threats from without nor secure peace within, what merit would there have been in acknowledging Qi’s leadership?

Thus, recording “rescued Zheng” expresses approval. Calling the participants “men” indicates that their commanders were of low rank and their forces small. Placing Qi before Song indicates that Qi led the military operation. And Duke Huan repelled the Yi and Di and brought peace to the central…

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
之大故也聖人能不為世道慮乎且邢丘之會
晉悼修文襄之業改命朝聘之數使諸侯之大
夫聽命焉孰不曰儉而有禮衆之所安也豈知
君臣之分等於冠屨而政柄不可一日下移也
況伯命維新又列國所由以一觀聽者乃曰重
煩諸侯而使大夫是使列國之君不自為政而
國之利器舉以示人矣則凡居然在會者得自
列於五等之尊而積微以著又安知有君耶後
此溴梁之會諸侯皆在而大夫獨盟禮樂征伐
===
不自諸侯而政自大夫出矣謂非此會為之作
俑乎故大夫稱人貶之也宋之盟向戌倡弭兵
之說子木起凌駕之謀使晉楚之從交見焉孰
不曰務德無爭盟之善者也豈知華夷之辨嚴
於否泰而大防不可一日决也況楚氛益熾又
中國所視以為向背者乃曰狎主夏盟而與同
好是使蠻夷之君爭長先歃而國之冠裳儕於
異類矣則凡俛焉從事者皆知有兩大之勢而
末流一逞又安知有伯耶後此于申之會大合

之大故也。聖人能不為世道慮乎？且邢丘之會，晉悼修文襄之業，改命朝聘之數，使諸侯之大夫聽命焉。孰不曰儉而有禮，衆之所安也？豈知君臣之分等於冠屨，而政柄不可一日下移也？況伯命維新，又列國所由以一觀聽者，乃曰重煩諸侯而使大夫，是使列國之君不自為政，而國之利器舉以示人矣。則凡居然在會者，得自列於五等之尊，而積微以著，又安知有君耶？後此溴梁之會，諸侯皆在，而大夫獨盟，禮樂征伐不自諸侯，而政自大夫出矣。謂非此會為之作俑乎？故大夫稱人，貶之也。
宋之盟，向戌倡弭兵之說，子木起凌駕之謀，使晉楚之從交見焉。孰不曰務德無爭，盟之善者也？豈知華夷之辨嚴於否泰，而大防不可一日决也？況楚氛益熾，又中國所視以為向背者，乃曰狎主夏盟而與同好，是使蠻夷之君爭長先歃，而國之冠裳儕於異類矣。則凡俛焉從事者，皆知有兩大之勢，而末流一逞，又安知有伯耶？後此于申之會，大合
translation_en:
…a grave matter indeed. Could the Sage fail to be concerned for the course of the world? At the meeting at Xingqiu, Duke Dao of Jin renewed the enterprise of Dukes Wen and Xiang, revised the prescribed frequency of court audiences and diplomatic visits, and had the grandees of the feudal lords receive his commands. Who would not have said that this was economical yet ritually proper, and agreeable to all? Yet how could they understand that the distinction between ruler and minister is like that between cap and shoes, and that the reins of government must not pass downward even for a single day? Moreover, the hegemon’s commands were newly promulgated, and this was an occasion through which the various states would attain unity in what they saw and heard. Yet he said that it would be too burdensome to trouble the feudal lords, and summoned their grandees instead. This caused the rulers of the various states to cease conducting their own government and exposed the potent instruments of state to others. Thus all those grandees comfortably seated at the meeting could rank themselves with the honored holders of the five grades of nobility. As small encroachments accumulated into manifest usurpation, how would they any longer acknowledge their rulers? At the subsequent meeting at Jiuliang, the feudal lords were all present, yet the grandees alone entered into the covenant. Ritual, music, and punitive expeditions no longer proceeded from the feudal lords: government issued from the grandees. Can one say that this meeting did not set the pernicious precedent? Thus the grandees are designated merely as “men”: this expresses censure.
At the covenant of Song, Xiang Xu advocated putting an end to warfare, while Zimu devised a scheme to gain ascendancy, having the states that followed Jin and Chu pay visits to both powers. Who would not have said that this was the pursuit of virtue without contention, an excellent covenant? Yet how could they understand that the distinction between the Chinese and the barbarians is as strict as that between Obstruction and Peace, and that this great barrier must not be breached even for a single day? Moreover, Chu’s threatening influence was growing ever stronger, and this was a matter on which the states of the Central Plain looked in deciding their allegiance. Yet they spoke of taking turns presiding over the covenants of the Chinese states and sharing friendly relations with Chu. This allowed a barbarian ruler to contend for precedence in being first to smear his lips with the sacrificial blood, and placed the capped and robed dignitaries of the states on a level with those of an alien kind. Thus all who bowed to these arrangements recognized only the power of the two great states. Once the resulting tendencies were given free rein, how would they any longer acknowledge a hegemon? At the subsequent meeting at Shen, a great assembly was convened …

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
諸侯而列卿獻禮伐吳滅賴雄長天下而霸不
自中國出矣謂非此盟為之濫觴乎故再言宋
者貶之也噫一會盟之間而君臣強弱夷夏盛
衰之機關焉聖人修經至是不得不重傷之也
抑悼之伯也魏絳智罃實助之故三駕之功成
於制楚邢丘之會政行姑息豈其疎於撫內耶
平之業不及悼公而趙武諸人偷見目前以幸
苟安遂使夷狄主盟而晉自是不能宗諸侯矣
故曰宋之盟趙武之偷也
===
禮記
天子以德為車以樂為御諸侯以禮相與
大夫以法相序士以信相考百姓以睦相
守天下之肥也
胡𤇍
同考試官主事吳　批　題旨正大而文之純樸
簡盡亦畧相當是宜以錄
同考試官檢討陳　批　渾厚爾雅得天下肥氣象
考試官學士張　批　詞贍而美亦文之肥者

punctuated:
諸侯，而列卿獻禮，伐吳滅賴，雄長天下，而霸不自中國出矣。謂非此盟為之濫觴乎？故再言宋者，貶之也。噫！一會盟之間，而君臣強弱、夷夏盛衰之機關焉。聖人修經，至是不得不重傷之也。抑悼之伯也，魏絳、智罃實助之，故三駕之功成於制楚。邢丘之會，政行姑息，豈其疎於撫內耶？平之業不及悼公，而趙武諸人偷見目前，以幸苟安，遂使夷狄主盟，而晉自是不能宗諸侯矣。故曰：「宋之盟，趙武之偷也。」

禮記
天子以德為車，以樂為御；諸侯以禮相與，大夫以法相序，士以信相考，百姓以睦相守，天下之肥也。

胡𤇍

同考試官主事吳，批：「題旨正大，而文之純樸簡盡亦畧相當，是宜以錄。」
同考試官檢討陳，批：「渾厚爾雅，得天下肥氣象。」
考試官學士張，批：「詞贍而美，亦文之肥者。」
translation_en:
…the feudal lords, while their ranking ministers presented ceremonial offerings. Chu attacked Wu and destroyed Lai, asserting supremacy over all under Heaven; hegemony no longer arose from the Central States. Can one say that this covenant was not the source of it all? Thus, mentioning Song a second time expresses censure. Alas! Within a single meeting and covenant lay the pivotal forces determining the strength or weakness of rulers and ministers and the flourishing or decline of the foreign peoples and the Chinese states. When the Sage edited the Classic, he could not but grieve deeply at this point.

Yet when Duke Dao exercised hegemony, Wei Jiang and Zhi Ying truly assisted him. Thus the achievement of the three campaigns lay in restraining Chu. At the meeting at Xingqiu, his government practiced indulgence: could he have been neglectful of nurturing those within his own domain? Duke Ping’s accomplishments fell short of Duke Dao’s, while Zhao Wu and the others shortsightedly considered only the immediate situation, hoping for a precarious peace. Consequently, they allowed the foreign peoples to preside over the covenants, and from then on Jin could no longer lead the feudal lords. Hence the saying: “The covenant at Song was the result of Zhao Wu’s negligence.”

Record of Rites (Liji)
“When the Son of Heaven takes virtue as his carriage and music as his charioteer; when the feudal lords deal with one another through ritual propriety, the grandees order their relations through established rules, the servicemen assess one another through trustworthiness, and the common people sustain one another through harmony—this is the flourishing of all under Heaven.”

Hu [?] (胡𤇍; the reading of the given name is uncertain).

Associate Examiner Wu, Secretary, comments: “The import of the topic is upright and grand, and the essay’s simplicity, sincerity, concision, and completeness are broadly commensurate with it. It therefore deserves inclusion in the record.”

Associate Examiner Chen, Examining Editor, comments: “Substantial, rich, and refined: it captures the atmosphere of ‘the flourishing of all under Heaven.’”

Examiner Zhang, Academician, comments: “Its language is abundant and beautiful; this too is an example of flourishing in literary composition.”

title: 嘉靖二十六年會試錄
text:
禮樂通乎造化則精粗之體備矣而人道因以
統於是其用顧不大哉今夫窮本知變著誠去
偽固知禮樂之可以治情也而不知其體之所
由來者大矣彼天地之情貞觀而不忒禮樂則
以順焉象其質而具故有秩也象其氣而作故
不乖也效法有定而動靜之道形矣神明之德
微妙而難求禮樂為能達焉主於辨者通乎其
散殊也主於和者通乎其合同也機緘相孚而
仁義之理著矣夫其氣之屈而具於地神之下
===
也惟禮順而達之以居乎鬼若有作之而使興
者氣之伸而行於天神之上也惟樂順而達之
以率乎神若有抑之而使降者則禮樂不專於
器也而包含者已運乎天地之精天地不秘其
道也而流行者皆寓於象數之末其凝是精粗
之體乎夫是以禮樂舉其全而統同辨異之用
以行故倫理通其大而至親至嚴之節不過領
乎父子焉愛不至於流而以天屬者固由之以
聯其恩也領乎君臣焉敬不至於離而以人合
